papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.
authors: Sezgin Er, Utku Turkbey, Alperen Gur, Omer Faruk Durugol, Suprosanna Shit, Murong Xu, Julia Wolleb, Jiayi Wang, Xiaoliang Wang, Hadrien Reynaud, Teodora Spasojevic, Dong Yang, Andriy Myronenko, Pengfei Guo, Yufan He, Can Zhao, Marc Edgar, Andreas Maier, Michael Moor, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Daguang Xu, Bernhard Kainz, Bjoern Menze, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
bullets: Addresses the limited anatomical and abnormality coverage of existing CT AI systems.
Recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts across 28 CT protocols.
Uses multiple-instance learning and an interpretable concept bottleneck linking spatial evidence, findings, and report generation.
Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations without manually annotated lesions.
Achieved strong concept recognition, localization, benchmark, and report-generation performance on held-out and independent evaluations.

papers.title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
papers.tldr: FORA is a general-purpose CT model that recognizes, localizes, and reports a broad range of radiological findings across multiple examination types using only routine report supervision.

papers.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
authors: Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Existing results are difficult to compare because papers use different sampling, resolutions, test splits, and alignment procedures.
The arena evaluates five tasks—including monocular depth, 3D/4D reconstruction, and SLAM—on 23 public datasets plus new captures spanning indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes.
Its deterministic alignment and common metrics address evaluation failures that can substantially distort reported errors.
Across 52 models, single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but remains challenging in large, uncontrolled scenes.
Progress increasingly depends on cross-frame and cross-view consistency: feed-forward 3D/4D models match or exceed monocular specialists and outperform video depth models.

Our estimator, R-GTSAM followed by the robust refit, stays exact under outliers and jumps, is unaffected by orientation noise, and matches evo under position noise.

papers.title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?
papers.tldr: SpatialArena provides a standardized, robust benchmark for comparing geometric foundation models across diverse 3D perception tasks and scenes.

papers.abstract: Segmenting a 3D object into semantically meaningful parts requires joint reasoning about geometric structure and semantic context. Pretrained 3D experts provide spatially grounded region proposals, while 2D experts provide semantic cues for identifying object parts. The challenge is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a framework that can both produce meaningful part segmentations and progressively refine them. We present PartAgent, a training-free agentic framework for 3D part segmentation built upon two complementary modules: (i) Structural-Semantic Expert Integration combines regions predicted by the 3D expert with multiview semantic evidence from the 2D expert through image-to-surface correspondences, constructing compositional part partitions at multiple granularities. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 across the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods.
authors: Yang Cao, Zhe Zhu, Yiheng Zhang, Zhengqiang Zhang, Haoyuan Li, Le Wan, Dan Xu
bullets: Combines spatially grounded 3D region proposals with semantic cues from 2D experts via image-to-surface correspondences.
Builds compositional part partitions at multiple granularities through Structural-Semantic Expert Integration.
Uses observation-driven actions—including inspection, evidence repair, composition, and reselection—to refine and verify segmentations.
Achieves 68.41 mIoU on PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT and the highest mIoU across four evaluated datasets, averaging 69.36.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PartAgent. (A) Structural–Semantic Expert Integration (SSEI) uses multiview semantic evidence to refine 3D expert regions and combine them into candidate segmentations at multiple granularities, then selects an initial segmentation P0. (B) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement (CLR) uses a VLM to examine the current segmentation and its supporting evidence and choose targeted actions. Proposed segmentation updates are verified before adoption, and feedback guides subsequent actions.

Figure 2. From a 3D expert to an agentic framework. (a) A 3D expert directly segments the object into parts. (b) PartAgent integrates predictions from frozen 2D and 3D experts and iteratively refines the segmentation through an observation-driven loop.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison. Comparison with SAMPart3D [46], PartField [22], P3-SAM [23], and PartSAM [50]. On the Hunyuan3D fish, PartAgent keeps the dorsal and tail fins as one part each. On the well, PartAgent separates the roof fittings and segments the roof surface and stone wall as one part each. On the chest, PartAgent separates the lid from the body and keeps the handle and latch distinct.

Figure 4. Observation-driven closed-loop refinement. Left: The agent inspects the rear wheel and identifies incorrect part groupings. Middle: It regroups existing 3D regions to separate the fender from the tire and merge the two regions belonging to the same wheel. Right: After the proposal passes multiview verification, the updated state and feedback guide inspection of the exhaust.

Figure 5. Progressive improvement through closed-loop refinement. Loop 0 denotes the SSEI initialization before closed-loop refinement. Loop 1 groups the cable and its connector into one part. Loop 2 merges fragments within the enclosure and within the control panel. Loop numbers denote agent decision rounds. Insets show the same boxed regions at each loop.
Figure 7. Performance across refinement loops.

Table 1. Comparison on PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT [23]. All six methods are evaluated on the same watertight meshes. For each category, we report Mask Match mIoU averaged over its objects (%, ↑). Overall is the average across all objects. Bold marks the highest score. Parentheses show the gain over the best baseline.
Table 6. 2D expert and VLM substitutions. P3-SAM is fixed. Each variant changes only the indicated component.
Table 3. SSEI and CLR ablations. Partition and Mask denote Partition Match mIoU and Mask Match mIoU, respectively (%, ↑).

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agentic framework for 3D part segmentation that integrates 3D and 2D experts, relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial understanding for embodied agents.
papers.title: PartAgent: Agentic 3D Part Segmentation via Expert Integration and Closed-Loop Refinement
papers.tldr: PartAgent is a training-free 3D part-segmentation framework that integrates 3D geometry with multiview 2D semantics and iteratively refines partitions through closed-loop agentic actions.

papers.abstract: Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-$\Omega$, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.
bullets: Separates scene layout prediction from asset generation, addressing a key limitation of existing 3D scene composition methods.
Takes one or more scene images, object masks, and one asset per object from any source.
Jointly predicts every object’s rotation, translation, and per-axis scale in a single forward pass of about one second.
Processes asset renders and scene images together with a multi-view geometry model, deriving poses in closed form from predicted cameras.
Improves fixed-asset scene layouts over native layouts from five scene-generation methods; reduces scene-level Chamfer distance versus SceneMaker by 52% on IndoorMix and 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

papers.selection_reason: Feed-forward 3D scene layout composition from arbitrary assets and views; directly relevant to 3D vision and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition with Any Assets from Any Views
papers.tldr: X-3DComposer rapidly predicts editable 3D object layouts from images and arbitrary assets without requiring depth, true-scale CAD models, or iterative refinement.

papers.abstract: Multi-view feed-forward models show strong scalability, but their reliance on costly geometric annotations limits data scaling. Existing 3D self-supervised approaches reduce this reliance through cross-view completion (e.g., CroCo, MuM, Muskie) or novel-view synthesis (e.g., RayZer, E-RayZer), typically learning image representations and cross-view interactions jointly. We argue that learning single image representations from scratch is unnecessary for 3D pretraining methods, as doing so fails to benefit from the continuing advances in 2D foundation models (e.g., DINO, CLIP, frontier VLMs). We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$\Omega$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.
authors: Zichen Zou, Xiaosong Jia, Wen-Ming Chen, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang
bullets: Addresses the annotation cost that limits scaling of supervised multi-view 3D learning.
Adds a randomly initialized multi-view transformer while reusing pretrained 2D image representations.
Trains with masked self-distillation: a student predicts masked views using complete anchor views, guided by an EMA teacher.
Outperforms supervised VGGT-Ω training and several prior self-supervised methods across model sizes up to 1B parameters.
Additional unlabeled videos improve generalization, with representations transferring to diverse downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Pretrains multi-view transformers via masked self-distillation on frozen 2D encoders, advancing scalable 3D foundation models.
papers.title: MaskedVGGT: Masked Multi-View Transformers Are Scalable 3D Learners
papers.tldr: MaskedVGGT scales 3D pretraining by freezing a strong 2D encoder and learning cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data via masked self-distillation.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian splats enable real-time rendering but require substantial storage. Existing compression methods either encode the primitives of a given splat or optimize a compact representation independently for each scene. Yet a Gaussian splat is only one realization of a scene: different arrangements of primitives can produce nearly identical rendered views. We exploit this freedom on the decoding side with SplatTok, a learned scene-resynthesis codec. Trained across thousands of real-world scenes, a transformer encodes an existing splat into compact, spatially anchored latent tokens, and a shared decoder synthesizes a new set of standard Gaussian primitives without preserving correspondence to the input. The representation is learned through rendering supervision rather than primitive reconstruction. At compression time, a quantization-aware latent search refines only the scene code, keeping the networks frozen, and closes most of the encoder's remaining error. On standard benchmarks, using only renders of the input splat for the latent search, without the original training images, SplatTok matches the PSNR of the feed-forward codec FCGS with 4 to 6.5 times smaller files, compressing input splats about 75 to 110 times. With the training images, it exceeds the PSNR of the per-scene method HAC++ with 13 to 41% smaller files. A single model trained on DL3DV generalizes to unseen scenes with millions of Gaussians and supports multiple target rates without retraining.
authors: Sai Karthikey Pentapati, Shashank Nelamangala Sridhara, Birendra Kathariya, Peng Yin, Guandao Yang, Alan C. Bovik
bullets: Addresses the high storage cost of 3D Gaussian splats and the unnecessary need to preserve primitive correspondence.
Uses a transformer encoder and shared decoder trained across real-world scenes with rendering-based supervision.
Performs quantization-aware latent search at compression time while keeping the networks frozen.
Matches FCGS quality with 4–6.5× smaller files using only input-splat renders, and surpasses HAC++ quality with 13–41% smaller files when training images are available.
A single model generalizes to unseen large scenes and supports multiple target rates without retraining.

papers.selection_reason: Learned scene-level compression and resynthesis of 3D Gaussian splats; fits 3D foundation/generation.
papers.title: SplatTok: Data-Driven Compression of 3D Gaussian Splats with Scene-Level Tokens

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes from RGB video requires reasoning about both 3D geometry and motion across viewpoints, yet existing methods either split reconstruction and tracking into fragmented pipelines or face prohibitive dense spatiotemporal decoding costs. We introduce MoGe-4D, a feed-forward framework that unifies geometry and motion prediction via ordered queries of paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps. Each query maps source pixels to a target time simultaneously in both camera frames, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while flexibly serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. For efficient dense querying, MoGe-4D decouples scene modeling from query decoding: a high-capacity context encoder caches coarse global spatiotemporal features once, while a lightweight query encoder rapidly decodes dense point maps at flexible resolutions. Furthermore, as supervising dense 4D queries demands continuous 3D correspondences whose raw trajectory storage is prohibitive, we introduce RigIDTrack, a synthetic data pipeline and dataset that compresses surface dynamics into rigidity-regularized affine bodies, recovering exact arbitrary-frame 3D trajectories with $\sim15\%$ storage overhead over RGB-D video. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.
authors: Ruicheng Wang, Linlin Xin, Sicheng Xu, Jianfeng Xiang, Zelong Lv, Yu Deng, Yue Dong, Guangzhong Sun, Tong Zhang, Jiaolong Yang
bullets: Predicts paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps to jointly model geometry, motion, camera pose, depth, registration, and tracking.
Uses cached global spatiotemporal features plus a lightweight query encoder for efficient dense decoding at flexible resolutions.
Introduces RigIDTrack, a synthetic pipeline and dataset that represents surface dynamics with rigidity-regularized affine bodies and compact trajectory storage.
Reports state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, reconstruction performance matching dedicated 3D foundation models, and substantially faster inference than prior 4D baselines.

papers.abstract: LiDAR reconstruction supports closed-loop autonomous driving simulation, but hours of per-scene optimization make large asset libraries costly to build and maintain. We present Instant LiDAR, a feed-forward pipeline that reconstructs multiple LiDAR scans as reusable Gaussian assets in minutes without per-scene optimization. LiDAR measurements provide strong geometric priors, but directly initializing Gaussians from them yields poor reconstruction due to nonuniform sampling and a limited field of view. Sparse returns leave surface gaps, while combining scans expands coverage but introduces redundant primitives. To address these challenges, Instant LiDAR combines measurement-anchored Gaussian prediction, sampling-aware Gaussian scales, and multi-frame consolidation. The predictor refines attributes anchored to recorded returns, while the scales adapt spatial support to LiDAR sampling. Multi-frame consolidation merges overlapping predictions into a compact asset spanning the driving log. Compared with NuRec, Instant LiDAR reconstructs scenes approximately 46 times faster on Physical AI (PAI) and 70 times faster on Waymo. It also achieves comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.
authors: Xin Kang, Jiahui Huang, Jiawei Ren, Sipeng Zhang, Yu Chen, Weihua Zhang, Junjie Lai
bullets: Eliminates costly per-scene optimization, reducing reconstruction to minutes.
Addresses sparse, nonuniform LiDAR sampling and limited field of view.
Combines measurement-anchored Gaussian prediction, sampling-aware scales, and multi-frame consolidation.
Runs approximately 46× faster than NuRec on PAI and 70× faster on Waymo.
Maintains comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D garments for digital characters requires preserving a reference design while adapting the garment to the target body's shape and pose. Sewing-pattern methods can struggle to reproduce unfamiliar designs and fine details, while image-to-3D generators offer rich shape priors but typically lack explicit 3D body context. We present \textbf{BodyWeave}, a framework that unifies garment generation and fitting through native 3D body conditioning. Building on 3D generative priors, BodyWeave uses the body as a spatial reference throughout geometry generation: a \textbf{Global Body Adapter} guides garment placement and extent in the shared coordinate frame, while \textbf{Local Body Attention} guides surface refinement using nearby body geometry. A \textbf{Surface Penetration Loss} supervises decoded surfaces to reduce body intersections, and the resulting geometry conditions material synthesis to produce garments with physically based rendering attributes. To support learning across designs and wearers, we construct \textbf{GarmentWeave3D} with 293K aligned garment--body observations, including 114K same-design cross-body pairs. Evaluations on out-of-domain \textbf{Artist-Created Garments} demonstrate high geometric fidelity and low body penetration. Cross-body evaluations demonstrate accurate adaptation to new wearers with consistent garment--body spacing, while appearance comparisons show faithful fabric reproduction. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/bodyweave-page/

Builds GarmentWeave3D with 293K aligned garment–body observations, including 114K same-design cross-body pairs.
Reports high geometric fidelity, low penetration, accurate cross-body adaptation, and faithful fabric appearance on artist-created garments.

papers.abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) enable dense reconstruction in a feed-forward pass, yet their effective span is limited by cross-view attention. Local consistency has been expanded through geometric alignment of video chunks and recursive updates of an implicit memory, and large-scale scenes with pose graphs. However, both strategies are prone to drift, largely due to the lack of metric-scale observability from monocular geometry. We present Xtream,a hybrid streaming pipeline that maintains an explicit metric state through a factor graph over keyframes, while using a 3DFM as a geometric front end. Xtream incorporates metric information in two ways: through metric scale predictions from 3DFMs; or through inertial measurements if available. Across the large-scale benchmarks of VBR, Oxford Spires and KITTI, Xtream achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3DFM-based online reconstruction, reducing average absolute trajectory errors compared with published baselines and concurrent work. https://ernestolozano.github.io/xtream
authors: Ernesto Lozano, Alberto Jaenal, Javier Civera
bullets: Addresses drift in long-range reconstruction caused by limited cross-view attention and unobservable monocular metric scale.
Uses a 3D foundation model as a geometric front end within a streaming pipeline.
Maintains an explicit metric state over keyframes using a factor graph.
Incorporates metric scale from 3D foundation models or inertial measurements when available.
Evaluated on VBR, Oxford Spires, and KITTI, with lower average absolute trajectory errors than published baselines and concurrent work.

papers.tldr: Xtream enables drift-resistant large-scale streaming 3D reconstruction by combining a 3D foundation model with an explicit metric factor-graph state.

papers.abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.
authors: Xize Duan, Binke Hou, Xingqiao Huang, Xinyuan Guan, Jiaxin Huang, Kaiyuan Hu, Zipeng Sun, Hong Kang, Meng Bi, Xue Liu, Yili Jin
bullets: Learns compact relations between distinct physical points using cross-view 2D point prediction.

A linear readout trained on 16 scenes generalizes to 39 held-out scenes, recovering displacement length and angle (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78).
Geometry remains organized across ARKitScenes and ScanNet++, and distinct-point relational prediction outperforms matched same-point correspondence learning in controlled comparisons.
Organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context; point-transfer accuracy alone is insufficient.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D points from a set of photos in one forward pass. Many cameras store a portrait shot sideways, with an orientation tag telling viewers how to turn it, and this tag can be ignored, lost or wrong. We measure how rotated photos affect five such models on three datasets. A few rotated photos lower camera pose accuracy for every model, and the sideways photos already in a standard benchmark do the same. Even the most robust model still loses accuracy. The failure is also silent: the models' confidence does not reliably flag it, and most official image loaders ignore the tag. The fixes we test each correct only part of the problem. These findings call for orientation checks in reconstruction pipelines and benchmarks.
bullets: Evaluates five multi-view 3D foundation models across three datasets under photo-rotation errors.
Even a few rotated images reduce camera-pose accuracy for every tested model.
Sideways photos already present in a standard benchmark also harm performance.
Model confidence does not reliably reveal the failure, while common image loaders may ignore orientation tags.
Tested corrections address only part of the issue, motivating orientation checks in pipelines and benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes robustness of multi-view 3D foundation models to rotated photos.
papers.title: Which Way Is Up? Rotated Photos Silently Hurt Multi-View 3D Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Rotated photos silently degrade camera-pose accuracy in multi-view 3D foundation models, and current confidence measures and fixes do not reliably prevent the problem.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometry models such as VGGT recover camera parameters, depth maps, and point maps from one to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, making them powerful backbones for multi-view 3D perception. However, VGGT's global attention is quadratic in the number of frames and dominates end-to-end runtime on long sequences, which has motivated a range of training-free efficiency methods such as token merging. These methods, however, come with a drop in accuracy that makes them hard to use in place of VGGT. We propose GPA-VGGT, a training-free acceleration method that replaces global attention in early blocks with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set. In the remaining blocks, we merge only keys and values while preserving all queries, restore the attention mass of the tokens each merged key represents, and randomly project the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching cost. Across diverse multi-view geometry tasks, GPA-VGGT provides training-free acceleration at speedups comparable to prior work while preserving the information required for precise geometric estimation, retaining over 99% of VGGT's pose accuracy under AUC@3.
bullets: Targets VGGT’s quadratic global-attention runtime on long multi-view sequences.
Uses frame attention with shared cross-frame keys/values in early blocks.
Later merges only keys and values, preserves all queries, and restores represented-token attention mass.
Randomly projects the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching overhead.
Achieves speedups comparable to prior training-free methods across multi-view geometry tasks while preserving precise estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of GPA-VGGT. Early blocks 0–8 replace global attention with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set containing special tokens and content-adaptive pooled image-token summaries. Later blocks 9–23 preserve all queries and merge only K/V tokens, using a weaker merge ratio in the core blocks 13–16. (a) Pooled summaries are constructed by assigning patch tokens to stride-8 seeds according to cosine similarity and averaging the K/V tokens within each content-adaptive cluster; the summary size determines the + log s correction. (b) K/V matching is computed after a 128-dimensional Gaussian projection, while all queries are retained for global attention.

Figure 5. Qualitative reconstruction under estimated camera poses. Each column shows the point cloud produced by the corresponding method, and red boxes indicate the enlarged regions below. GPA-VGGT most closely matches the geometry reconstructed by vanilla VGGT.

Figure 2. Two sources of accuracy degradation in existing token-merging methods. Top: Query merging collapses the block-12 outputs of 83 tokens into 12 shared outputs, whereas retaining all queries while merging only K/V preserves the output diversity of the unmerged model. Bottom: Omitting the + log s correction disproportionately allocates attention to the first frame. Restoring the correction recovers an attention distribution close to that of the unmerged model.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime scaling with the number of input frames. Although existing acceleration methods substantially reduce end-to-end runtime, they incur pronounced camera-pose degradation under the strict AUC@3 metric. GPA-VGGT achieves comparable runtime while maintaining camera-pose accuracy close to that of vanilla VGGT.

Figure 3. Effect of cross-frame context in the early blocks. Top: Replacing global attention with frame attention substantially displaces the block-8 output field from the full-global-attention reference, whereas the shared cross-frame K/V set largely preserves it. Bottom: Pairwise alignment of per-frame drift directions. Cross-frame special tokens partially align the drift, and image-token summaries further reduce its variation, preserving a coherent geometric reference across views.

papers.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.
authors: Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common representation for 4D spatiotemporal vision.
Uses a multimodal VAE to fuse visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into one structured latent representation.
Frames perception and generation as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space.
A single model achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent generation, and controllable editing across representative benchmarks.
Positions the shared latent protocol as a foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. WorldLatent training pipeline. (a) WorldVAE training: Multiple 4D spatiotemporal modalities, including monocular RGB video, depth maps, and camera Plücker coordinates (ray direction d and moment m), are compressed via modality-specific encoders (E1– E4) and fused by a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) into a unified latent bottleneck, z4d (WorldLatent). Modality-specific decoders (D1–D4) then reconstruct the original modalities from this shared latent space. (b) Any-to-4D generative modeling: With the WorldVAE frozen, a unified diffusion model is trained within the learned latent space. It takes Gaussian noise, text prompts (Ctext), and partial or empty 4D latents c4d(S) (e.g., S = ∅ for text-to-4D generation, RGB-only for perception, or depth-only for editing) to synthesize the full 4D latent z4d. Finally, the frozen decoders (D1–D4) map z4d back into temporally coherent video, 3D geometry, and camera trajectories.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of zero-shot video depth estimation. Results are shown across the MPI Sintel, Bonn, and ScanNet datasets. For each clip, we display the input RGB frames, ground-truth depth, predictions from the teacher model (DA3-Giant) and WorldLatent-14B (Ours).

Figure 5. Any-to-4D: text-to-4D world generation with WorldLatent. Given only a text prompt, our model jointly denoises appearance, depth, and camera rays from noise, producing an RGB video together with aligned depth maps and a 3D scene with camera trajectory.

Figure 4. Any-to-4D: world editing and depth-conditioned re-rendering with WorldLatent. (1) Given an input RGB video, our model first performs 4D perception to estimate dense depth maps. (2) Conditioned on these predicted depth maps and new text prompts, the same model then performs 4D re-rendering to synthesize appearance-edited RGB videos. For each example, we show the input video, the predicted depth and camera outputs from our 4D perception stage, and the re-rendered videos across diverse text prompts.

Figure 6. Linear subspace decomposition of WorldLatent. Visualization across videos re-rendered from an identical depth sequence under different text prompts (Row 1). The 16-D appearance projection Π∥z4d (Row 2) varies markedly with visual style, whereas the orthogonal 16-D geometry-and-camera projection Π⊥z4d (Row 3) remains nearly invariant.

Panels (from left to right, top to bottom) show: input RGB, ground-truth depth, WorldLatent-14B (Ours), DA3-Giant (Teacher), VGGT-1B, CUT3R-512, MonST3R, DUSt3R, MASt3R, Video-Depth-Anything-L, DepthCrafter, Marigold-v1.1, and Metric-VDA-Large.

For each input RGB video (kitchen inspection, cloth folding, and multihuman tracking), we show our estimated depth maps and 3D geometry with camera poses (top row). The estimated depth is then combined with two new text prompts to re-render the scene (bottom row), changing its appearance while keeping its geometry and motion.
Figure 10. Additional text-based 4D generation results. For each text prompt, we show the generated RGB video (top), depth maps (middle), and 3D geometry with camera poses (bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Unified 4D latent space for world perception and generation, relevant to world models and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
papers.tldr: WorldLatent unifies 4D perception and generation in a shared latent space, allowing one model to perform both tasks and support controllable 4D editing.

papers.abstract: 3D indoor scene synthesis requires generating objects to form a complete and coherent scene. Existing approaches rely heavily on manually annotated datasets, leading to high costs and limited generalization. We present SceneCast, an annotation-free framework that trains on large-scale, unlabeled videos, addressing two key challenges: (1) Videos provide only partial views of a scene, requiring the model to extrapolate unseen 3D regions, which is inherently error-prone; (2) Raw videos available online are uncurated, suffering from uncontrolled conditions and variable data quality. First, we design a Transformer-based model that predicts objects sequentially and is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), where an LLM acts as a spatial common-sense evaluator. The LLM provides reward signals through chain-of-thought reasoning and code-executable geometric checks to refine object configurations. Second, we introduce \trim, a data curation approach that generates training videos with controllable video generation models. Crucially, it retains only high-quality prefix clips via multi-criteria quality assessment with an entropy-based weighting strategy. Evaluated on curated synthetic video sets, our annotation-free approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality.
authors: Ziyang Zong, Canming Xia, Haoran Xu, Guang Tan
bullets: Addresses costly annotations and limited generalization in existing indoor scene synthesis methods.
Uses a Transformer to sequentially predict objects and extrapolate unseen 3D regions from partial video views.
Fine-tunes scene configurations with RL using LLM rewards based on spatial reasoning and executable geometric checks.
Curates synthetic training videos by retaining high-quality prefix clips selected with multi-criteria, entropy-weighted assessment.
Outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality on curated synthetic video sets.

figures.caption: Figure 1. SceneCast overview. (a) Our generation model predicts 3D objects sequentially, starting from an initial set of objects. The model is fine-tuned with a reinforcement learning phase with LLM feedback. (b) Our ViTrim strategy removes low-quality tail segments from generated video using multiple quality assessment criteria, ensuring only valid clips are used for training.

Figure 2. SceneCast pipelines. (a) Transformer-based autoregressive 3D indoor scene completion backbone network. (b) LLM-driven reinforcement learning fine-tuning loop incorporating CoT spatial reasoning, automatic geometric code execution, and multi-dimensional reward fusion. (c) ViTrim pipeline for high-quality video segment selection.

Figure 3. Generation samples from an empty scene. SceneCast performs well in producing reasonable and complete object layouts, with correct collision avoidance. ATISS and DiffuScene generate misaligned objects and unnatural layouts. Perhaps restricted by the video generation model, VIPScene generates a small number of objects with narrow coverage of the scene, missing objects that are commonly found in realistic scenes (e.g., wardrobe for bedroom, sofa for livingdiningroom). SAGE [52] lacks the understanding of the actual physical space, resulting in the generation of duplicate or poorly arranged objects (e.g., bedroom without bed, impassable passageway).

papers.selection_reason: Presents SceneCast, a framework for 3D indoor scene synthesis using synthetic videos and LLM-based rewards. This fits the 3D Vision topic as a foundation model for scene generation.
papers.title: SceneCast: Learning Indoor Scene Synthesis from Curated Synthetic Videos with LLM Reward
papers.tldr: SceneCast learns coherent 3D indoor scene synthesis without manual annotations by combining curated synthetic videos with LLM-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.
authors: Qingqiao Hu, Jialin Li, Meilong Xu, Kehan Qi, Yipeng Zhang, Lin Tian, Hongwei Bran Li, Klaus Mueller, Xiaoling Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of giving 2D-input MLLMs informative, token-efficient views of 3D prediction errors.
Represents each volume with three orthogonal planes intersecting at a point, preserving detail around error regions.
An MLLM judges tri-plane predictions while a visual harness converts judgments into precise voxel-level 3D clicks and validates predictions.
Evaluated on 690 ROIs from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities.
Achieves about 10 Dice points over the strongest baseline with frontier MLLMs, with larger gains for targets smaller than 3 cm; also outperforms a recent 3D agent using flash-level MLLMs.

papers.tldr: TriSegAgent uses compact tri-plane views to let MLLM agents iteratively correct 3D segmentations efficiently and accurately.

papers.abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
authors: Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule, Srinath Neelamagam, Aniket Bera
bullets: Noise-only and real dark frame pairs produce nearly identical, high self-consistency, masking the absence of reliable scene structure.

A single inflated statistic is interpreted in opposite ways by keyframing and relocalization, starving keyframes while accepting almost every relocalization candidate.
Reading the statistic at keyframe-pair baselines separates confident collapse from working runs on ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation, in-sample.
Low-light weights and threshold retuning increased tracking but did not recover accurate geometry; the failure signature also reproduced on the two darkest of four Jetson robot routes.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes silent failure and confidence miscalibration in learned dense visual SLAM; relevant to embodied perception and 3D foundation model reliability.
papers.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
papers.tldr: Under photon starvation, dense learned visual SLAM can generate highly consistent but incorrect geometry, causing silent failure in real-time edge deployment.

papers.abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.
authors: Zeyu Ren, Jie Ni, Rui Qian, Jiahao Wei, Hao Tang, Yongtai Liu, Zeyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of estimating geometry and semantics with separate networks or passes.
Uses an Omni Diffusion Transformer with separate token streams for point maps, surface normals, and instance maps.
Employs stream-masked interactions, camera-ray token encoding, and DINOv3-based grounding attention.
Trained on 139K synthetic geometry images, it achieves state-of-the-art point maps and the best average rank for surface normals.
Outperforms SAM on large objects and predicts all three maps 5.7× faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

papers.selection_reason: Generalist one-step model jointly predicting point maps, normals, and instance maps qualifies as a broad 3D perception foundation model.
papers.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
papers.tldr: PINE jointly predicts scene geometry and object instances in one diffusion-model forward pass, achieving strong accuracy with substantially faster inference.

papers.abstract: Modifying 3D assets requires enacting targeted structural transformations while strictly preserving the geometric identity of unedited regions. While recent probability flow models enable training-free editing, bounding these modifications within a high-dimensional latent space presents severe mathematical challenges. Current inversion-free trajectories rely on global velocity updates, which often cause spatial bleed into preserved structures and induce trajectory under-commitment, causing edits to stall mid-path. To resolve these dual failures, we introduce FocusFlow, a segmentation-free framework that structures the integration trajectory into two disjoint phases. During early coarse structure formation, FocusFlow applies Feature-Divergence Localization (FDL) to spatially gate the velocity field using intrinsic cross-attention. Once coarse structure has formed, FocusFlow applies Reference Generation Guidance (RGG), a trajectory-correction term that drives convergence to the target shape by pulling the trajectory toward an explicit clean-latent target. Evaluated on the joint Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny benchmarks, FocusFlow obtains the best preservation scores and the largest edit magnitude among compared methods, suggesting that it can reduce the traditional preservation-modification trade-off. By providing stable, localized geometric control without manual spatial annotations, this phase-scheduled approach lowers technical barriers to the modification of synthetic 3D media.
authors: Tri Ton, Siwoo Lim, Joshua Tian Jin Tee, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Addresses spatial bleed and stalled edits in inversion-free probability-flow editing.
Uses Feature-Divergence Localization to gate velocity updates during early coarse structure formation.
Applies Reference Generation Guidance later to pull the trajectory toward a clean latent representing the target shape.
On Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny, reports the best preservation scores and largest edit magnitude among compared methods.
Requires no segmentation or manual spatial annotations, though its scope is evaluated on these benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes FocusFlow for training-free 3D asset editing using feature-divergence localization, offering a method for controllable 3D generation and editing.
papers.title: Training-Free 3D Editing via Feature-Divergence Localization and Trajectory Correction
papers.tldr: FocusFlow enables training-free, localized 3D editing by combining feature-based spatial gating with trajectory correction to preserve unedited geometry while completing target edits.

papers.abstract: Unified 3D understanding and generation require compact sequences preserving spatial structure. Dense grids yield long sequences, while serialization can separate spatial neighbors. We propose Sparse Proximity Aware Compression (SPAC), a shared sparse SDF vocabulary combining sparse encoding with reversible spatial merging. A Sparse SDF VQ-VAE quantizes near-surface features while retaining explicit coordinates, using reconstruction supervision for surface fidelity and detail. 3D Byte-Pair Encoding (3D-BPE) merges recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets before serialization. Macro tokens expand exactly into leaf tokens and coordinates. After Morton serialization, a shared LLM reads geometry for captioning and predicts tokens that decode into meshes for text-conditioned generation. With fixed geometry, architecture, and band width in voxels, sparse encoder cost grows approximately quadratically with resolution. 3D-BPE reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4 percent, including coordinates, text, and control tokens. SPAC achieves strong results in both 3D captioning and text-conditioned mesh generation. Ablations show gains over leaf tokens and Morton 1D-BPE in both tasks. The project page at https://yangjj007.github.io/spac/ .
authors: Junjie Yang, Rui Qian, Yijiang Li, Jinyi Xu, Yuhao Yan, Xinjian Yi, Yanfeng Li, Mingxuan Li, Xiang Wan, Jicong Fan, Siqi Liu, Ahmed Elazab, Changmiao Wang
bullets: Targets long sequences from dense 3D grids and spatially disconnected serialization.
Uses a sparse SDF VQ-VAE with explicit coordinates and reconstruction supervision to preserve surface detail.
Applies 3D-BPE to merge recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets; macro tokens decode exactly to leaf tokens and coordinates.
Reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4% and achieves strong captioning and text-conditioned mesh-generation results.
Ablations report gains over leaf-token and Morton 1D-BPE baselines; encoder cost still grows approximately quadratically with resolution under fixed settings.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive diffusion world models deliver strong video generation performance, yet they typically output only RGB frames rather than explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representations, creating a gap between learned visual world dynamics and usable 3D assets for downstream robotics, simulation and rendering. To bridge this gap, we introduce ArgsWorld, an autoregressive diffusion model that also produces an explicit 3DGS scene. For each generation chunk, the diffusion transformer jointly processes clean historical image latents and noisy latents for new views. It keeps the historical image latents fixed and refreshes the scene features so that the Gaussian representation can be revised as new regions come into view. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Distribution matching supervises direct image latents and latents of Gaussian renderings at both generation and additional cameras. ArgsWorld unifies 3D scene reconstruction from posed images, scene generation from image or text prompts, and scene extrapolation across camera segments with disconnected endpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that ArgsWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks. Project page: https://m4a1tastegood.github.io/ArgsWorld/
authors: Weiming Chen, Shuaiyan Liu, Xinyu Shao, Zhewen Chen, Tian Guan, Yonghong He, Xitong Ling
bullets: Addresses the gap between RGB-only video world models and usable 3D scene representations.
Jointly processes fixed historical image latents and noisy new-view latents while refreshing Gaussian scene features as regions are revealed.
Uses 3D Self-Forcing Distillation with single- and multi-view data, plus distribution matching for direct and Gaussian-rendered image latents.
Supports 3D reconstruction, image- or text-prompted scene generation, and camera-segment extrapolation with disconnected endpoints.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks.

papers.abstract: As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on converting or captioning pre-existing 3D assets, consisting mostly of single-turn code data for static single objects and struggling to scale task diversity and scene complexity, leaving such training data scarce. We present 3DCodeFactory, an automated framework that directly constructs diverse, complex 3D training data from abundant raw text (e.g., diffusion prompts and product descriptions). The framework first leverages an image generator to synthesize 3D reference images from raw text as visual anchors, guiding the generation of concrete modeling specifications and interactive functional requirements; meanwhile, it jointly constructs visual, specification, and functional rubrics from the reference images and requirements to automatically score and filter multi-turn agent rollouts. Based on this framework, we release 3DCodeFactory-Data, comprising 5,045 high-quality task instances and multi-turn interaction trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on 3DCodeFactory-Data significantly improves performance on BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench, consistently outperforming models trained on existing open-source 3D code datasets, with our 27B model further surpassing the same-series 2.4T flagship Qwen3.8-Max in overall performance.
authors: Zhaoyu Wang, Xueru Wen, XingYu Li, Jie Lou
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of training data beyond static, single-object 3D code generation.
Uses image-generated 3D references to guide modeling specifications and interactive requirements.
Automatically creates visual, specification, and functional rubrics to score and filter agent rollouts.
Releases 3DCodeFactory-Data with 5,045 high-quality task instances and interaction trajectories.
Fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models improve performance across BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench; the 27B model surpasses Qwen3.8-Max overall.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page: https://github.com/KTH-RPL/VG3R
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Lin Lian, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Patric Jensfelt, Kwanghee Won
bullets: Addresses the slowness and incomplete camera modeling of prior video-generation-based 3D reconstruction methods.
Corrects decoded inverse-depth distortion using clip-level shift prediction.
Predicts per-frame camera parameters with a multi-layer camera head that fuses features across transformer blocks.
Using Wan2.1, reconstructs scenes without iterative denoising and reports the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among comparable video-generation methods.
Runs about 4× faster than Aether and 14× faster than Geo4D, while remaining competitive with geometry foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview. VG3R encodes the input video with the frozen VAE of Wan2.1 and processes its latents with a LoRA-adapted transformer at a fixed timestep, with blocks ordered from bottom to top. The final-block features are decoded into inverse depth x̂ through the output layer and VAE decoder D. ClipShift uses these features to predict a single shift ĉ for a video clip, recovering depth up to a global scale. LayerTap combines features from multiple transformer blocks and pairs each latent frame with the first to predict per-frame cameras. Depth and cameras yield the reconstructed point maps. Gray losses are used only during training.

Figure 7. Reconstructions of the methods built on video generation models on 7-Scenes heads-seq-01 and redkitchen-seq-12 and on NRGBD morning apartment and grey white room, in the format of Fig. 4: every method fuses the point maps of all frames with its own predicted cameras, without confidence filtering or other post-processing, and is aligned to the ground truth by a similarity transform.

(ii) Normalization sets the farthest surfaces to zero inverse depth, so directly taking 1/x̂ places them at infinity and distorts the room, even with ground-truth cameras and scale alignment (gray: ground truth). (iii) VG3R predicts a clip-level shift ĉ to restore the inverse-depth offset and reconstructs the room using its own predicted cameras. Its camera head also reads the highlighted intermediate transformer blocks in (i).

papers.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu
bullets: Adapts Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and referring segmentation.
Uses a shared low-rank adapter, public data, and task contracts that align each task’s encoder, instruction, and decoder before training.
Geometry is learned early, but absolute depth scale remains unstable; ensembling predictions improves unaligned depth accuracy without retraining.
Depth and 2D segmentation compete for adapter capacity, and weight merging does not remove this trade-off.
Lower validation flow loss correlates with worse Cityscapes mIoU, making the loss unreliable for checkpoint selection; code, data, contracts, and evaluations are released.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Open Vision Banana overview. A source image x and a task instruction pq condition a frozen generative backbone (Qwen-Image-2.1 in all experiments; the backbone is a configuration choice) that carries one newly initialized rank-64 LoRA adapter δ shared by all tasks. The source enters as visual tokens and reference latents, the instruction as the text condition, and the target latent is generated from noise in 50 flow steps. The generated RGB image r̂q is converted by a parameter-free decoder Dq into a structured prediction ŷq: metric depth, a class-ID map, instance masks, or a binary mask. Bottom: a task contract Cq = (Eq, pq, Dq; Sq) ties encoder, instruction, and decoder to one specification and is validated before training. The scene is a rendered illustration; its RGB tiles are produced by the contract encoders from exact annotations and are not model predictions.

Fig. 3. Training data and task mixture of the main runs. (a) The 1,098,435 training records by task and source; one record is an image–instruction–target triple, so an image can appear in several records. Small sources are listed to the right of their bar; “Indoor observed” combines ARKitScenes, DIODE, and SUN RGB-D frames with at least 98% observed depth, and “Earlier pool” is the segmentation data of the earlier OVB stages. (b) Each task’s share of the pool (light) against its per-update sampling probability (dark), and the expected number of times each record is drawn over the 3.2M draws of a 100k-update run. Sampling reweights the pool: semantic segmentation and editing replay are drawn more often than their size implies, referring segmentation less often.

Fig. 4. Training trajectories of the two 100k-update runs (A: lr 3 × 10−5, B: lr 1 × 10−5; EMA “best” checkpoints, external evaluation). (a) Median-aligned NYUv2 δ1 is flat at 0.89–0.93 from the first evaluated checkpoint, while unaligned δ1 moves between 0.11 and 0.49: training changes the scale, not the geometry. (b) Cityscapes mIoU declines in both runs while depth improves; ReasonSeg peaks early in B and recovers late in A.

Fig. 5. Qualitative results: metric depth and semantic segmentation of Qwen-Image-2.1 with run B at 20k updates (EMA adapter, merged) on benchmark validation images. Depth is the RGB code before decoding.
Fig. 6. Qualitative results: instance and referring segmentation, same model as Fig. 5. Instance colors are arbitrary per instance and need not match the ground truth.

Fig. 2. Task contracts, contract check, and training. (a) Each task is an explicit, decodable RGB code given by a specification Sq, an encoder Eq, an instruction pq, and a decoder Dq; the depth card shows the colormap path along the edges of the RGB cube, each vertex labeled with the metric depth it encodes under Eq. (2). (b) Checks that run on the training manifest and configuration before the first update. (c) Training: an annotation is encoded into an RGB target and then into a latent b by the frozen autoencoder; conditional flow matching updates the shared adapter while the backbone stays frozen. Run A uses peak lr 3 × 10−5 (shown) and run B uses 1 × 10−5; editing replay is included with the intent of preserving generation, which we have not measured (Sec. 6).

Table 8 gives all metrics and Table 9 the gap to interpolation. Cityscapes is above interpolation for every merge, ReasonSeg below for every merge, and unaligned NYUv2 δ1 below for all merges except P6. P2, P3, and P4 show unstable DIODE AbsRel (1.1–2.9), while P1 and P5 stay at 0.50–0.56, close to the 17.5k checkpoint (0.51), and P6 is 0.79.

papers.selection_reason: Unified perception through generation in RGB space, including metric depth and segmentation, directly relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana shows that an open 7B diffusion generator can unify depth and segmentation perception tasks, but shared-adapter interference, unresolved depth scale, and misleading validation loss limit performance selection.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/
authors: Changyu Du, Stavros Nousias, Syed Salman Ahmed, Kai Dietmair, Mohammad Alrabab'h, Andr\'e Borrmann
bullets: Introduces 1,028 reconstructions across 128 real-world scenes, five domains, and varied spatial scales, using expert-curated BIM references.
Agents measure scans with Python, create labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
Parallel asynchronous collaboration enables a lead agent to delegate, model concurrently, and integrate versioned worker proposals.
The leading agent achieves 96% scan coverage within 5 cm but only 63% semantic mIoU; no agent passes all engineering checks on over 38% of scenes.
Larger scenes reduce coverage and engineering conformance, while smaller-model teams improve performance, especially on larger scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of S2Bench. S2Bench pairs scans of 128 scenes across five built-environment domains and spatial scales with expert-curated reference models (top). A coding agent builds a component model by writing and inspecting code in a live CAD/BIM kernel (middle). Despite high geometric fidelity, agentbuilt models can fail semantic accuracy (1: door as wall) or engineering consistency (2: open wall joint).

Figure 2. Reconstruction framework. (a) Within an isolated workspace, a harness runs one agent or a team to measure scans in Python and iterate code in Rhino 8, receiving structured feedback (execution errors, validity checks, and agent-written validation) and rendered views before exporting the program, model, and IFC. (b) Single-agent timeline and revisions. (c) Team run on the same scan: the lead (solid icon) delegates regions to three workers, keeps modeling, and merges their parts under a shared 45-minute deadline.

Figure 3. Reconstructed models compared with the input scan and reference. Colors denote component semantic classes, and tunnel and interior views are cut open for visibility. * and ** mark two Qwen outputs whose raw-coordinate 5 cm scan coverage (R5) is 0% due to frame/unit errors and are transformed for display only: (*) rotated 180◦ to undo a flipped local frame, and (**) scaled by 1,000 from metres to millimetres. Additional comparisons across 48 scenes appear in Supp. Figs. 11 to 14.

Figure 6. What agents do, and where errors enter. (a) An interior region in the scan and five reconstructed models, with rings marking scan door locations. (b) Sample outputs by Sol and Opus alongside each agent’s mean share of meshes and kernel solids across 128 scenes. (c) Share of runs (%) with scan checks or declared interference, contact, and support checks, and median program executions.

Figure 9. Kimi K3.1 Pro on Japan RC Bridges Bridge_3 (bridge). The run takes 43 minutes and executes the model program 8 times. The delivery has 9 components, lies within 5 cm of 63.3% of the scan points, and reaches 32.4% mIoU. The agent first reads the span as one slab (step 3), then finds vertical faces below both deck edges and models them as edge girders (step 4). It builds the components as hexahedra between fitted planes and declares contact and interference checks (step 6). When a thickness check fails, it sets the expected value to the value of the model (steps 7–8). The comparison with the scan shows misfits at the abutment tops, and the agent finds that its earlier sections were clipped and revises the end blocks (steps 9–12).

Figure 10. GPT-6.1 Sol on STSD horse-1-6_2 (tunnel). The run takes 27 minutes and executes the model program 9 times. The delivery has 276 components, lies within 5 cm of 99.7% of the scan points, and reaches 47.3% mIoU. The agent fits the tunnel axis (step 3) and a lining profile. It enters the stations of the ring joints as a list of constants (step 5) and models the joints as bands 8 mm wide (step 6). It assigns the invert to the tunnel wall (step 6). Two declared checks fail and are repaired in the geometry: an interference between rail and invert (steps 6–7) and the contact of the walkway brackets (steps 9–10). The remaining clusters of unexplained points receive a decision by position for the report (step 12).

Figure 4. Coverage and IoU per class (Sol and Opus mean). Bars span from class IoU to 5 cm coverage (per-agent values in Supp. Tab. 11).

The delivery has 508 components, lies within 5 cm of 92.2% of the scan points, and reaches 27.8% mIoU. The agent measures the scan for 15 minutes before its first program execution and then extends the model in stages: walls, slabs, openings, and objects from clusters of unexplained points. It searches for doors as open gaps, drops a detector for closed doors (steps 6–7), and later notes an undetected closed door in an elevation sheet (step 11). Its elevation images color scan points by offset from its fitted wall plane: white within the wall, green in front, red behind, and black where there are no points. It repairs a failed interference check between doors and walls (steps 12–13) and reports that the door count is short. The run ends shortly after the five-minute notice of the harness (Sec. papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
