papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

bullets: Existing VLMs struggle with metric 3D inference because uncalibrated views leave geometry ambiguous.
StereoVLM learns from binocular observations through correspondence, disparity, calibration-conditioned depth, and semantic spatial reasoning.
The authors introduce Stereo3D-Bench, evaluating point-, object-, and spatial-reasoning capabilities.
Disparity supervision generalizes better to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision.
Interventions show performance relies on cross-view geometry, while hierarchical supervision improves broader spatial and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.
authors: Zunhai Su, Keyu Fan, Ruishan Guo, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jingzehua Xu, Bohan Sun, Hansen Feng, Ruihan Hu, Yik-Chung Wu, Ngai Wong
bullets: Streaming geometry transformers face growing KV caches and sensitivity to quantization across cache locations, causing cache–geometry mismatch.
Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization preserves sensitive cross-view evidence.

Across five benchmarks and two backbones, it achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings and can outperform unquantized inference.
The optimized backend reaches 5.05× physical KV compression, 23.1% lower latency, and up to 5.4× larger batch size under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Growers and traders rely on root morphology to assess wild ginseng, yet breakage can obscure important structural traits. We study point cloud completion to provide geometric references for morphological analysis. Does providing more observed points always improve 3D completion? We test whether selected subsets improve recovery of the original missing region while keeping the pretrained completer fixed. We introduce BioCL-POS, an external selector that predicts how the completer responds to candidate inputs. For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. We use these spatial responses to estimate recovery quality and supervise them with measurements from actual completions. At inference, we select an input from the observed geometry and run the completer once. We evaluate four frozen completers on controlled gaps in ginseng and tree data at 5%,10%, and 20% omission, and examine 30% omission on ginseng. At 5--20% omission, we outperform full-input completion and all five alternative selectors on both datasets with all four completers. We achieve lower mean reconstruction error and higher mean F-score and coverage. We thus show that selecting observations can improve geometric recovery without retraining the completer, providing more accurate geometric references for subsequent morphological analysis.
authors: Yulu Wang, Tingting Yao, Taolue Liu
bullets: Addresses whether using all observed points is always best when reconstructing missing root geometry.
Uses an external selector to predict a completer’s spatial response to candidate observation subsets.
Selects one input based on predicted recovery quality, then runs the pretrained completer once.
Outperforms full-input completion and five alternative selectors across four frozen completers on ginseng and tree data with 5–20% omissions.
Improves reconstruction error, F-score, and coverage; performance is also examined at 30% omission on ginseng.

papers.abstract: Point cloud denoising and upsampling require samples that accurately recover the underlying surface from noisy or sparse observations. A central challenge in both tasks is preserving surface coverage while refining point locations. We introduce GAAFormer (Geometry-Anchored Attention Transformer), a unified generative octree transformer that performs both tasks with a shared network. Its decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry, providing spatial context for occupancy prediction and point generation. Fixed voxel windows and alternating shifts preserve the grouping of surviving nodes as the output tree changes. The design retains the encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count of a serialized-attention backbone. We establish a deletion-consistency property of the neighborhood rule and evaluate both tasks using the same model. On PUNet, GAAFormer achieves a mean Chamfer distance (CD) of $6.0643\times10^{-5}$, reducing CD and Hausdorff distance by 3.35% and 19.34%, respectively, relative to the serialized backbone. For upsampling, it achieves CD values of $0.8475$, $1.7057$, and $1.0147$ ($\times10^{-5}$) on PU-GAN, PU1K, and Sketchfab, respectively, with improvements in CD, Hausdorff distance, and point-to-surface distance over the same backbone on PU-GAN and Sketchfab. These results establish a single architecture for point cloud denoising and upsampling. Within the shared encoder-decoder, the same geometry-anchored attention module improves both noise removal and dense point generation without task-specific redesign or additional parameters.
authors: Haoxi Tian (School of Civil Engineering,Geomatics, Southwest Petroleum University)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering accurate surface geometry while preserving coverage in noisy or sparse point clouds.
Uses a generative octree Transformer whose decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry for occupancy prediction and point generation.
Fixed voxel windows, alternating shifts, and a deletion-consistent neighborhood rule preserve grouping as the output tree changes.
Retains the serialized-attention backbone’s encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count.
Improves denoising and upsampling metrics over the serialized backbone, with gains reported in Chamfer, Hausdorff, and point-to-surface distances on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Moving objects introduce cross-frame inconsistencies that complicate camera estimation and static geometry recovery in driving scenes. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods explicitly separate static and dynamic primitives, but often estimate camera parameters and geometry from shared features that jointly encode both components, leaving static reconstruction susceptible to dynamic interference. To address this challenge, we propose S2D-Splat, a feed-forward framework for static-first Gaussian reconstruction with layer-wise feature guidance. Our framework separates static and dynamic features before camera and geometry estimation, enabling the static branch to recover camera parameters and static 3D Gaussians with reduced dynamic interference. Intermediate static features are cached at each layer and reused as fixed conditioning at corresponding layers of the dynamic branch. This asymmetric information flow preserves the established static representations while providing stable geometric context for reconstructing dynamic 3D Gaussians. An instance-level motion decoder further queries the fused static and dynamic representations to estimate object trajectories, supporting motion-aligned Gaussian fusion and temporal interpolation. Experiments on Waymo and zero-shot evaluations on nuScenes and the MM-AU accident dataset demonstrate that S2D-Splat outperforms existing approaches on most evaluated metrics and generalizes to highly dynamic, pre-collision driving scenarios.
authors: Jinheng Li, Tianchen Deng, Bufan Zhang, Qu Chen, Jianwu Fang
bullets: Addresses camera and geometry errors caused by moving objects interfering with static-scene estimation.
Separates static and dynamic features before estimating camera parameters and 3D Gaussians.
Caches intermediate static features to condition the dynamic branch while preserving stable static representations.
Uses an instance-level motion decoder for object trajectories, motion-aligned Gaussian fusion, and temporal interpolation.
Outperforms existing methods on most evaluated metrics on Waymo and transfers zero-shot to nuScenes and MM-AU accident scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of S2D-Splat. Given unposed images, we encode each frame into patchified features and use SAM2 to classify tokens as static or dynamic, which a Motion-Static Separator then refines into clean static and dynamic tokens (camera in , static in , dynamic in , suppressed dynamic in ). The static tokens pass through alternating attention and are decoded by heads into camera parameters and a static Gaussian field, with each layer’s camera and static tokens cached in a Tokens Bank. The dynamic reconstruction mirrors this but takes the fused static and dynamic tokens as input, re-fusing the extracted dynamic tokens with the Tokens Bank after each layer to yield global tokens and a dynamic Gaussian field. From the global tokens, instance-specific queries retrieve each instance’s motion, and all components merge to form the full scene reconstruction.

Figure 1: We propose S2D-Splat, a feedforward Gaussian reconstruction framework that achieves precise dynamic-static decoupling and instance-level motion prediction for complex driving scenes. It disentangles multi-frame input into static and dynamic representations, reconstructs each representation independently, and fuses them into a global representation that guides a motion decoder to recover accurate and temporally consistent per-instance 3D trajectories (e.g., Query 1, Query 2).

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals. These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.
authors: Thomas E. Huang, Alex Zihao Zhu, Hao Xiang, Tianyi Cai, Jingwei Ji, Yuliang Zou, Jiafan Yu, Xin Huang, Mingxing Tan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring rich 2D VLM knowledge to outdoor 3D object detection.
Uses class-agnostic 3D proposals and spatially aware VLM embeddings from projected 2D regions for object-level distillation.
Generates proposal-level captions with an MLLM to add domain-specific semantic information and improve zero-shot capability.
Trains with a composite objective combining direct feature distillation and caption-based semantic alignment.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Data Generation Pipeline. (a) Generic Objects Extraction: We use RANSAC and DBSCAN on the raw point cloud to generate class-agnostic 3D proposals across the entire scene, which are then projected to all 2D camera views. (b) Visual Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to RoI pool features from the VLM vision encoder, creating the visual distillation targets f vis. (c) Language Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to crop and mask the images and then sent to a MLLM for captioning, which are then encoded by the VLM text encoder to create the language distillation targets etext.

Fig. 2. Overall Pipeline. During (a) training, our detector is supervised with three losses: class-agnostic bounding box loss Ldet along with two distillation losses, Visual Alignment loss Lvis and Language Alignment loss Llang, for feature alignment. During (b) inference, we directly use the trained detector to predict boxes and open-vocabulary embeddings. Text-based queries are encoded by the VLM text encoder, and cosine similarity between the embeddings and queries are used to assign the final class label.

Fig. 1. 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection Results. Given text prompts for each class, our detector can retrieve corresponding objects in 3D, without using any ground-truth data during training. Our detector can even generalize to novel object classes like TVs.
Fig. 4. TIPS Features. Comparison of visual features from TIPS [26] (middle) and CLIP [7] (right). TIPS produce features that are higher resolution and more spatially aligned.

papers.tldr: A two-part framework transfers 2D vision-language semantics to 3D proposals through visual embedding distillation and MLLM-generated captions, achieving state-of-the-art open-vocabulary 3D detection on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.
bullets: Addresses 3D motion recovery and temporal prediction without per-scene optimization or predefined physical assumptions.
Fuses all camera observations into a shared world-coordinate voxel grid and predicts a continuous-time velocity field.
Integrates the learned field from observed states to estimate intermediate and future object positions.
Improves F1 on held-out PhysInOne scenes by 2.5% for in-between and 15% for future prediction over the strongest competitor.
Transfers zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, achieving a 12% future-prediction F1 improvement.

papers.title: AdaPixFlow: Learning Continuous-Time 3D Dynamics Across Scenes from Sparse Multi-view Observations

papers.abstract: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.
authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee, Guan-ming Su
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem of iteratively optimizing every glyph or icon for Gaussian scenes.
Encodes sampled surface anchors into a shared feature plane, then decodes neural Gaussians with surface normals.
Separates geometry conversion from material and lighting, while supporting compact image and video delivery.
Uses a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets, with font-family holdouts for evaluation.
Achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen assets; conversion takes 9.1 ms per prepared asset.

papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.tldr: FFGaussType converts glyph and SVG geometry into compact, renderable Gaussian assets in one fast forward pass instead of per-asset optimization.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.
authors: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Zhemeng Zhang, Hanxiao Jiang, Congcong Zhu, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Jingrun Chen, Rynson WH Lau
bullets: Addresses the limitation that matching observed video motion may not yield correct responses to new forces, especially in spring-based models coupling volume and shape changes.
Enriches local deformation modes while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation.
Uses offline calibration to translate shared relative response edits into stiffness updates for interpretable material editing and transfer.
On synthetic scenes, reduces Poisson’s-ratio error by 75.8% and Young’s-modulus relative error by 22.1% versus PhysTwin.
A new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark and real-world tests show improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MorphTwin, a method for reconstructing interactive physical twins from video by enriching local deformation modes, which is relevant to simulation-based manipulation and 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
papers.tldr: MorphTwin reconstructs deformable physical twins from video with independently controllable deformation responses, improving material accuracy and future-motion prediction over PhysTwin.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.
authors: Ayman Alkhateeb, Hadi Amirpour, Christian Timmerer
bullets: Addresses fine-scale detail loss caused by the finite projected footprints of 3DGS Gaussians.
Uses progressive multi-aperture rendering with covariance contraction, uncertainty-guided feature aggregation, and transmittance/depth conditioning.
Acts as a lightweight plug-in for pre-trained 3DGS models without retraining.
Outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines on Mip-NeRF 360, with larger gains for lower-quality Gaussian representations.
Maintains real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of AGSR. Covariance contraction produces multi-aperture RGB, transmittance, and depth renderings with progressively smaller projected footprints and correspondingly higher effective bandwidth. Cross-aperture variations form a structural uncertainty field that guides a three-stage geometry-aware fusion network. Higher-bandwidth observations are fused sequentially and refined through residual PixelShuffle reconstruction to produce the final super-resolved output.

Fig. 1: Projected Gaussian covariances influence the effective bandwidth of individual rasterization kernels. By systematically contracting the covariance, AGSR generates multiaperture observations that reveal structural cues attenuated by native rasterization. The resulting uncertainty field guides geometry-aware super-resolution for enhanced detail reconstruction.

Fig. 3: Visual comparison of 2× and 4× super-resolution on 3DGS representations trained on highly subsampled images (tf = 8). AGSR exploits structural cues revealed by multi-aperture rendering to recover fine-scale detail that is poorly reproduced by degraded Gaussian representations. Quantitative metrics (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS) are reported below each crop.

Fig. 4: Quantitative performance (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) of AGSR compared with native 3DGS and bicubic baselines across varying training degradation factors (tf ). As the training factor increases, the quality of the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates substantially. AGSR becomes increasingly advantageous as the underlying representation degrades, with the strongest gains observed under moderate and severe degradation, outperforming the baselines across most settings and metrics.

TABLE I: Complexity analysis of the progressive aperture fusion network. We report the parameter count, computational complexity (GMACs), and full-pipeline inference speed (FPS) in both FP32 and FP16 precisions. Parameter counts and GMACs correspond to the cumulative deployed inference model required to produce each stage’s output. papers.abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
authors: Xiaoxin Mi, Zhen Cao, Chong Liu, Yuhao Li, Zhen Dong, Bisheng Yang, Yang Jia, Shengwu Xiong
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing datasets, including limited semantic richness, modality diversity, and scenario complexity.
Covers approximately 100 km of Chinese highways and urban streets.

Annotates 15 road-element categories, including boundaries, crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, and 10 direction-symbol types.
Supports research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction, road mapping, topology reasoning, map updating, and street-scene generation.

papers.abstract: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.
authors: Yinan Wang, Rohan Kadkol, Hyunjin Yoo, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Lalonde, James J. Clark
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between combining independently trained radiance-field parameters and combining their rendered images.
Uses shared scene geometry and separate, identically initialized appearance networks with merge-aware training.
Relights a target HDR environment by computing basis-light coefficients and merging the corresponding appearance networks.
Supports both NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, requiring one rendering pass per viewpoint.
Demonstrates competitive relighting quality on synthetic and real multi-light captures.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Qualitative comparison on the Neural Gaffer objects. Each row shows an object relit under a new environment map (left) and seen from a held-out view. Every method uses the setting reported in Tab. 1. Our results come from a single render of the merged network, with no optimization for the new lighting. All methods handle the backpack well. The shiny helmet and iron are harder. Our models get the overall color and shading right but miss the sharp reflections, because our basis lights are smooth.

Figure 1. Mergeable radiance fields. (a) One radiance field, a NeRF or a set of 3D Gaussians, is shared by K basis illuminations Li. For every element j that contributes to a pixel (a sample along its ray for NeRF, a Gaussian that overlaps it for 3DGS), the field provides a feature zj and the viewing direction dj . Each basis light has its own small appearance MLP with parameters ϕi, trained on the images Ii of the scene under Li. All MLPs start from the same initialization. To make them mergeable, some of the training samples are rendered with a random convex combination ϕmix of the MLPs and supervised by the same combination of the basis images, which is the true image under the mixed light (bottom row). (b) To relight, we approximate a new environment map LA by a non-negative combination of the basis lights with weights βi, and take the same weighted sum of the MLP parameters, ϕM = ∑ i βiϕi. The merged MLP ϕM then renders the relit image in a single pass with the unchanged radiance field. (c) Three scenes relit under four unseen environment maps at a held-out view, one render each.

papers.abstract: When reconstructing high-quality 3D assets from images, existing approaches often excel at one objective while compromising another, and frequently overlook the intrinsic quality of the reconstructed surfaces. We present MODL, a framework that jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh. Our approach combines Laplacian-preconditioned optimization for smooth vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing to preserve fine details and well-shaped triangles. The triangle mesh is optimized subject to multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints, but without segmentation, geometric supervision or alpha-blending. Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets demonstrate that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis while producing geometrically accurate models with superior intrinsic mesh quality. Our results highlight the potential of direct mesh optimization to unify photorealistic rendering, geometric reconstruction, and practical 3D asset creation.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between novel-view appearance and intrinsic mesh quality in image-based 3D reconstruction.
Optimizes a watertight triangle mesh using Laplacian-preconditioned vertex updates and curvature-adaptive remeshing.
Uses multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints without segmentation, geometric supervision, or alpha-blending.
Evaluations show competitive novel-view synthesis alongside geometrically accurate models and superior mesh quality.
Scope: focused on reconstructing textured objects from images.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of the output mesh geometry and appearance between several GS methods and MODL.
Figure 5. Output 3D assets for MODL on the Aria DTC [9] dataset.

Figure 2. Radar chart of the metrics assessing 3D asset quality. BER, SIR, and AR focus on mesh quality, CD measure geometric accuracy, and PSNR portrays image synthesis capability (see Section 5.3). Methods using TSDF Fusion for post-processing provide competitive geometric accuracy and intrinsic mesh quality, but are lacking in well-formed triangles and rendering capabilities. Triangle Splatting [20] without TSDF Fusion is the antithesis, providing the best rendering capabilities and well-formed triangle shapes, but lacks in mesh quality (since the output is a triangle soup) and geometric accuracy. MeshSplatting [19] provides a nice balance between rendering and geometric quality, but the meshes are nonmanifold and have poor connectivity overall. MODL yields the most balanced 3D assets in terms of the combined mesh, geometric, and photometric quality.

Figure 3. The remeshing operations of Botsch and Kobbelt [2]. To maintain a desired target triangle edge length, edges are: (a) split if the actual edge length exceeds the target length; (b) collapsed if the current edge length is smaller than the target length. In practice, we use a buffer size around the target edge length such that triangle edges that are close to this length are not split or collapsed. Following the Botsch and Kobbelt [2] algorithm: (c) edges are flipped when doing so improves the vertex valence distribution of the mesh; and (d) vertices are moved towards their one-ring neighborhood centroid in a local tangent plane and are then projected back onto the surface.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Zahra Montazeri, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Milos Hasan
bullets: Targets reconstruction errors in scene layout, scale, lighting, and unseen-surface completion.

Agents generate parameterized Blender programs, with visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail selection.
Adds inferred unseen regions, fitted lighting, motion support, programmatic checks, and visual comparison-based revision.
Evaluated on 100 scenes, showing better original-view fidelity than direct-agent reconstruction and stronger novel-view content similarity than compared video-to-3D methods.

papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Zahra Montazeri, Milo\v{s} Ha\v{s}an
bullets: Addresses the limitations of meshes, analytic materials, and illumination-baked Gaussian representations for complex appearance and light transport.
Uses a fine-tuned video diffusion model to generate structured RGBA turntable sequences with known pose, camera, and lighting.
Reconstructs selected video-VAE latent frames as millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features.
A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer support novel-view rendering and relighting.
Demonstrates interactive scene integration for assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs.

The MLP labeled “4L × 64” is the per-asset decoder distilled from the nine-layer, width-512 shared decoder described in Section 3.4 for final rendering. (d) The resulting asset supports novel views and lights through stochastic Gaussian ray tracing.

papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.
bullets: Addresses the need for one reusable model across localized and global tasks and multiple imaging modalities.
Combines 3D architectural advances, self-distillation, and cross-modal curricula, trained on permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes.
Evaluated strictly frozen across segmentation, classification, and registration on MRI and CT, with zero-shot evaluation on PET.
Achieves the best or tied-best average rank in every task group and performs at specialist-model levels across modalities.
Shows strong label efficiency, matching top-performing TotalSegmentator CT models with one-tenth of the labels.

papers.abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from aligning only pooled point-cloud descriptors.
Computes neighborhood averages and residuals at multiple encoder stages before pooling.
Uses branch-level cross-modal alignment, cross-level consistency, and adaptive fusion.
Supports both graph encoders and point Transformers through a shared intermediate-feature interface.
Evaluations show transfer value across classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning.

papers.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
authors: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses rule-state persistence across saving and loading and rule-to-visual realization, including unseen affected objects.
Represents rules, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph linked to video generation and perceptual feedback.
Uses dynamic object binding, state-constrained generation, attribute state replacement, and counterfactual reconstruction training.
Introduces RuleVerse, a rule-driven interaction dataset built from GTA-V and Habitat with detailed state and event annotations.
Experiments show improved consistency of saved/restored rules and accurate realization of rule outcomes on specified objects and attributes.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of WorldRuler. papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
bullets: MatterChat uses a large bridge and separate contrastive alignment; this work instead learns representation selection jointly on downstream tasks.
Different target properties benefit from representations at different depths of Zatom-1, while CHGNet and Zatom-1 provide complementary information.
Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, including up to 47.8% lower RMSE, with fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.
Adding UMA-S shows flexibility across encoder combinations; the three-encoder setup reaches 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our proposed Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) methodology. (a) Frozen domain encoders (Zatom-1 and CHGNet) extract complementary atom-level representations from a crystal structure. Here, features from all 16 Zatom-1 layers are retained, and CHGNet features are projected from 64 to 512 dimensions. (b) The property requested by the prompt selects a learned task residual, which is added to 32 latent queries. Two Perceiver blocks apply cross-attention to the structural features, followed by latent self-attention and a feed-forward network. These taskconditioned queries allow the bridge to weight encoder sources and layer depths differently for each property. (c) The fused latents are projected into the language-model embedding space and combined with prompt embeddings. A frozen language model then generates the response. The trainable components are optimized jointly using a downstream language-modeling objective.

Figure 4: Performance comparison of multimodal fusion strategies across six classification tasks. The grouped bars evaluate the baseline Matterchat, basic fusion mechanisms (Weighted Sum, Concatenation), and the proposed TCAF architecture with and without task conditioning. papers.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models

papers.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.
authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limits of appearance-only guidance for diagnosing geometry, material, and illumination errors.
Combines geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues during iterative scene refinement.
Uses Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, evidence, and revision history, including partially visible or unseen sources.
Requires no additional training or differentiable rendering.
Reports improved reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, with benefits for editing, object insertion, and relighting.

figures.caption: Figure 10. Application of harmonious object insertion. Our method (b, d) enables physically realistic lighting, reflection, occlusion and geometric projection, while (c) generative model-only method struggles with these real-world principles.

Figure 7. Application of texture editing. Our method supports texture replacement with multiple reference images with precise and executable code reconstruction, while directly applying even front-tier generative models leads to inaccurate structure.

Figure 6. Qualitative ablation of key designs. Our full framework reproduces scene layout and illumination more precisely, while removing individual components introduces errors in basic scene layout (c), light placement (c-f), and light source shape (e).
Figure 11. Limitation on complex invisible lighting reasoning. Although effective, our framework still struggles with inferring complex invisible objects from scarce light and shadow cues.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison between other SoTA image-to-code baselines. Across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, our LightHarness better preserves object arrangement and characteristic lighting effects, including strong back-lighting, localized illumination, and structured cast shadows, achieving more faithful reconstructions of scene structure and appearance.
Figure 5. Hard case verification. Our method more faithfully reconstructs the diagonal shadow and surrounding building structure relative to other methods.
Figure 9. Application of relighting with realistic shadow.

Figure 2. Conceptual comparison of image-to-code paradigms. (a) Appearance feedback emphasizes rendered–reference similarity. (b) Tool-grounded refinement uses perception and spatial analysis to improve layout. (c) LightHarness combines enriched evidence and persistent memory for explicit lighting reasoning throughout reconstruction.
Figure 8. Application of relighting with realistic reflection.
Table 2. Quantitative ablation experiment. We evaluate on a 16-image subset for efficiency. Our full model achieves the best. BT scores are re-normalized here.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison of image-to-code reconstruction. We report four appearance consistency metrics covering PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and DreamSim, and measure novel-view consistency by a mean-centered Bradley-Terry (BT) score which is estimated from pairwise judgments using an additional ±15◦ view following SceneRig [19]. Bold and underline indicate the best and second-best.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a VLM-based agentic framework for 3D scene reconstruction, incorporating geometric and lighting reasoning, fitting 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
papers.tldr: LightHarness improves image-to-code 3D scene reconstruction by using agentic, evidence-guided reasoning about lighting alongside geometry and materials.

papers.abstract: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.
authors: Claudia Cuttano, Tamy Boubekeur, Elena Garces, Giuseppe Vecchio
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed disentanglement of appearance factors from a single RGB image.
Trains a shared decoder to reconstruct intrinsic maps from DINOv3 features, separating reconstruction from decomposition without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision.
Uses lightweight, modality-specific projections to predict teacher representations from RGB and support partially annotated data.
Predicts all intrinsic properties in one forward pass with a compact 165M-parameter model, reported as 100× faster than diffusion-based methods.
Achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, improved resolution robustness, and interpretable modality-specific feature spaces.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RAID overview. (a) We first learn an X → X reconstruction autoencoder across RGB and intrinsic signals, i.e. albedo, irradiance, normals, roughness, and metallicity. A frozen DINOv3 backbone with trainable AdaptFormer modules encodes each modality into a shared, decodable feature space; one DC-AE decoder reconstructs the input modality from that space. (b) We then freeze the reconstruction model and learn to infer its features from RGB. A student encoder and modality-specific projections predict the features that the teacher extracts from the corresponding GT maps. Feature alignment guides these predictions, while supervision on the decoded maps enforces pixel alignment. At inference, the teacher is removed: the student, projections, and same shared decoder produce all five maps.

Figure 6. Qualitative robustness to input resolution. We compare RGB↔X, MVInverse, and RAID with and without multi-resolution training at input resolutions from 256×256 to 2048×2048. At each resolution, we show the predicted albedo and surface normal maps. RGB↔X exhibits artifacts at both extremes, whereas MVInverse degrades at high resolution. The single-resolution variant of RAID produces more consistent predictions than either baseline, suggesting that our adaptation to intrinsic decomposition preserves the resolution robustness of the pretrained DINOv3 representation. Multi-resolution training further improves prediction consistency.

Figure 5. Feature-space selection. Given an image and a query patch +, we compute cosine similarity between the query and patch features in each modality-projected feature space (red: high, blue: low). The resulting maps show that albedo, normal, irradiance, and metallicity projections induce different selection axes, grouping regions according to the corresponding physical property.

Figure 4. Resolution robustness and memory scaling. Albedo PSNR (↑) and LPIPS (↓) on Hypersim and InteriorVerse for input resolutions from 512 to 2048 pixels. Marker area encodes peak inference GPU memory. We compare our models trained with and without multi-resolution supervision against MVInverse and RGB↔X (InteriorVerse only). Our model is more stable across resolutions; multi-resolution supervision further improves highresolution accuracy while keeping peak memory below 3GB.

Figure 3. X → X autoencoder reconstructions. The reconstruction stage receives a map X as input and reconstructs the same signal at the output. The autoencoder preserves the spatial structure and modality-specific details of the input maps. These reconstructions indicate that heterogeneous intrinsic signals can be represented in a shared DINOv3 feature-to-map space, which is later used to supervise the RGB-to-intrinsics student.
Figure 7. Additional qualitative results. Intrinsic maps predicted by RAID for additional input images.

Table 1. Comparison on InteriorVerse and Hypersim. RAID offers the best overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off, maintaining competitive albedo and normal estimation while achieving the best material estimates (roughness and metallicity) on InteriorVerse and irradiance estimates on Hypersim. With only 165M parameters, it is the smallest and fastest model in this comparison, delivering over 100× the throughput of the fastest diffusion baseline [41] on InteriorVerse. Compared with the feed-forward baseline [36], it uses about one-sixth as many parameters and achieves 2× FPS at 1024×768. For albedo and irradiance, we report PSNR, RMSE, and LPIPS; for metallicity and roughness, PSNR, RMSE, and MAE; and for normals, mean angular error and pixel accuracy at 11.25◦ and 30◦. FPS is measured on an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU at 640×480 on InteriorVerse and 1024×768 on Hypersim. Best results bold, 2nd best underlined.

Table 2. Choice of pretrained representation. We compare DINOv3 with leading Vision Foundation Models spanning selfsupervised and image–text pretraining. With each VFM, we train a reconstruction autoencoder and then an RGB student to predict the teacher features. DINOv3 consistently achieves the best performance across all modalities on Hypersim. Best result in bold.

Table 3. Ablation of the reconstruction teacher and output loss. No teacher regresses maps directly in pixel space, while No pixel loss uses teacher feature alignment alone. Combining feature alignment with supervision on the decoded maps (RAID) gives the strongest overall performance, leading across all four modalities on InteriorVerse and on irradiance on Hypersim. Direct regression achieves higher albedo PSNR and slightly lower mean normal error on Hypersim at the cost of a separate decoder per modality.
Table 4. Data statistics. Number of training and test images, together with the available intrinsic-map annotations for each dataset.
Table 5. Training configuration. Both stages use the same six training datasets and keep the DINOv3 backbone frozen.
Table 6. Reconstruction upper bound. X → X reconstruction of ground-truth maps by the teacher, compared with RGB → X prediction by RAID. Both use the same decoder.

papers.selection_reason: Applies a strong pretrained representation (DINOv3) to solve the ill-posed problem of single-image intrinsic decomposition, fitting the 3D foundation models subtopic.
papers.title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition
papers.tldr: RAID performs fast single-image intrinsic decomposition by predicting intrinsic representations from RGB with a compact DINOv3-based model instead of using iterative diffusion.

papers.abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.
bullets: The study probes 15 functional attributes across elements in 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings, holding out entire buildings for evaluation.
Models are compared using a shared linear readout, including hand-crafted descriptors, supervised point networks, frozen pretrained transformers, and random-weight controls.
From-scratch networks do not clearly beat descriptors, which reach 0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements.
Frozen Utonia reaches 0.732 mAP, with its gain over matched random-weight controls attributed to pretraining.
Pretrained features improve as labeled buildings increase; in tested settings, fine-tuning reduces their advantage.

Top: Google Street View (© Google), used to verify the labels; A has an opening sash. Bottom: the same windows in the LiDAR scan. (c) P (operable): the predicted probability that A (red) and B (blue) are operable, from a linear layer on each feature source.
Figure 2: Left: mAP vs. number of labelled training buildings (5 draws; all: ∼18; band: ± sd). Right: fine-tuning, added descriptors and context (mAP).

papers.selection_reason: Probes whether 3D point representations and pretrained 3D models encode architectural function, relevant to 3D perception and foundation-model evaluation.
papers.title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
papers.tldr: Frozen self-supervised 3D point features encode architectural function better than hand-crafted descriptors or models trained from scratch, especially with limited labeled buildings.

papers.abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.
authors: Jaehyun Kim, Wonseok Kang, Jeongmin Lee, Tae-Wan Kim
bullets: Compares eight learned 3D models with geometric estimation across five test sets, varying reference counts, pose components, and reference inputs.

With two references, geometric estimation plus one additional reference is more accurate at fine pose thresholds than every tested model on Cambridge and NAVER B1, and is never significantly worse as a fallback.
With three references, the better approach depends on the scene; translation magnitude helps most when references are spread out rather than top-ranked retrieved images.
At NAVER Gangnam Station, retrieval from multiple locations causes models to fail at different stages; robust alignment narrows Pi3X and MapAnything’s gap to adding references.
Controlled tests show alignment restores several models’ performance, but not Depth Anything 3; pose-conditioned Pi3X additionally requires masking distant poses during input-pose normalization.

papers.title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
papers.tldr: Geometric localization can outperform learned 3D models with fewer references, while learned pose cues help mainly when references are selected appropriately and model inputs are well aligned.

papers.abstract: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
authors: Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Recovers dense geometry, camera poses, metric scale, point tracks, and moving-object masks from single- or multi-image inputs.
Uses a geometry branch plus a geometry-conditioned motion branch that lifts image correspondences into 3D.
Achieves the best overall average rank on geometry benchmarks and competitive 2D/3D tracking and segmentation performance.
The full system has about 0.5B parameters and can process scenes with thousands of images despite training on at most 64 views.
The paper also describes its data and training recipe, design studies, and releases code and models.

papers.abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.
bullets: CBCT typically obscures non-calcified abnormalities, which are usually assessed with MRI.
A two-stage pipeline combines anatomy-focused 3D masked-autoencoder pretraining with automated, targeted cropping of the temporomandibular joint.
In 212 paired CBCT–MRI joints, the approach detected synovial effusion with ROC AUC 0.793 using patient-isolated cross-validation.
The signal emerged only with the proposed physics-guided pretraining and captured 3D anatomical chirality and intra-patient consistency.
The study supports opportunistic screening of occult soft-tissue disease from routine radiographic scans, demonstrated in the TMJ.

papers.title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
papers.tldr: Physics-guided self-supervised learning extracts MRI-verified soft-tissue pathology signals from routine CBCT scans despite limited paired data.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.
authors: Kailai Zhou, Ziqi Chen, Xiaoning Xu, Yuefeng Wu, Zixuan Fu, Zijun Lin, Zhihao Li, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Xun Cao, Bihan Wen
bullets: I-JEPA can improve semantic recognition while degrading 3D geometric representations.
CascadeJEPA addresses this by encoding full-grid spatial context and using cross-attention between cascaded prediction stages.
The approach largely preserves the original I-JEPA architecture while enabling richer patch-level interactions.
Experiments show substantial gains across multiple 3D geometric tasks without sacrificing strong semantic recognition.
Benefits also extend to future feature forecasting and world-model planning.

This unidirectional coupling promotes richer patch-level interactions while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture.

papers.abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.
bullets: LAS identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as key sources of generation difficulty and performance variation.
DSADiff combines these factors into a unified generation-difficulty representation.
The representation guides both feature modeling and training-strategy optimization across samples with different structures and difficulty levels.
Across three CSP benchmarks, including Carbon-24, DSADiff improves Match Rate and RMSE, with up to a 9% Match Rate gain.
The method reports new state-of-the-art performance and offers a framework for analyzing and reducing bias in complex materials spaces.
