papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.
bullets: Uses paired RGB–event recordings to match a frozen RGB teacher’s final tokens, avoiding depth and pose ground truth while training only about 1% of parameters.
Introduces sparsity-aware adaptive gating to adjust shared transformer refinement per patch according to event density.
Trained only on simulated data, it generalizes zero-shot to real MVSEC and DSEC data.
Reports the lowest pointmap error among evaluated event-based methods; on DSEC, it achieves 0.15 AbsRel versus 0.30 for the strongest baseline with about one-tenth the parameters.
Also obtains the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC, and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

papers.title: Déjà-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating

papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.
authors: Yiyuan Ge, Changxing Ding, Ziyu Hao, Zijie Zheng, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action-relevant supervision in unlabeled human videos for robot policy pretraining.
Lift aligns shallow policy features with intermediate representations from multiple 3D foundation models to create dense 3D representations.
See adds depth-map reconstruction and hand-region guidance for spatial understanding and task-relevant attention.
Act uses these representations for robotic manipulation across diverse simulated and real-world tasks.
The abstract reports significant gains over current state-of-the-art methods, without specifying quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview of LSA. (a) In the data engine phase, we utilize two 3D FMs to extract depth maps and camera intrinsics, respectively. Combined with the extracted 2D wrist coordinates, we obtain 3D hand motion trajectories. Furthermore, we also extract dense geometric representations and depth maps. (b) In the pretraining phase, we first align the policy’s shallow-layer representations with the intermediate representations of the two 3D FMs pre-computed during the data engine phase. Then, we introduce depth-map reconstruction to equip the model with precise structural knowledge, and utilize hand heatmaps to guide the model’s attention toward interaction hotspots. Following this, we predict the 3D hand motion trajectories. (c) Finally, we freeze the pretrained LSA and combine it with a policy head to perform closed-loop robotic control.

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.
authors: Yumin Zheng, Qingtian Zhu, Ziyan Zhu, Kailu Song, Yinqiang Zheng, Jun Ding
bullets: Addresses the challenge that serial ST data are dense within sections but sparse along the axial direction.
Uses a conditional implicit neural representation with graph-autoencoder latent compression, pseudo-label signature conditioning, and depth-dependent FiLM modulation.
Applies correlation alignment to encourage consistent cross-slice covariance in latent features.
Evaluations on held-out measured sections show improved reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation versus general-purpose INRs and adapted ST baselines.
Scope: designed for pre-registered ST sections and estimates, rather than directly measuring, continuous 3D expression.

papers.abstract: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.
authors: Bart M. N. Smets, Gijs Bellaard, Pieter Wils
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between overly restrictive built-in equivariance and costly data augmentation.
Introduces an architecture that can become equivariant to selected symmetry groups based on the training data.
Provides a post-training fingerprint indicating which symmetries are relevant and to what degree.
Demonstrates the architecture and fingerprinting process on image classification.

papers.abstract: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at https://github.com/guxiang2002/AerialOcc
authors: Fan Liu, Xiang Gu, Baoyu Lv, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuye Ma, Yuhui Zheng
bullets: Addresses the fragmentation of drone perception systems built around separate models or task-specific heads.
Represents spatial existence and semantics to connect coarse scene understanding with fine-grained object localization.
Introduces AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments.
Reports competitive performance across diverse perception tasks with one unified architecture.
Models and data are publicly available; specific quantitative results are not stated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at https://github.com/anwaarua/life4d.
bullets: Addresses the lack of validity estimates for geometry that has not been recently observed.
Models persistence, modification, growth, removal, and replacement using continuous-time, class-specific transition priors.
Combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence; functional anchors support prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies.
Reduces combined error and calibration error in controlled experiments and achieves 9.8% combined error with 0.016 ECE on Urb3DCD-v2, outperforming reported baselines.
Re-survey prioritisation provides only modest gains over random selection with two observations; code and an evaluation protocol are released.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Shanxin Yuan, Mona Jaber, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Addresses quadratic cross-frame attention costs and accuracy degradation on long videos.
Uses a training-free Pinned Key Set of 31 frames, cached once and reused by independently processed frames.
Supports online streaming by updating pinned frames during recording.
An Alignment Score detects failures, while Alignment Refocusing fine-tunes six global blocks to improve robustness.
On long ScanNet videos, it matches or improves baseline success rates while achieving substantially higher speed and scaling to thousands of frames on one GPU.

papers.abstract: Automated lidar feature detection from lidar point clouds can support archaeological surveys, but models trained in one landscape may transfer poorly to another because of differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition characteristics, and feature morphology. We address this problem for cross-region detection of ancient terraces using transductive unsupervised domain adaptation that exploits an unlabelled target survey. We propose MELD (Multi-level Embedding-space Latent Diffusion), which trains separate diffusion denoisers on target-domain representations at four hierarchical PointNet++ feature levels. These target distribution priors are then used to refine source representations during supervised training and target representations during inference, allowing adaptation to act directly on the multi-scale features consumed by the segmentation decoder. We additionally investigate local geometric descriptors derived from K-nearest-neighbour neighbourhoods, including surface normals, slope, and aspect. MELD is evaluated bidirectionally between the Teyuna and Miraflores lidar surveys in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia, against a source-only model and nine configurations of established domain adaptation approaches. MELD raises F1 over the source-only model from 0.397 to 0.459 for Teyuna-to-Miraflores transfer and from 0.557 to 0.594 in the reverse direction, achieving the highest F1 among the evaluated adaptation methods in both directions. Adding local geometry further raises F1 to 0.542 and 0.606, respectively. Multi-level ablation shows that refining all four PointNet++ levels provides the strongest performance in both directions. These results show that explicit modelling of target feature distributions in hierarchical point cloud feature space, complemented by local geometry, provides an effective route to cross-region archaeological mapping without target labels.
authors: Sina Mohammadi, Roderik Lindenbergh, Javier Ruiz-P\'erez, Marco Madella, Sebastian Fajardo
bullets: Addresses poor transfer caused by differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition, and terrace morphology.
Uses transductive unsupervised adaptation with an unlabelled target survey and diffusion denoisers at four PointNet++ feature levels.
Refines source features during training and target features during inference, with optional local geometry descriptors such as normals, slope, and aspect.
Across bidirectional Teyuna–Miraflores transfer, F1 improves from 0.397 to 0.459 and from 0.557 to 0.594; local geometry raises these to 0.542 and 0.606.
All four hierarchical feature levels perform best in ablation, supporting multi-scale target-distribution modelling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: High-level overview of the MELD framework. During joint training, unlabeled target/test features train the level-specific diffusion denoisers, while labeled source features are refined by the target-trained denoisers and decoded under source ground-truth supervision. The diffusion loss updates the denoisers, whereas the segmentation loss updates PointNet++ through the straight-through refinement path. A held-out source-validation set ranks checkpoints by adapted validation F1. At inference, the top three paired PointNet++ denoiser checkpoints are applied independently to all target/test points using deterministic target-guided DDIM refinement; their terrace-class probabilities are averaged point-wise and thresholded at 0.5 to obtain the final binary prediction. No target labels are used for adaptation or checkpoint selection. Preprocessing and the PointNet++ backbone are detailed in Figure 3, target domain latent diffusion adaptation in Figure 4, and source-feature refinement with the straight-through estimator in Figure 5; adapted inference is described in Section 3.5.

Figure 3: PointNet++ segmentation backbone. Each 20m × 20m point cloud tile is converted by sampling or padding into a fixed 4096-point input patch, which is then normalized. The patch may contain either only xyz coordinates (C = 3) or xyz coordinates augmented with optional KNN-derived geometric features (C = 9), including normals, slope, and sine/cosine of aspect. The encoder comprises four set-abstraction (SA) layers that progressively reduce the number of points while increasing feature dimensionality, producing hierarchical latent features Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4. The decoder then uses four feature-propagation (FP) stages with interpolation and skip connections to recover pointwise features at the original resolution. A per-point classification head, implemented with 1× 1 convolutions, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout, and log-softmax, produces per-point class log-probabilities; applying exp(·) yields the corresponding per-point class probabilities. The generic Zl notation used in this figure denotes the multi-level encoder features that serve as latent representations in the target-adaptation and source-refinement stages, where they are written explicitly as Zl tar and Zl src in Figures 4 and 5, respectively.

Figure 1: Reference terrace annotations for the two study regions. Left: Teyuna (Ciudad Perdida); right: Miraflores. Reference terrace annotations are shown over the labelled study extents. Mapped terraces cover approximately 6.5% of the labelled Teyuna extent and approximately 1.5% of the Miraflores extent.

Figure 5: Source refinement for supervised segmentation training. A labeled sourcedomain input patch Xsrc is passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain hierarchical latent features Zl src for l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each feature level, the encoder output is tokenized into U l 0,src, partially noised to a shared starting depth tl0, and then refined token-wise through a deterministic DDIM reverse process using the level-specific target-trained denoiser Dl. The refined token matrix Ũ l 0,src is unflattened to Z̃l src and supplied to the decoder through a straight-through estimator (STE), so that the decoder uses the refined features in the forward pass while segmentation gradients flow back to the original encoder features during backpropagation. The decoder output is supervised by the source ground-truth labels using the class-weighted NLL loss Lseg. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are refined. During training, source refinement is stochastic overall because the initial Gaussian perturbation is sampled randomly, whereas the subsequent DDIM reverse trajectory is deterministic conditional on the resulting partially noised token.

Figure 4: target domain latent diffusion adaptation. Unlabeled target domain input patches Xtar are passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain multi-level latent features Zl tar, l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each level, the target features are detached from the backbone and flattened into token matrices U l 0,tar, so the target domain diffusion objective does not propagate gradients into PointNet++. Each token is independently assigned a diffusion timestep tli and perturbed with Gaussian noise according to the forward diffusion process. A level-specific denoiser Dl(·, ·;ϕl), conditioned on the noisy token and its timestep embedding, predicts the added noise. Within each level, the same denoiser is shared across all tokens, while denoiser parameters are not shared between feature levels. The level-wise noise-prediction losses are computed as mean-squared error between the sampled and predicted noise and are combined into the total diffusion loss Ldiff . Consequently, target domain adaptation updates only the denoiser parameters ϕl, allowing the denoisers to learn the latent feature distribution of the unlabeled target domain for subsequent source-feature refinement and adapted inference. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are active; the level-ablation experiments use the corresponding subsets of these levels.15

Figure 6: Precision–recall curves for the three principal configurations, averaged over three random seeds. The left panel shows Teyuna → Miraflores and the right panel Miraflores → Teyuna. Solid lines show the mean across three random seeds, and shaded regions indicate one standard deviation across seeds. The compared configurations are sourceonly PointNet++, MELD, and MELD+geometry.

Table 1: Cross-region terrace detection (point level, all points): F1 as mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. Single applies adaptation at the deepest level (l = 4); multi at all four levels (l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}). Mean is the unweighted average of the two directions. Best result per column in bold. The target-only oracle (italic) is an in-domain supervised reference trained with five-fold cross-validation on the evaluation region of each direction; it is not a competing UDA method and is reported for context only.

Table 2: MELD level ablation: effect of activating diffusion adaptation at different PointNet++ feature levels (no KNN features; adaptation enabled). The first column lists the active level set. F1 as mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. Best result per column in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MELD, a multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation method for cross-region point cloud segmentation, effectively combining 3D perception with foundation model techniques.
papers.title: Multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation for cross-region point cloud segmentation of ancient terraces
papers.tldr: MELD adapts lidar point-cloud terrace segmentation across archaeological regions by refining hierarchical features with target-domain latent diffusion, improving cross-region F1 without target labels.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
authors: Muhammed Izzet Sezer, Sevval Belkis Dikkaya
bullets: Global attention in multi-view 3D transformers is costly because its complexity grows quadratically with the number of images.
The study identifies three layer roles: scene-wide averaging, cross-image point matching, and anchoring to the first image.
RAWATTA uses 8-bit attention by default and retains 16-bit precision when a worst-case calibration check requires it.
RAWATTA-Fast additionally approximates attention in selected averaging and anchoring layers while preserving full keys for matching layers and the first image.
On VGGT, RAWATTA is faster than the released implementation, loses at most about one AUC@3 pose-accuracy point, and supports 200 images on a 12 GB GPU where the baseline runs out of memory at 100.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free attention approximation for multi-view 3D transformers, improving efficiency while preserving accuracy, relevant to efficient AI and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.tldr: RAWATTA accelerates multi-view 3D transformers without retraining by adapting attention precision and approximation to each layer’s functional regime.

papers.abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.
authors: Zhuangzhuang Ma, Rukuan Chai, Qianqian Ma, Yanghua Wang, Branko Bijeljic, Martin J. Blunt
bullets: Addresses noisy, low-contrast CT images where conventional segmentation requires image-specific manual tuning and independent 3D models can confuse segmentation errors with physical change.
Combines spatial and temporal information in a 4D transformer framework to resolve ambiguous phase assignments across image sequences.
More accurately measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries than a comparable spatial-only 3D model in mineral-dissolution experiments.
Captures permeability increases consistent with reference segmentations and flow simulations, and transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining.
Reduces spurious rock and porosity fluctuations while identifying filling events in fluid-displacement datasets.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework for micro-CT images that leverages spatiotemporal information. This applies foundation model architectures (transformers) to 3D vision tasks, specifically segmentation.
papers.title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
papers.tldr: A transformer-based spatiotemporal segmentation method uses information across time to more reliably quantify pore evolution and fluid displacement in time-resolved micro-CT images.

papers.abstract: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.
authors: Sheng Tang, Shengzhe Wei, Tiancheng Chen, Wenhua Jin, Xinyang Lu, Tinghao Jiang, Shuoxuan Feng, Yupeng Liu, Yu Zhang, Xingshuo Chang, Keren Zhou, Yuhan Xiong, Jiahao Li, Haoming Liu, Jituo Tian, Hui Liang, Chaoqun Tang, Feng Tian, Wentao Ouyang, Kaojin Zhu, Xiaolin Chai, Peihuang Fu, Miao Zheng, Yunbo Hu, Feixue Cai, Zizhen Zou, Weigang Wang, Yexuan Yang, Haoyu Feng, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Targets scene-level camera pose, geometry, and dynamic 3D reconstruction from images and videos.
GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, dynamic 3D points, and scene flow.
PoseEngine refines these predictions through geometric optimization for downstream 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting.
Achieves best reported depth, relative-pose, dynamic-point, and scene-flow metrics across the evaluated benchmarks.
PoseEngine is substantially faster than GLUEMAP in the reported comparison, with Flash offering a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.
authors: Linda Forster, Nicholas J. LaHaye, Marcin J. Kurowski, Anna Jungbluth, Bernhard Mayer, Anthony B. Davis
bullets: Addresses uncertainty in climate predictions caused by limited measurements of low-level cloud internal structure.
An ML emulator converts radiances from nine viewing angles into cloud optical-thickness projections, which SART inverts into 3D extinction.
Trained using radiative-transfer simulations of synthetic 3D cloud fields.
Reaches 13.3 km⁻¹ RMSE in 3.5 seconds, versus 22.7 km⁻¹ in about 30 minutes for AT3D—over 500× faster.
Scope: the approach is demonstrated with synthetic training observations and aims to support scalable cloud-structure observations.

papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
authors: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna B\"o{\ss}end\"orfer, Mirko M\"ahlisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
bullets: Targets ground-to-aerial localization when GNSS is unreliable, especially in forests, fields, and rural tracks.
Provides 9,356 georeferenced scenes near Munich across four seasons, pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and 3D LiDAR.
Includes paved/unpaved terrain labels and seasonal variation to study terrain structure and appearance gaps.
Fine-tuned state-of-the-art baselines degrade substantially off-road, while the proposed RGB–LiDAR baseline improves localization performance.
Data and baselines are publicly released for future research.

papers.abstract: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
bullets: Addresses limited latent capacity for modeling fine details in complex 3D objects.
Uses continuous coordinate-based scene representations to tokenize arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference.
Explores trade-offs among compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality through ablations.
Achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits.
Also supports high-quality generative modeling with an autoregressive 3D generator.

figures.caption: Figure 6 Qualitative generation comparison. A generative model trained on split-and-scale can reproduce fine details. In contrast, competitor methods suffer from either poor detail or poor material estimation. Asset credits (wribeast, 2020; slasmir, 2020; bobrik00, 2020).

Figure 5 Qualitative reconstruction comparison. Figure 3 Quantitative comparison versus naive token count scaling. We train a split-and-scale model that outputs 1024 latents per voxel. We compare with LiTo-1024, LiTo-8192, LiTo-32768 that use 1024, 8192, 32768 tokens during training, respectively. We also evaluate these models with naive inference-time scaling. Note that training LiTo-32768 requires larger memory than all other methods, and its training takes 2.7× more time. All models are trained to the same number of iterations. As shown, the performance of the proposed method (blue curve) increases consistently as we increase number of tokens during inference, whereas naive scaling quickly hits bottleneck.
Figure 8 Quantitative geometry comparison versus naive token count scaling. We compare the quality of sampled point clouds from split-and-scale versus comparable LiTo models (Chang et al., 2026).

Figure 9 Quantitative comparison versus naive token count scaling. Following the recipe in Section 3.2, we train a split-and-scale model that outputs 1024 latents per voxel at inference. For comparison, we train 1024 and 8192 token LiTo models (Chang et al., 2026) that use a similar amount of memory/compute during training. In both (a) equal compute time and (b) equal iteration scenarios, split-and-scale can be seen to scale with token count better than the baseline models. Although it cannot be trained within the memory limits of an 80GB GPU, we include a 32768 token variant of LiTo (Chang et al., 2026) as a performance upper-bound; split-and-scale is still competitive.

Figure 4 Visualization of our proposed generation procedure. To reduce memory requirements, we propose autoregressive voxel-based generation with flow matching-based sampling and cross-attention conditioning. Given an input image, we start by first generating coarse 43 occupancy. For the occupied voxels, we then autoregressively sample voxel latents conditioned on previously-generated latents, until all voxels are filled. Asset credit (Studio, 2022).

Figure 2 Naive scaling vs. split-and-scale. (Left) Naive scaling increases number of latents by using more queries to the tokenizer. As the tokenizer is not trained with the higher number of queries, the quality improvement is limited. (Right) Split-and-scale encodes/decodes subregions of the scene with the same tokenizer/decoder and the designed number of queries, effectively increasing latent capacity. Figure 1 Split-and-scale reuses the same tokenizer across spatial scales to effectively increase latent capacity at inference time. Recommend viewing the figure on monitor, zoomed in. Asset credit (Cherchye, 2016).

Figure 7 Failure cases. (a) In tokenization, because each voxel is independently processed, subtle seams can appear in areas with significant view-dependent appearance. papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
bullets: Addresses failures of existing 4DGS methods on splitting, merging, opening, and closing interactions.
Introduces TopoEgo, a benchmark covering fission, fusion, opening, and closing in egocentric video.
Assigns independent rigid motion to interacting parts and activates or deactivates Gaussians as surfaces change.
Outperforms existing 4DGS approaches across topological changes, particularly in post-event frames.
Code and data are planned for public release.

Topological Boundary Resolution creates support for newly formed or exposed surfaces and temporally deactivates obsolete or concealed support.

papers.abstract: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.
bullets: Targets task-specific monocular geometry architectures with a unified, scalable alternative.
Uses one backbone to jointly denoise, reason about, and understand images and depth.
Supports image-plus-depth generation, depth estimation from photographs, and image synthesis conditioned on depth.
At sufficient scale, surpasses specialist models on established depth benchmarks while retaining generative capabilities.
Releases two models for community use.

papers.abstract: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.
bullets: Targets engineering studies with limited simulations, where conventional surrogates must be retrained for each problem.
Uses procedural priors over generic laws and boundary-element models on morphed 2D/3D meshes, with quantile field predictions from context examples.
Handles variable context sizes, scalar inputs, input/output fields, mesh sizes, and mesh connectivity in a single checkpoint.

On five unseen PLAID datasets, error improves with more context and beats the nearest context simulation from K=32; performance matches reduced-order models on two datasets but trails them for low-rank fields.
Maintains low peak memory on million-node AhmedML meshes; geometry/load-specific procedural fine-tuning reduces 2D_M​​SHE stress error by 2.7× without using target outputs.

papers.abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
authors: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Jiale Cao
bullets: Benchmarks 242 tasks across scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos.
Scores both hidden scene facts via rule-based checks and their visibility in rendered proxy videos via VLM judgment.
Analysis covers 11 frontier coding agents and finds multimodal understanding—especially space and camera motion—strongly differentiates performance.
Agents handle basic staging and camera work but struggle with challenging requests and rarely correct errors after inspecting renders.
Results motivate stronger spatial/camera reasoning, explicit checks, and item-by-item render verification.

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.
authors: Hong Shang, Zijian Zhan, Sen Jia, Xiang Fan, Jintao Meng, Yang Zhou, Xiang Zhou, Tianyu He, Xinran Chen, Qiaoling Zeng, Keyan Yu, Jianhua Yao, Dong Liang
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of deep-learning MRI reconstruction caused by limited, biased, and costly clinical data.
Co-designs simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms to replace historical data scaling with compute scaling.
Evaluated across 14 public and in-house datasets spanning multiple centers, vendors, field strengths, anatomies, protocols, and downstream tasks.
Reports recovery of fine anatomical detail and suppression of aliasing artifacts where conventional methods fail, including a blinded radiologist study.
Attention analyses suggest the model learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SIM, a compute-scalable framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction. a, The physics-simulated data engine transforms arbitrary images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements (X) and ground-truth targets (Y ). This pipeline strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics to align simulated and real measurement characteristics, effectively closing the simulation-to-real gap. Simultaneously, it expands image and acquisition diversity to overcome historical data bottlenecks, enabling models to learn fundamental inverse mappings. b, SIM adopts the multi-channel Vision Transformer (mcViT)—a high-capacity architecture with minimal MRI-specific inductive bias—to absorb diverse simulated data and learn robust reconstruction priors at scale, replacing hand-crafted architectures designed for data-scarce regimes. c, Pairing large-scale simulated data with high-capacity architecture reveals power-law scaling relationships with dataset size, model size, and patch count, mirroring scaling behaviors in natural language and vision. Crucially, these scaling gains transfer directly to real clinical data, confirming that the simulation engine effectively bridges the simulation-to-real gap. d, Comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across public and in-house datasets—spanning diverse scanner hardware, populations, anatomies, protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular imaging tasks, and a clinical reader study—demonstrates that SIM achieves vastly superior generalizability over traditional real-data learning paradigms.

Fig. 3 Scaling laws in reconstruction. a, In-distribution scaling for simulated data. Reconstruction performance improves smoothly as dataset and model size increase in tandem. Scaling model size yields sustained performance gains when not bottlenecked by data diversity, analogous to scaling laws observed in LLMs[48]. b, In-distribution scaling for real fastMRI. Scaling model size fails due to pronounced overfitting (Extended Data Fig. A1b) from inadequate data diversity; despite comparable dataset size to simulated data, real fastMRI exhibits high inter-dataset similarity. c, Transfer scaling comparing training data. Scaling behavior learned on simulated data transfers effectively to diverse real-world datasets, successfully bridging the sim-to-real gap. Real fastMRI alone shows no scaling benefit and transfers poorly to OOD test sets; combining fastMRI with simulated data restores OOD scaling, demonstrating that high-diversity simulated data are essential to unlock scaling laws in MRI reconstruction. d, Transfer scaling comparing model architectures. When trained on 1.1 million simulated samples, conventional architectures designed for small-data regimes with hard-coded domain priors (such as E2EVarNet) are outperformed on OOD test sets by mcViT—a generic Vision Transformer with minimal inductive bias—underscoring the need to co-design data and models for scaling regimes. Experiments in a–c utilize mcViT. Across a–d, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. ID, in-distribution.

Fig. 4 Zero-shot reconstruction. a, Quantitative comparison. Both SIM and SIM-Zero (trained exclusively on simulated data) outperform all competing baselines across 8 out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks, with SIM exceeding the top baseline by 1.06–3.95 dB in PSNR and 0.008–0.045 in SSIM, and SIM-Zero performing only marginally below SIM. Error bars indicate mean ± s.d. Full comparisons against 9 state-of-the-art methods are in Extended Data Fig. A3. ID, in-distribution. b, Qualitative comparison. Representative reconstructions, error maps, and reference images. SIM recovers fine anatomical detail matching ground truth without perceptible aliasing artifacts (see Extended Data Fig. A4 for additional visual comparisons). XGY, Xingaoyi. c, Cross-protocol transfer. Models were trained on fastMRI Brain data partitioned by protocol (T1, contrast-enhanced T1 [CE], T2, FLAIR). E2EVarNet trained on real data exhibits a diagonal performance, degrading on unobserved protocols due to overfitting. Conversely, SIM displays uniform performance across protocols due to domain-agnostic simulated data. Across a–c, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 2 Data simulation pipeline, feature representation, and ablation study. a, Data simulation pipeline. The workflow transforms arbitrary natural images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements and ground-truth targets. The physical mapping between measurement and target strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics. FT, Fourier transform; iFT, inverse Fourier transform; rss, root-sum-of-squares. b, Data visualization in a shared representation space. While real datasets show a clustered distribution with limited diversity, simulated data display diverse local contrast patterns relevant to clinical imaging at the patch level. Each dot represents a 14 × 14 image patch in the DINOv2 feature space[55] after dimension reduction using principal component analysis and linear discriminant analysis to two primary discriminant axes, color-coded by dataset source. LDA, linear discriminant analysis. c, Ablation study demonstrating the effectiveness of key simulated data design features in closing the simulation-to-real gap, as well as the impact of model architectural choices and learning objectives engineered to leverage simulated training data. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 8 Visualization of SIM attention maps. a, Attention maps of individual heads across layers, demonstrating that SIM intrinsically captures generic image structures and spatial relationships tied to undersampling physics via large-scale domain-agnostic training, thereby achieving physically explainable and broadly generalizable reconstruction. b, Attention maps aggregated across all layers and heads, showing that SIM dynamically adapts its attention to aliasing source regions as changes in acceleration alter the spatial aliasing distance. Two example query patches are shown under effective acceleration factors of 3.2× and 4.2×. For a and b, arrows and boxes on input images indicate query patches. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 5 Zero-shot quantitative MRI. a,b, Representative single-echo reconstructions, derived T ∗ 2 maps, and corresponding error maps evaluated on the public AHEAD dataset (MP2RAGEME sequence, Philips 7 T) (a) and an in-house cohort (MULTIPLEX sequence, UIH 3 T) (b). SIM’s zero-shot capability enables reliable downstream parametric mapping. Skull stripping is applied, and display windowing and leveling are adjusted per echo image and matched between reconstructions and reference images. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. c, Quantitative comparison of T ∗ 2 mapping across all slices evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1×. SIM consistently outperforms baselines across sequences and acceleration factors. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 7 Zero-shot clinical applications. a, Representative reconstructions of SIM and E2EVarNet at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1× for an in-house Alzheimer’s disease cohort with three contrasts: T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and T2-FLAIR. Red arrows indicate residual aliasing artifacts. b,c, Quantitative evaluation in terms of PSNR (b) and SSIM (c). papers.selection_reason: Introduces Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework using physics-simulated data to achieve zero-shot generalization for MRI reconstruction across diverse scanners and populations.
papers.title: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction
papers.tldr: SIM uses physics-based simulated MRI data and scalable learning to enable robust zero-shot reconstruction across diverse scanners, anatomies, protocols, and clinical settings.

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.
authors: Jiayun Wang, Ram Daftari, Weijie Gan, Valentin Duruisseaux, Ruibo Wang, Armeet Singh Jatyani, Boris Bonev, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Addresses the high GPU cost of full-volume 3D MRI reconstruction, which often leads to slice-wise 2D processing that misses through-plane structure.
Uses resolution-agnostic neural operators with continuous-basis 3D convolutions that can be sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions.
Combines a k-space neural-operator head with image-space operator cascades and interleaved physics-based data consistency.
Trained on low-resolution volumes and deployed directly at higher resolution without retraining.
Outperforms classical and CNN baselines across knee and brain MRI benchmarks; gains over a 3D CNN reach 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4× acceleration on SKM-TEA, and persist at 8× and 16×.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a–c) Three deep learning architectures for 3D MRI reconstruction. (a) 2D CNN: GPUmemory limits force slice-wise 2D models that stack into a volume, losing inter-slice consistency. (b) 3D CNN: fixed discrete kernels are tied to the training grid, so cross-resolution transfer is unreliable. (c) 3D Neural Operator (KIR-NO, ours): discretization-agnostic — trained on memoryfriendly coarse volumes and deployed at higher resolutions without retraining. (d) Resolution robustness: PSNR at quarter/half/full resolution on SKM-TEA (quarter-trained); KIR-NO leads throughout. (e) Convergence (SKM-TEA, half-res, 4×): first epoch to reach each PSNR threshold; KIR-NO reaches 34 dB ∼6× faster than the 3D CNN. (f) Qualitative: a knee slice with error maps for 2D CNN, 3D CNN, and KIR-NO; KIR-NO has the lowest residual.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on knee (top) and brain (bottom) MRI reconstruction. Reconstructions of a representative slice with corresponding error maps (warmer colors indicate larger residuals). All models are trained and evaluated on half resolution data. The top left number is the PSNR (dB) on the shown slice. The ground truth (GT) is compared to classical baselines (Zero-Filled, ℓ1-Wavelet) and learned baselines — 2D E2E-VarNet, 3D E2E-VarNet, and our KIRNO. Classical methods show strong aliasing; KIR-NO has the smallest residuals on both samples. Dataset-level results are in Tables 1 and 2.

Figure 2: Our KIR-NO architecture. Undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements k̃ are first refined by a k-space neural-operator head NOk (Eq. 1), then mapped to image space (inverse Fourier transform F−1 and coil combination) and refined by an unrolled cascade of image-space neural operators NOi (Eq. 2, where ℓ indexes the cascade) interleaved with data-consistency updates, producing the final 3D reconstruction x̂. Operator layers learn continuous kernels built on discrete-continuous convolutions, in contrast to fixed-resolution conventional CNN kernels.

Figure 3: 3D Morlet-wavelet DISCO basis. Left: cross-section slices through individual basis functions. Right: a 3D DISCO kernel formed as a learned linear combination of these functions. The discretization shown is for illustration only; the basis is continuous, so the same learned coefficients can be sampled at any target resolution.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes KIR-NO, a resolution-agnostic neural operator framework for 3D MRI reconstruction, enabling effective coarse-to-fine training and deployment across different resolutions.
papers.title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
papers.tldr: KIR-NO enables memory-efficient low-resolution training of full 3D MRI reconstruction models that transfer zero-shot to higher-resolution scans.

papers.abstract: In the era of large models, stereo matching is developing towards generalizable foundation models trained on million-scale synthetic images. However, how model performance scales up with synthetic data is still underexplored. In this work, we preliminarily investigate the in-domain and cross-domain data scaling laws in stereo matching. A realistic synthetic dataset, named XStereo, containing 200 thousand samples is first built to serve as a high-quality benchmark for data scaling research. In-domain training on five large-scale datasets demonstrate a two-regime scaling behavior with data, transitioning from the standard power law to saturation, where the critical transition point is approximately invariant under a fixed model. Cross-domain performance exhibits a substantially weaker and less predictable dependence on the source-domain data scale. The distribution and coverage diversity are more effective for diminishing domain gaps. More instructive suggestions are provided for high-efficiency data construction and training. The insightful findings are significant verification and extension of the existing scaling laws in both language and vision, paving the way to efficient and stronger stereo matching. The XStereo dataset is public at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Tong-Zhao/XStereo.
bullets: Introduces XStereo, a realistic synthetic benchmark with 200,000 samples for studying stereo data scaling.
Finds two in-domain scaling regimes: a power-law improvement followed by saturation.
Reports that the transition point is approximately stable for a fixed model.
Shows cross-domain performance depends weakly and unpredictably on source-domain data size.
Suggests prioritizing distribution diversity and coverage for efficient data construction and training.
