papers.selection_reason: Stereo matching scaling laws and dataset support generalizable 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Data Scaling Laws in Stereo Matching: From In-domain Fitting to Cross-domain Generalization
papers.tldr: The study shows that stereo-matching performance follows predictable scaling with in-domain synthetic data but is less predictable across domains, where diversity and coverage matter more than scale alone.

papers.abstract: Radar systems can recover scene geometry and recognize predefined categories, but these outputs do not provide a persistent spatial representation for open-ended language queries. Such queries require linking observations from different viewpoints to the same physical locations. We present TextRadar, a framework that constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from panoramic radar observations. The field combines occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations, allowing the reconstructed scene to be queried with new descriptions. A single-frame radar distillation model predicts aligned ranges and language features from each radar observation. Using radar-estimated poses, we register these predictions to reconstruct the field from radar alone in a new scene. Experiments on approximately 20k synchronized observations across seven buildings demonstrate scene-level natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization. Analysis of camera-to-radar concept transferability shows stronger agreement for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially persistent, language-queryable representations in radar-based scene understanding.
Distills each radar observation into aligned geometry and language features, then registers them using radar-estimated poses.
Constructs a scene-level field combining occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations.
Demonstrates natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization across seven buildings and about 20k synchronized observations.
Concept transfer is stronger for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

figures.caption: Fig. 13 Overview of the TextRadar framework. A rotating mmWave radar provides high-resolution panoramic RF measurements, while a front-facing camera supplies multiscale language supervision during data collection. Building on these inputs, TextRadar jointly learns geometry and language-aligned embedding from RF measurements and builds a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field, which supports several tasks.

Fig. 3 Scene-level natural-language querying of small structures and objects. The field localizes architectural structures, including (a) “Stairs” and (b) “Windows,” as well as compact objects, including (c) “Trash bin” and (d) “Human.” The RGB images provide representative observations of the queried regions, with dashed boxes indicating the corresponding targets. For categories with multiple instances, such as stairs and windows, the system simultaneously highlights geometrically separated regions throughout the scene.

Fig. 2 Scene-level natural-language querying of large building structures. The reconstructed geometry is colored according to the cosine similarity between the scene-level feature at each surface point and the CLIP text embedding of the query. Warmer colors indicate higher semantic relevance. The queries (a) “Ceiling” and (b) “Floor” activate complementary upper and lower surfaces across multiple corridors and room regions. The spatially coherent responses over distant parts of the environment show how the persistent occupancy-language field associates related structures across a common 3D coordinate system.

Fig. 5 Natural-language querying of high-level concepts. The prompts describe human configuration, affordances, and functional regions: (a) “Standing” localizes a standing person, (b) “Going down” highlights a descending staircase, (c) “Things to sit” retrieves a bench and other seating, (d) “Taking a rest” identifies a shared seating area, (e) “Entrance to other places” highlights doorways and passages, and (f) “Working region” identifies the occupied workspace in a laboratory office. These examples show responses to contextual prompts beyond direct object and material names.

Fig. 9 Radar-camera feature disagreement. The top row highlights concepts dominated by visual content: (a) televisions and monitors, (b) information signs, and (c) exhibition boards. The bottom row highlights appearance-dependent concepts: (d) ribbed texture, (e) yellow color, and (f) roughness and grid patterns. Dashed boxes mark the relevant regions in the RGB observations. While the camera-derived features clearly distinguish these regions by displayed content, color, or fine surface appearance, the radar-predicted features often assign them similar embeddings and thus fail to distinguish them.

Fig. 1 TextRadar constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from radar observations. A robot collects panoramic mmWave measurements along a trajectory (left). Surface geometry and language features predicted from these measurements are integrated in shared 3D coordinates (center). The right panels illustrate natural-language querying, prompt-free semantic visualization, and camera-to-radar concept transferability. The query “Things to sit” highlights a bench, while the feature visualization reveals semantic organization without specifying a prompt. Comparisons of radarpredicted and camera-derived features show stronger agreement for structures, objects, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

Fig. 8 Prompt-free semantic visualization of material-related regions. The examples show (a) wood doors, (b) a glass window, and (c) a metal cabinet. The highlighted material regions occupy distinct portions of the projected feature space and therefore appear with colors different from their surrounding walls and structures. The agreement between the radar-predicted and camera-derived PCA images indicates material-related information being retained beyond range geometry alone.

Fig. 6 Prompt-free semantic visualization of general indoor structures. For each example, the rows from top to bottom present the rendered panoramic RGB image, the predicted range image, the three-component PCA projection of the radar-predicted CLIP features, and the corresponding camera-derived reference projection. The predicted and reference features are projected using a shared PCA basis, and the three principal components are mapped to RGB channels. Similar colors therefore indicate nearby positions in the projected semantic feature space, rather than predefined semantic classes. Large structural regions, including ceilings, floors, walls, corridor openings, and wall-mounted structures, form spatially coherent groups in the radar-predicted visualization and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference.

Fig. 4 Geometry and natural-language queries. Each example shows, from top to bottom, the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the range image predicted from the radar measurement, the query-relevancy map obtained from the radarpredicted CLIP-aligned features, and the corresponding map obtained from the camera-derived reference features. Warmer colors indicate higher cosine similarity to the text query. The queries cover materials, including (a) “Glass,” (b) “Metal,” and (c) “Marble”; objects, including (d) “Trash bin,” (e) “Chairs,” and (f) “Human”; and structures, including (g) “Stairs,” (h) “Floor,” and (i) “Ceiling.” The radar-predicted maps localize both compact objects and extended structural regions, remain spatially consistent with the recovered geometry, and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference maps.

Fig. 7 Prompt-free semantic visualization of structures and objects. The examples examine (a) stairs, (b) humans, and (c) chairs, with two scenes shown for each concept. The dashed boxes in the rendered RGB image indicate the structures or objects of interest. A shared PCA projection is used for each prediction-reference comparison, allowing their color organization to be compared directly. Stairs, human silhouettes, and individual chairs emerge as coherent regions whose boundaries follow the corresponding geometry, despite some differences in their sizes, shapes, and spatial extents.

Fig. 11 Example scenarios in our dataset. The dataset spans common indoor environments, including hallways, lounges, offices, classrooms, and open floor areas. These examples are captured by the front-facing camera on the robot and illustrate the visual context used to generate language supervision.

Fig. 12 Radar-camera feature disagreement around glass. Each column presents one example, and the rows show the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the radar-predicted range image, and the pixelwise cosine similarity between radarpredicted and camera-derived CLIP features. Dashed orange boxes indicate glass windows. Warmer colors represent stronger feature agreement, and cooler colors represent weaker agreement. Similarity decreases around the indicated glass regions, where the two sensors observe different scene content.

Fig. 10 Hardware platform for data collection. The mobile robot carries a rotating mmWave MIMO radar, a 3D LiDAR, and a front-facing camera. A stepper motor rotates the radar, while the battery and WiFi router rotate with the radar to prevent cable twisting and are placed behind it for weight balancing. Radar commands are sent through the wireless router. (a) Front view. (b) Rear view.
Table 2 Per-building radar-camera concept agreement. Each building is the held-out test split in the leave-one-building-out protocol.

Table 1 Category-wise radar-camera concept agreement. Camera-derived CLIP relevancy is the reference signal, and every property is evaluated within the entity that carries it. Values are means over the seven held-out buildings and the complete prompt bank.
Table 3 Per-building geometry and multiscale CLIP feature prediction in held-out environments. Each building is evaluated as the held-out test split in the leave-one-building-out protocol.

Table 4 Model and decoder ablation for range and CLIP feature prediction. We compare a transformer-based dense prediction model, a CNN with separate task decoders, and our CNN with a shared decoder. Metrics are averaged over all held-out buildings and, for cosine similarity, all five scales.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TextRadar, a framework for constructing 3D occupancy-language fields from mmWave radar, enabling natural language querying of 3D scenes.
papers.title: 3D Occupancy-Language Fields from mmWave Radar
papers.tldr: TextRadar builds a persistent 3D occupancy-language representation from panoramic mmWave radar, enabling open-ended natural-language scene queries without cameras.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems need geometric perception that exploits available observations beyond images alone. Recent feed-forward 3D models incorporate geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and depth. However, handling noisy poses, preserving accurate priors, and recovering physical scale require more than simply accepting these inputs. We introduce \emph{Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded Transformer} (VPGGT), a VGGT-based framework that extends OmniVGGT for prior-aware embodied perception. We formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from ground-truth trajectories for training and introduce a parameter-free \emph{prior residual connection} (PRC) to mitigate \emph{prior dilution}, where predictions are less accurate than their supplied pose priors. Our noise formulation targets camera poses; supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption. We further introduce \emph{Metric Global Attention}, which conditions a global scale token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared metric scaling factor for the geometric outputs. Experiments across four datasets show that \emph{PRC} improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC over a matched training baseline when camera priors are provided for all views, under both exact and corrupted poses. These results support explicit prior access during refinement as a useful addition to feature-level conditioning.
bullets: Addresses noisy camera poses, prior dilution, and missing physical scale in prior-aware geometric perception.
Introduces sensor-motivated camera-pose corruption for training while leaving supplied intrinsics and depth uncorrupted.
Adds a parameter-free Prior Residual Connection to retain and refine pose priors explicitly.
Uses Metric Global Attention to predict a shared scale factor from available pose and depth scales.
Across four datasets, PRC improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC with exact or corrupted pose priors.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VPGGT. Images and optional camera or depth priors are encoded and processed by a shared alternating-attention backbone. PRC places available camera priors in the camera head’s refinement state after its initial prediction. A Scale Encoder conditions a global token on available metric-scale statistics, using learned placeholders when they are absent. The camera, depth, and pointmap heads predict geometry, and a scale head supplies a shared factor that converts translations, depths, and points to metric units.

Figure 5: Pose-prior corruption in the training data. Two examples are shown for each dataset. Within each panel, the left plot displays the complete trajectory, while the right plot displays a selected segment of the same ground-truth and corrupted trajectories. Colors identify the ground truth and corruption realizations, as indicated by the plot legends. Ground-truth and corrupted poses share a coordinate system, without independently fitted trajectory or scale alignment. Spatial units and segment information are provided in the plots.

Figure 2: Prior dilution during camera refinement. A0 is released OmniVGGT; A1 uses the same checkpoint with PRC enabled, without additional training. All views receive camera priors; no depth is supplied. Colors distinguish methods and markers distinguish datasets. Dashed lines show input-prior scores. Reset is a state intervention, not a learned iteration.
Figure 4: Prior Residual Connection. PRC retains feature-level conditioning and supplies aligned camera priors as the state from which subsequent residual updates are predicted.

Table 1: Ablation of auxiliary information guidance. Depth and pose accuracy with varying prior coverage. Bold identifies the better score between the matched-training OmniVGGT-trained and PRC-only models at identical input settings; released-model and input-prior references are not ranked. Blue parentheses report PRC-only gains over OmniVGGT-trained, in percentage points, with full camera priors and no depth input. Depth is median-aligned per frame; RTA and AUC use sign-free translation errors.
Table 6: Base pose-corruption parameters before severity scaling. Time-scaled white increments use a reference interval of 0.1 s.

ATE is in millimeters for C3VD and meters for the other datasets. All three metrics are lower-is-better; different input settings are not ranked against one another.

papers.selection_reason: Explicitly targets prior-aware geometric perception for embodied systems, with direct relevance to spatial intelligence and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Deep Prior Learning for Embodied Perception
papers.tldr: VPGGT improves embodied 3D perception by explicitly preserving camera-pose priors and recovering metric scale under noisy pose inputs.

papers.abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu, Ayush Tewari, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the split between feedforward geometry predictors and generative visual models for partial 4D scene observations.
Uses modality- and time-dependent noise levels to jointly model video and geometric representations.
Learns from heterogeneous datasets with varying subsets of visual and geometric annotations.
Supports inference-time search over plausible scene hypotheses, using RGB-derived geometric evidence without ground-truth geometry.
Outperforms non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including sparse-observation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled generation. Given the first and last RGB frames and a target camera trajectory, we compare generated intermediate frames against ground truth and baseline video generation methods. UGG better preserves scene identity and dynamic content compared with the generic video completion baselines.

Figure 3: Conditional completion with noise as masking. We specify each task by the clean/noisy pattern over RGB, depth, camera-ray, and text tokens. Clean tokens provide observed context, while noisy tokens are denoised as missing targets, enabling generation and prediction with the same model architecture.

Figure 2: Generative-predictive transformer. We model RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned tokens, with camera pose represented as dense ray maps. Partial observations are zero-noise context tokens, while missing modalities are noisy tokens to be denoised. A unified transformer processes all tokens with modality-specific projections and feed-forward layers together with shared multimodal self-attention, enabling information exchange across modalities. The decoded RGB, depth, and ray maps form a complete 4D scene representation for cross-modal generation, geometric prediction, and inference-time consistency search.

Figure 1: A unified model for generation and prediction. We formulate visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion in a single joint model over RGB, depth, and camera pose. Given arbitrary partial observations, ranging from a text prompt to RGB sequences with geometric cues, our model jointly uses these modalities to infer a complete 4D scene representation, enabling both generation from sparse inputs and geometric prediction from observations.

Figure 6: Depth prediction qualitative comparison. The white box marks the region shown in the zoom-in columns, ordered as GT, Ours, ChronoDepth, and Geo4D from left to right. Our predictions preserve sharper local structures and object boundaries in the highlighted regions. Evaluation results. Table 2 reports camera pose estimation results. In the dense setting, UGG achieves lower ATE and RPEt than the external baselines across all five datasets. For example, ATE is reduced from 0.190 to 0.087 on ScanNet++ compared with Geo4D. papers.selection_reason: Introduces UGG, a unified generative model for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations (depth, pose). This fits both World Models (predicting dynamics) and 3D Vision (geometric understanding).
papers.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
papers.tldr: UGG unifies 4D scene generation and geometric understanding by modeling RGB video, depth, and camera pose as conditional completion in one generative framework.

papers.abstract: Estimating 3D head expression from a single image requires mapping visual appearance to underlying facial geometry. We propose ViGA-FLAME, a two-stage framework that aligns semantic visual features with a structured geometric latent space. First, a Parametric-Geometric Variational Autoencoder (PG-VAE) learns a unified representation of canonical head surfaces and FLAME parameters, supporting both detailed surface reconstruction and interpretable parameter recovery. Supervision on geometry and parameters, together with consistency between the two decoding branches, connects surface detail with parametric structure. Second, a trainable Visual-Geometric Adapter (ViGA) maps features from a pretrained semantic visual encoder into this latent space. Asymmetric attention enables ViGA to align semantic image features from the visual encoder with the structured geometric information represented in the PG-VAE latent space, without altering the original visual stream. By grounding image evidence in this latent prior, ViGA-FLAME enables robust 3D head expression estimation across severe facial deformations and large viewing angles, efficiently improving robustness over competing feed-forward methods.
authors: Wen Hao He, Jiacheng Wu, Jie Chen
bullets: Uses a two-stage framework combining geometric representation learning with visual-to-geometric adaptation.
PG-VAE jointly represents canonical head surfaces and FLAME parameters through geometry, parameter, and cross-branch consistency supervision.
A Visual-Geometric Adapter uses asymmetric attention to align semantic image features with structured geometric latents without modifying the original visual stream.
Targets robustness under severe facial deformations and large viewing angles.
The abstract reports improved robustness over competing feed-forward methods, without providing quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.

EO pretraining significantly helps some pairs but hurts others—even for MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery.
Effects are strongest with 1–5% labels, concentrate on small man-made objects, and persist across token pooling and attentive probing.
Frozen-embedding silhouette score strongly predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval performance on four of five datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
authors: Xianping Ma, Yu Zhang, Mingzhe Jiang, Wanxin Xie, Qing Zhu, Nan Xu, Xiaokang Zhang, Yuanxin Ye
bullets: Reframes cross-modal pairing from exact instance alignment to class-consistent semantic alignment.
Uses a latent-factor analysis to show semantic structure is preserved while instance-specific correlations are averaged out.
Introduces MixPair to continuously control the degree of exact versus semantic pairing.
Experiments find SemPair performs comparably to exact pairing, while transfer varies non-monotonically with the exact-pair ratio.
Suggests reducing reliance on costly instance-aligned multimodal data for scalable pretraining.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Semantic Pairing (SemPair) to relax cross-modal correspondence in remote sensing pretraining. This advances Multimodal Foundation Models (spatial understanding) and 3D Vision (scene understanding).
papers.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
papers.tldr: SemPair shows that multimodal remote sensing pretraining can learn transferable representations from semantically matched, non-identical cross-modal pairs rather than requiring exact instance correspondence.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.
authors: Ruxiao Duan, Yunwen Zhou, Erin Hong, Dongxu Zhao, Eric Turner, Federico Tombari, Alex Wong
bullets: Existing 3D reconstruction models often fail to generalize beyond perspective images.
Camera3R uses low-rank adaptation to extend pretrained reconstruction networks with minimal retraining.
The framework adds only 0.5% parameters and trains in less than a day, according to the abstract.
Experiments show adaptation to non-perspective cameras while preserving performance on perspective inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous cameras. Given an image sequence of arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, our method reconstructs the scene in a single forward pass.

Figure 2: Camera-agnostic feed-forward reconstruction. Given an input sequence from arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, we adapt a perspective-pretrained reconstruction network by camera-specific LoRA experts. Each frame is passed to a camera router, which selects the corresponding LoRA expert to adapt the model to the frame’s camera geometry, enabling pose and dense geometry (depth, ray directions, etc.) prediction from non-perspective cameras. Perspective frames bypass the adaptation, preserving the original behavior of the pretrained backbone.

Figure 3: Cross-camera data augmentation for model adaptation. Multi-view 3D reconstruction data from fisheye and panoramic sequences are augmented by synthesizing diverse camera projections. For fisheye sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, create additional fisheye distortions, and undistort the image to obtain perspective views. For panoramic sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, apply rotations, and render fisheye or perspective images by sampling from the panoramic sphere. Dense ground truth quantities such as depth and ray maps are transformed together with the image, providing geometrically aligned supervision across various camera models.

papers.abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.
authors: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Addresses the challenge of clinically meaningful 3D pathology localization from weak, scan-level supervision.
Generates pathology predictions and localization maps from pathology-conditioned query–image feature similarities.
Uses token-to-voxel upsampling for high-resolution maps and gradient-guided thresholding without extra learned parameters.
Across five tasks and 355 annotated CT scans, achieves 96.1% voxel-level AUROC and 34.5% AUPR, outperforming the compared saliency methods.
Reports classification AUROCs of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.
bullets: Addresses the irreversibility of feed-forward 3D reconstruction predictions.
Injects sparse geometric constraints through a lightweight point correspondence adapter.
Targets ambiguities from repetitive textures, symmetry, viewpoint changes, and textureless regions.
Introduces a challenging benchmark focused on failure modes of existing methods.
Reduces reconstruction error with as few as one correspondence click on standard and curated benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CLICK3R architecture. A shared ViT encoder processes the two input images. Correspondence prompts are tokenized using our correspondence tokenizer (Section 3.2). A symmetric point correspondence adapter, implemented as a lightweight transformer with self-attention and cross-attention (Section 3.3), updates the decoder-input features for each view. The asymmetric decoder then interprets the updated embeddings and passes them to the original DUSt3R [44] heads to predict 3D pointmaps and confidence.

papers.abstract: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.
bullets: Handcrafted reductions and sparse representations may discard weak but informative structure and preserve reduction-specific artifacts.
The paper defines structure as spectrum content recoverable after localized corruption, distinguishing it from unreconstructable noise.
Leakage-aware Spectral MAE pretrains on raw radar cubes using masking and corruption inspired by spectral leakage.
Organizing Doppler as a primary x-y-D dimension, with height as features, improves learning over naive channel stacking.
The approach consistently outperforms radar detectors and point-cloud SSL counterparts without handcrafted reductions.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have demonstrated strong generalization under large-scale pre-training, yet they struggle in long-tail scenarios such as low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation. We observe relational attention structure collapse, manifested as the failure of cross-view correspondences, as a primary cause of these limitations. While adaptation offers a practical way to bridge this gap, existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches mainly perform channel-wise feature adjustment and lack mechanisms to explicitly adapt relational structures, leaving correspondence failures unresolved. In this work, we formulate adaptation of 3D reconstruction models as a problem of correspondence recovery under domain shift and propose 3R-Adapter, a PEFT paradigm for long-tail 3D reconstruction scenarios. Our method consists of three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions. Extensive experiments on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods while maintaining efficient lightweight adaptation. Our code is released at https://github.com/PKU-OV3-LAB/3R-Adapter.
bullets: Targets long-tail settings including low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation.
Attributes failures to collapsed relational attention and disrupted cross-view correspondences.
Introduces three components: Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement.
Experiments report improved robustness over existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods while preserving lightweight adaptation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The data scaling bottleneck in 3D pre-training and our relational adaptation paradigm. (a) While foundation models thrive on massive data, they struggle to generalize to long-tail 3D domains due to the high cost of dense 3D ground truth. (b) Conventional PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA, Adapter) rely on implicit, channel-wise feature adjustment, which struggle to model the correspondence relationship in data-scarce scenarios. In contrast, our 3R-Adapter shifts the paradigm to explicit relational adaptation via Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement, effectively establishing robust cross-view correspondences without destroying pretrained priors.

Figure 3: The overall pipeline of the proposed 3R-Adapter. To enable efficient adaptation for complex long-tail scenes, our 3R-Adapter modulates the network via three cohesive modules: Deformable Retrieval extracts view-specific anchors and estimates spatial offsets alongside routing weights; Relational Rewiring establishes explicit geometric correspondences across views through deformable spatial sampling; and Consistency Refinement integrates the relational features back into the main stream via a learned gating mechanism, effectively enforcing cross-view consistency.

Figure 2: Relational attention structure collapse in long-tail scenarios. (a) In data-rich daytime scenes, the pre-trained 3D reconstruction model produces concentrated cross-view attention, allowing a selected query token to attend to consistent physical counterparts across reference views. (b) For selected low-light queries, the attention distribution becomes diffuse and fragmented, indicating degraded relational routing and unreliable correspondence modeling. This observation suggests that long-tail adaptation requires explicitly restoring cross-view relational structures, motivating the design of 3R-Adapter.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on joint human-scene reconstruction. 3R-Adapter produces more consistent human mesh recovery and cleaner scene geometry under complex human-scene interactions.

papers.abstract: Creating high-quality 3D content has traditionally required specialist expertise and experience with complex tools. The growing ecosystem of AI-assisted creativity demands accessible and intuitive 3D generation systems. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between LLM reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations.
Introduces Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), built from flexible B-spline patches with interpretable, part-level semantics.
Supports interactive text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation without expensive fine-tuning or restrictive geometric priors.
Enables targeted natural-language edits at multiple granularities and explicit per-patch surface-detail control.
Experiments report strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of SurfScaff3D. SurfScaff3D iteratively constructs an HPS representation by programmatically generating surface geometry and verifying its local geometry through rendered views. HPS organizes geometry as a hierarchical semantic tree of B-spline surface patches with explicit patch-level control over surface variation, enabling both structured mechanical objects and organic shapes. The examples illustrate how frequency and amplitude help in modelling diverse objects. A critic evaluates rendered outputs and provides targeted feedback, forming a closed-loop refinement process that progressively improves prompt alignment and geometric fidelity. The critic loop executes for a fixed number of N iterations unless an early stopping criterion is met.

Figure 2. Qualitative Comparison of SurfScaff3D. We provide qualitative examples of SurfScaff3D against similar works, on the left we represent methods which allow greater geometric flexibility but require fine-tuning, in the middle we show methods which benefit from the zero-shot generalizability of modern LLMs but suffer from restrictive geometric priors. On the right we show SurfScaff3D using the open-source Kimi K2.6 [20] and Claude Sonnet 4.6 [4] as generation backbones, respectively. Each row corresponds to a single object prompt, all methods are generated using the identical prompts to ensure a fair qualitative comparison.

By modulating the local smoothness parameters sf and ωf , the model synthesizes complex, highfrequency organic geometry without losing geometric coherence.

Figure 10. Qualitative Samples for text-to-3D generation. We show samples generated by SurfScaff3D from the object categories of ShapeNetCore [8], Toys4K [34] and OmniObject3D [40] datasets. The corresponding MARVEL-40M+ level-3 text prompts are displayed below each result.

HPS is far more effective than both. All settings are evaluated without critic iterations and with the same set of in-context objects, to isolate the impact of the representations.

Table 4. Impact of Surface Variation. For each backbone, the two columns add up to the number of objects in the dataset (55, 105 and 71). Higher is better ↑.

papers.title: SurfScaff3D: Bridging Geometric and Semantic Representations for LLM-based 3D Object Generation

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses drift accumulation because streaming model predictions are fixed after emission and cannot be corrected by loop closures.
Uses causal streaming inference for frame tracking, while selecting keyframes to write into persistent SLAM state.
An asynchronous back end re-observes past frames with fresh context to verify loops, correct trajectories, and refine dense geometry.
Shares one frame-encoder pass across invocations; cached features also support loop retrieval without extra encoding cost.
Reports state-of-the-art results on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, with over 40% lower mean ATE than the best uncalibrated baselines and tracking above 28 FPS at 518×154 on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D.

papers.selection_reason: Builds real-time SLAM on a frozen streaming 3D foundation model.
papers.title: Map2SLAM: From Streaming Map Prediction to Real-Time SLAM
papers.tldr: Map2SLAM turns a frozen streaming 3D foundation model into a real-time, loop-closure-capable SLAM system by making its predictions revisable observations of persistent map state.

papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.
bullets: Addresses anatomy-agnostic encoders and local-only MoE routing in 3D medical VLP.
Uses a Histogram Representation Router to select experts based on global context and predicted anatomical composition.
Introduces an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector for fine-grained organ-level alignment without manual inference-time annotations.
Patch-level routing lowers routing complexity and enforces load balancing by construction.
Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, it reports state-of-the-art results across segmentation, classification, and detection, with generalization to MRI and ultrasound.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the A2MoE architecture. Given a 3D CT input XI n, the Histogram Representation Router (HRR) combines visual context and anatomical composition to predict stagespecific expert weights shared across spatial positions. These weights combine the outputs of all experts {E(s) k }Ks k=1. OQMSP uses shared organ queries Q to aggregate multi-scale encoder features Xs into organ-level visual embeddings Zvis. These are aligned with corresponding text embeddings ztxt, obtained through a frozen text encoder and a trainable linear projection, using Lalign. A parallel decoder combines encoder features with spatial skip connections and is supervised by Lseg. At inference, anatomical composition is predicted from image features.
Figure 4: Qualitative segmentation results. Comparison of A2MoE against the top four baseline methods. Key differences are highlighted in red bounding boxes (see Appendix F for more samples).

Figure 15: Critical difference (CD) diagrams comparing ten segmentation methods across six benchmark datasets for DSC (top; higher is better) and HD95 (bottom; lower is better). Average ranks are computed independently per dataset and then averaged across all six benchmarks; rank 1 denotes the best-performing method. Horizontal brackets connect groups of methods for which no statistically significant difference was detected (Friedman test followed by Nemenyi post-hoc test, α=0.05). Our proposed method A2MoE is evaluated in two configurations: #2 +A2MoE applied on top of SegMamba, and #3 +OQMSP, which further extends it with organ-query-guided semisupervised pre-training; #1 SegMamba serves as the baseline. The full model (#3 +OQMSP) achieves the best average rank on both metrics (DSC: 1.00, HD95: 2.25) and is statistically distinguishable from the majority of competing methods (p = 4.51 · 10−8 and p = 1.88 · 10−6, respectively).

Figure 1: Comparison of MoE routing strategies. A learnable class-to-expert affinity matrix A(s) introduces a structural prior via a log-probability term log(h̃Ã(s) + ϵ), biasing expert selection toward anatomically consistent assignments. papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}
bullets: Addresses box mislocalization and missed objects caused by sparse, partial LiDAR observations in driving scenes.
Aligns canonical amodal 3D asset geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR using image-to-rendered-view correspondences.
Improves consistency and efficiency by estimating each instance’s scale once, propagating it across dynamic-object frames, and aggregating observations for static objects.
Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on Waymo Open Dataset.

papers.abstract: We present a hypernetwork that generates the parameters of an implicit neural representation (INR) for a given signal in a single forward pass, without test-time optimization. Existing hypernetworks for this problem either ignore the chain-rule structure of the test-time optimization that produces an INR or, when they preserve it, instantiate the structure with MLPs whose parameter count grows quartically in target-network width. Our central contribution is to show that this parameter-count cost is structural to the MLP instantiation, not to the optimization-oriented principle of preserving chain-rule structure, and to resolve it by replacing the MLP body with attention. The resulting hypernetwork combines three design choices: an output-neuron-centric tokenization that aligns the token axis with each layer's output-neuron axis; an information-flow consistency rule that fixes the role of every cross-attention module from the representation its output should occupy; and a token-space iterative rollout that realizes the five quantities one optimization step on the target INR computes as five cross-attention modules with parameter count independent of target-network width. Across five 2D and 3D INR generation benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines; scales to target-network widths at which the MLP-based optimization-oriented paradigm exhausts GPU memory; and produces the highest result on NeRF generation without ground-truth INR weights supervision.
bullets: Existing optimization-oriented hypernetworks preserve test-time optimization structure but can require parameter counts that grow quartically with target-network width.
The method replaces the costly MLP body with attention while retaining the chain-rule structure of an optimization step.
It uses output-neuron-centric tokenization, information-flow-consistent cross-attention, and token-space iterative rollout.
Across five 2D and 3D INR benchmarks, it outperforms reported single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines.
It scales to target widths that exhaust GPU memory for MLP-based approaches and achieves the highest reported NeRF-generation result without ground-truth INR-weight supervision.

papers.abstract: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at https://mic-dct.dkfz.de/.
bullets: Analyzes 565k 3D radiological images from 1,034 public datasets.
Identifies challenges including reuse propagation, duplication, provenance fragmentation, leakage, bias amplification, and distorted distributions.
Finds at least 118k duplicate pairs through perceptual hashing and manual tracing.
Publishes perceptual hashes and a web tool to help researchers identify overlaps and shared provenance.
Introduces MAP, a portable metadata profile for recording provenance, overlaps, and deduplication decisions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cross-dataset overlap network revealed by exact and near-duplicate 3D medical images. Each node represents a public dataset or dataset collection, and edges connect datasets that share at least one image pair with perceptual Hamming distance ≤ 100 or identified through datasetspecific deduplication and manual overlap tracing. Node size indicates the number of images in a dataset, edge size indicates the number of duplicate links associated with a dataset, and shaded regions denote connected components in the overlap graph. The largest component contains 107 datasets, including widely reused datasets and collections such as AMOS, KiTS, and AbdomenAtlas, illustrating that public dataset collections are not independent flat unions but part of a densely connected reuse ecosystem. Because perceptual hashing detects visual identity rather than causal lineage, edges should be interpreted as evidence of image-level overlap rather than complete provenance relationships.

Figure 4: The MAP Profile can be fragmented into 7 constituent areas (Section E). Notably, the Source Dataset section encodes provenance, while Duplicate Handling makes the efforts of the authors transparent regarding their work in handling repeated samples. Finally, Preprocessing Steps clarifies the modifications made to the source images in the collection for downstream reference.

Figure 2: Structural Provenance Documentation via Metadata Profiling. (A) Provenance is currently reconstructed manually from papers, websites, notes and correspondence, and documented ad hoc across heterogeneous tools. (B) We screen dataset collections for overlap by perceptual hashing against a reference hash database (Section 3) and record provenance and deduplication decisions as structured, machine-readable MAP metadata (Section 4).

Figure 1: Dataset Collections in Medical Image Analysis. Large-scale medical datasets are increasingly dataset collections formed through the aggregation of images, labels and metadata from multiple sources. However, limited provenance can introduce hidden dependencies and duplicates. In this paper, we (1) highlight the risks of dataset reuse, (2) detect duplicates via perceptual hashing, (3) document provenance through structured metadata profiles, and (4) provide associated tooling through a web-based platform (Section A).

papers.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.
authors: Mohamed Adjel (LAAS-GEPETTO), Kahina Chalabi (LAAS-GEPETTO), Vincent Bonnet (LAAS-GEPETTO)
bullets: Targets real-time human mesh recovery for mobile applications such as AR/VR, robotics, biomechanics, and exergames.
Uses lightweight single-image regressors based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) model, trained only on public SAM 3D Body annotations.
Reports competitive accuracy: 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB, and 41.7 mm on RICH.
Runs at 5.5 ms per person on a Galaxy S23 NPU and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU.
Provides open-source code and models, plus unified latency and reproduction evaluations across multiple methods and hardware targets.

papers.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.
authors: Yunhan Yang, Yunfei Zhao, Zeqiang Lai, Jiachen Xu, Minxiu Wang, Xintong Han, Xiangyu Yue, Xihui Liu, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses fragile post-hoc mesh segmentation affected by geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and scarce part annotations.
Uses a unified latent space for geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, leveraging richer visual and geometric priors.
Generates geometry, texture, deformation, and surface part IDs in one pass without a separate segmentation stage.
Adds point-prompt editing and subdivision, plus amodal completion of partial part masks using dynamic part tokens and local/global attention.
Experiments report meaningful segmentations, precise boundaries, interactive editing, and globally consistent completion.

papers.abstract: Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.
authors: Weidan Xiong, Kaijie Qu, Shihao Feng, Shunqi Fan, Rongyu Xiong, Hui Huang

Provides an interactive tool for texture-aware 3D editing and model retrieval.
Experiments report significant improvements over existing methods, though the abstract gives no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark
authors: Abdiaziz Muse, Tooba Javed, Tao Pu, Jiju Poovvancheri, Dong Chen
bullets: Contains approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 Halifax buildings across four seasons, day/night conditions, and varied weather.

Benchmarks point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer models.

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
authors: Zuhao Liu, Melih Darcan, Zhengdi Yu, Riza Alp Guler, Tolga Birdal
bullets: Addresses the need for hand-pose priors that account for the interacted object, beyond unconditional pose models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes HaNDF, an object-conditioned neural distance field that serves as a generative prior for hand-object interaction, enabling pose refinement and manipulation synthesis.
papers.title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
papers.tldr: HaNDF models plausible hand articulations conditioned on interacting objects using a geometry-aware neural distance field.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
bullets: Addresses the sensitivity of imitation-learned visuomotor policies to camera and robot-base viewpoint changes in mobile manipulation.
Separately reconstructs static scenes and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting and feed-forward 3D foundation models.
Uses kinematics-based action retargeting to render novel viewpoints and pair them with geometrically consistent transformed actions.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, plus simulation-based fidelity validation.
More than doubles average success over the strongest baseline and retains non-trivial success at large base displacements where baselines fail.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MOMASPLAT. 3D Reconstruction: We build 3D models of the environment from the navigation and manipulation data. We estimate camera poses via structure-from-motion and fit a 3D Gaussian Splatting model of the static scene, Gscene. For the dynamic objects, we segment each manipulated object and estimate its per-frame pose trajectory with a feed-forward 3D foundation model; since the scene and object poses lie in separate reference frames, we align them with a Sim(3) transformation and fit a separate object model Gobj. Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses: Given a robot base pose, T̃ , sampled around the original demonstration poses (left), we render the scene and object from the new viewpoint, transform the source end-effector trajectory into the new base frame to render the robot from a simulator, and composite the three streams into a photorealistic novel observation. Paired with the transformed actions ã1:Lj , this forms a synthetic demonstration; repeating across sampled poses yields the generated dataset. Imitation Learning: the policy is trained on the union of source and generated demonstrations.

Fig. 4: Policy success across base poses. For each task, we evaluate 12 unseen base locations distributed across categorical distance bins that vary per task, with 3 trials per pose, and report success rate by distance to the nearest demonstration pose. The shaded gray region denotes the original base poses; locations 5–50 cm away are unseen deployment poses. MOMASPLAT maintains substantially higher success as the base pose shifts away from the source demonstrations (where Source Only is labeled “Original data only”).

Fig. 1: MOMASPLAT. Starting from mobile-manipulation data collected at the original base pose (white and red robot), MOMASPLAT synthesizes demonstrations from sampled novel base poses (yellow-outlined gray robot). The top-right sequence shows the source manipulation demonstration, while the bottom-right shows the corresponding synthesized trajectory, including the dynamic object as it is moved by the robot. Augmenting the source manipulation dataset with these demonstrations enables execution from unseen deployment-time base poses (blue-outlined gray robot).

Fig. 5: Spatial distribution of policy evaluation poses. Top-down view of each task showing the table and target-object locations, the original demonstration base poses, and the test base poses used for policy evaluation. Original demonstration poses are marked with circles, while evaluation poses are marked with squares; arrows indicate the robot heading at each pose. Evaluation poses are colored by MOMASPLAT policy success rate, providing spatial context for the distance-based results in Fig. 4.

Fig. 3: Tasks and scenes used in our experiments. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world manipulation tasks across three scenes (top: scenes; bottom: per-task close-ups), covering manipulation of both rigid and articulated objects. The simulated scene and its task, SIM PICK-PLACE BOTTLE (right of the dashed lines), are used to measure the fidelity of MOMASPLAT’s generated demonstrations against ground truth.

TABLE I: Generated-observation fidelity against simulator ground truth. Mean ± std over 75 generated demonstrations spanning viewpoints with distances of 0.4–27.3 cm from the reconstruction views. Full image, object, and robot use every tenth frame (2486 total frames), with object and robot restricted to their masks; scene PSNR evaluation uses one frame per demonstration (75 in total).
