papers.title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: MOMASPLAT augments mobile-manipulation demonstrations with viewpoint-consistent synthetic trajectories that include dynamic object interactions, substantially improving robustness to unseen robot base poses.

papers.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SplatAnything
bullets: Existing methods normalize global radial distance but leave neighboring Gaussian spacing inconsistent across scene scales and camera setups.
This mismatch shifts Gaussian-scale targets and creates ambiguous supervision.
The proposed GSNorm canonicalizes a robust scene-level Gaussian-spacing statistic as a consistent spatial reference.
A benchmark evaluates diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and extrapolated viewpoints.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, with especially strong gains under large scale and viewpoint variations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of SplatAnything. Given N input images and optional camera parameters, a frozen geometry foundation model first estimates multi-view geometry. We convert the geometry from its native radial-distance-normalized space to the proposed Gaussian-spacing-normalized space and predict per-pixel Gaussian attribute through a Gaussian backbone and a lightweight GShead.

Figure 2: Normalization space. (a) Radial Distance Normalization canonicalizes a global radial statistic but leaves Gaussian spacing varying across scenes and camera configurations, resulting in inconsistent supervision targets. (b) Gaussian Spacing Normalization canonicalizes a representative statistic of Gaussian spacing, providing a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction.
Figure 5: Qualitative comparisons across diverse scenes and viewpoints with multi-view input.
Figure 14: More qualitative results of our method. SplatAnything feed-forward reconstructs highquality 3DGS representations generalizing to arbitrary scenes, scales, and viewpoints in a few seconds.
Figure 9: Target-view sampling modes used during training. Blue cameras denote the source views provided as input, while red cameras denote the target views used for rendering supervision.

Figure 8: Source-view trajectory patterns (16 views per panel), visualized in an approximately top-down projection. Dots and arrows denote camera centers and viewing directions, respectively; the gray polyline connects consecutive views, and color indicates capture order. For inward-orbit, × marks the approximate viewing center.
Figure 10: Qualitative comparisons of different normalization spaces.

Figure 13: Qualitative results of SplatAnything for panoramic images reconstruction. SplatAnything can reconstruct high-quality 3DGS representations from panoramic images with different field of view, demonstrating its strong generalization ability.
Figure 4: Median Gaussian spacing across scene types. RDNorm leaves up to 4.5× variation in median Gaussian spacing across scene categories, whereas GSNorm canonicalizes it by construction.
Figure 12: Qualitative comparisons across diverse scenes and viewpoints with monocular input.
Figure 11: Qualitative comparisons across diverse scenes and viewpoints with multi-view input.
Table 11: Median forward-pass latency per scene (ms) of different methods under different numbers of input views. The fastest method within each pose setting is highlighted in bold.

papers.title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
papers.tldr: SplatAnything improves feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting across varied scenes by normalizing Gaussian spacing for more consistent prediction.

papers.abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing models to capture clinically relevant anatomy across hierarchical scales in 3D scans and reports.
Routes both image and text tokens through local and global anatomy-organized Soft Mixture-of-Experts layers.
Uses anatomy-level and global contrastive alignment to learn unified vision-language representations.
Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision and evaluated on segmentation, classification, and detection across 6 datasets.
Reports consistent improvements over 11 state-of-the-art methods; the approach is scoped to 3D medical imaging and the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the MedHiVE framework. A hierarchical encoder processes a 3D CT scan and anatomy masks alongside a full report representation zTi and anatomy-specific snippet representations zTi,a, extracted through a frozen text encoder. The global vision representation zIi is contrasted with zTi , while local vision representations zIi,a are aligned with zTi,a for each anatomical structure a. This yields anatomy-aware vision-language representations that enhance downstream segmentation, classification, and detection.

Figure 4. An overview of the 2D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6]. We consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups to facilitate analysis and model training (see Table 3). These projections illustrate the spatial distribution of the anatomies across representative slices.

Figure 2. Overview of the HiVEL layer. Global and anatomylevel vision tokens and text tokens are routed to E global experts FFNG and F local experts FFNL via first-level routers. The resulting slots are concatenated and processed by a second-level router. Global vision and text tokens are fused with H shared experts FFNS outputs via residual connection, yielding enhanced vision tokens x̂ and text tokens t̂. Vision tokens are used at all stages s ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, while text tokens are enabled at s ∈ {3, 4}.
Figure 6. Text preprocessing pipeline.

Figure 10. Qualitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. We benchmark MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE exhibits superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging its ability to capture long-range dependencies for large-scale dental arches while preserving high-fidelity boundaries in smaller, individual tooth structures. While competing methods frequently suffer from topological discontinuities (e.g., fragmented roots) or oversegmentation in high-density regions, our approach maintains global structural integrity and local connectivity. The zoomed-in regions (red boxes) highlight MedHiVE’s robustness in resolving ambiguous inter-proximal boundaries where baseline models typically fail to maintain clear separation.

Figure 9. Qualitative multi-class segmentation results on the KiTS 2023 internal test set. We evaluate the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth annotations and four state-of-the-art baselines for the joint segmentation of the kidney parenchyma, cysts, and tumor masses. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency by effectively modeling the hierarchical dependencies between nested structures; it captures the global morphology of the kidney while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for small, low-contrast cysts and heterogeneous tumor regions. Unlike competing methods, which frequently exhibit topological fragmentation or semantic leakage (e.g., misclassifying tumor voxels as healthy tissue), our approach preserves structural integrity across varying object scales. The zoomed-in insets highlight MedHiVE’s ability to resolve ambiguous boundaries in complex cases of multi-focal cystic disease, where baseline models suffer from oversegmentation and loss of connectivity.

Figure 8. Qualitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT validation set. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines across 15 abdominal organs. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging long-range dependency modeling to maintain the global anatomical context of large-scale organs (e.g., liver, stomach) while ensuring high-fidelity boundary localization for small, low-contrast structures (e.g., adrenal glands, gallbladder). While competing methods frequently suffer from inter-class leakage and topological discontinuities in anatomically crowded regions, our approach preserves structural integrity and inter-organ spatial relationships. The highlighted regions (red boxes) illustrate MedHiVE’s robustness against oversegmentation at organ interfaces, where baseline models often fail to resolve clear semantic boundaries due to similar intensity profiles in non-contrast CT.

Figure 7. Qualitative segmentation results on the PANORAMA test sets. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against the ground truth and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, accurately capturing long-range dependencies in large-scale structures (e.g., the pancreas parenchyma) while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for fine-grained objects like PDAC lesions and pancreatic ducts. Unlike competing methods that suffer from topological discontinuities or oversegmentation, our approach consistently preserves structural integrity across varying object scales.

Figure 3. Qualitative segmentation results on four datasets, from top to bottom: PANORAMA, AMOS, KiTS and GEPAR3D. Comparison of MedHiVE with the top five baselines. Red boxes highlight significant artifacts or missing components in baseline predictions. MedHiVE shows superior consistency with the ground truth in these challenging regions.

Figure 11. Qualitative comparison of visual grounding performance on external in-house abdominal CT scans with kidney lesions. Each row displays a representative abdominal CT slice paired with its corresponding part of radiology report describing kidney tumors or cysts; in the absence of voxel-wise annotations, the report serves as the reference. Grounding predictions are shown for MedHiVE (left), Merlin (center), and fVLM (right). All models are fine-tuned on KiTS 2023. MedHiVE segments lesions consistent with the radiology reports, whereas Merlin and fVLM overshoot the lesion extent or place predictions in a kidney the report leaves unremarkable (red boxes).

Figure 5. Visualization of the 3D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6], shown from the front, left, right, and back views. These projections highlight the global structural consistency and anatomical coherence of the segmented structures. Consistent with the 2D setting, we consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups for clarity and downstream processing (see Table 3). The multi-view renderings provide a qualitative assessment of segmentation quality across the full 3D volume.

Table 4. Quantitative segmentation and detection performance on the PANORAMA test sets (NIH, MSD, and In-house). Evaluation metrics include mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm), while PDAC detection efficacy is measured via Sensitivity and Specificity (%). The best results are highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, particularly in the challenging task of PDAC segmentation, where it significantly outperforms existing Transformer and Mamba-based architectures. Notably, our method achieves a substantial boost in mDSC for the In-house PDAC dataset (65.8%) and the Overall PDAC average (54.2%), representing a major improvement over the second-best performing models. Additionally, MedHiVE exhibits the lowest mHD95 and the highest sensitivity for patient-level detection, underscoring its clinical utility in identifying low-contrast ductal adenocarcinomas across diverse multi-center cohorts.

Table 5. Quantitative segmentation results on the KiTS dataset. Performance is evaluated across three distinct labels: Kidneys, Tumor, and Cyst. Results are reported in DSC (%) for individual classes, with mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) representing the overall average performance. MedHiVE achieves the highest performance in mDSC and mHD95, consistently outperforming both CNN-based and advanced sequence-modeling baselines. Specifically, the model shows a marked improvement in the segmentation of small, irregular structures compared to pure Mamba or Transformer architectures. The achievement of the lowest mHD95 further validates our method’s precision in boundary localization, demonstrating its robustness in handling the high anatomical variability and complex pathologies inherent in kidney tumor imaging. The best results are bolded.

Table 6. Quantitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT dataset. The evaluation encompasses 15 distinct anatomical structures across a wide range of scales and morphologies. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves superior overall performance, demonstrating a high degree of robustness across both large, high-contrast organs (e.g., Liver, Spleen) and smaller, more complex structures (e.g., Adrenal Glands, Duodenum). Notably, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art for the Pancreas and Duodenum, which are traditionally challenging due to their low-contrast boundaries and proximity to the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, the significant reduction in mHD95 compared to both Transformer-based and pure Mamba-based baselines indicates a superior ability to preserve global topological consistency while maintaining fine-grained local details. MedHiVE exhibits competitive or superior Dice scores across the majority of classes, underscoring the generalizability of our proposed architecture.

Table 7. Detailed quantitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. Results are categorized by individual teeth following the FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall segmentation accuracy and the lowest mHD95 among all compared methods. The performance is notably consistent across different tooth types, effectively bridging the gap between large molars and smaller incisors. In particular, our model demonstrates superior precision in the upper and lower left quadrants, where it maintains high fidelity for complex occlusal surfaces and inter-proximal spaces. The significant reduction in the average Hausdorff distance suggests that MedHiVE is less prone to the isolated voxel noise and topological errors that often degrade the clinical utility of baseline segmentation outputs.

Table 1. Comprehensive performance comparison across segmentation, classification, and detection tasks. Segmentation performance is reported in mDSC (%), while PDAC classification and detection are reported via Sensitivity (%), Specificity (%), and mAP (%). VRAM is measured in gigabytes (GB) (↓), and speed in million voxels per second (MV/s) (↑). The best results are bolded.

Table 8. Quantitative segmentation performance on the ToothFairy2 dataset subset. Evaluation follows the FDI World Dental Federation notation across the upper and lower dental arches. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates a clear state-of-the-art advantage, particularly in maintaining structural continuity across the most challenging anatomical sites. Our method significantly outperforms all baselines in the posterior extremities, specifically the third molars (FDI 18, 28, 38, 48), where standard models typically struggle with severe under-segmentation or total loss of connectivity. Furthermore, MedHiVE attains the second-best mHD95 among all methods. These results validate the robustness of our approach in handling the high morphological variability and lower image quality characteristic of the ToothFairy2 benchmarks, ensuring precise tooth-by-tooth delineation across the entire oral cavity.

Table 12. Ablation study on the AMOS-CT validation set across 15 organ classes. We evaluate the impact of the Text (T) supervision and Contrastive Loss (CL) components on segmentation accuracy (mDSC) and boundary precision (mHD95). The results demonstrate that incorporating textual representations (Config #2) consistently improves performance for anatomically complex organs, while the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest overall accuracy and a significant reduction in Hausdorff Distance (mHD95 from 5.0 to 3.6 mm). This suggests that the joint contrastive objective effectively regularizes the latent space, particularly benefiting small-scale structures such as the adrenal glands and duodenum. B, T, and CL indicate baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 10. Ablation study on the PANORAMA and in-house datasets demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate our proposed method across three diverse test sets: NIH (public), MSD (public), and a multi-institutional In-house dataset. Segmentation quality is measured through mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm). Additionally, we report patient-level PDAC detection performance using Sensitivity/Specificity (%). The results indicate that while text guidance (T) significantly improves tumor localization, the addition of contrastive learning (CL) is crucial for refining boundary transitions, as evidenced by the reduction in mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 11. Ablation study on the KiTS dataset demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate the incremental contribution of text-based prompts (T) and contrastive learning (CL) over the baseline (B) architecture. Segmentation performance is reported via class-specific DSC (%) for Kidneys, Tumors, and Cysts, alongside aggregate mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) metrics. The results indicate that text guidance (T) primarily benefits cyst segmentation, while the addition of contrastive learning (CL) yields the largest gain for tumors and further reduces mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 14. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D dataset, including ToothFairy2 subset across 32 individual tooth classes (FDI notation). We evaluate the contribution of Text (T) conditioning and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained dental segmentation. While the baseline (Config #1) performs adequately on centralized teeth, the integration of textual representations (Config #2) provides a significant performance boost in boundary precision, reducing mHD95 from 6.5 to 2.0 mm. Notably, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) demonstrates superior robustness in segmenting distal molars (e.g., FDI 18, 28, 38), which are typically prone to severe imaging artifacts and morphological variation. This confirms that the contrastive objective effectively regularizes the feature space for anatomically rare or obscured structures. This indicates that the benefit of the anatomy-level contrastive objective can depend on overlap between the pre-training anatomy inventory and the target structures. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 13. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D test set, excluding ToothFairy2 subset across 32 dental classes (FDI notation). We quantify the influence of Textual Supervision (T) and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained segmentation. The inclusion of text-conditioned representations (Config #2) yields substantial gains in semantic recognition across the dental arch. Crucially, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest boundary fidelity, reaching sub-millimeter precision (mHD95: 0.5 mm). This indicates that the contrastive objective mitigates surface errors effectively in anatomically complex regions, such as the lingual surfaces of incisors (FDI 11, 21) and the occlusal pits of molars (FDI 36, 46), where baselines exhibit higher spatial variance. As this dataset covers dental anatomy absent from our pre-training inventory, the anatomy-level contrastive objective is expected to contribute less here. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.
Table 3. List of selected anatomies.

Table 9. Comparative quantitative analysis of tooth segmentation on the full dataset, including GEPAR3D [42] and ToothFairy2 [8, 9, 31] subsets. Evaluation is conducted for individual teeth using FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results bolded. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall mDSC, particularly in the segmentation of molars and premolars. MedHiVE achieves the second-best mHD95, indicating precise boundary localization. Notably, the performance gap is most pronounced in the posterior regions, where complex root morphologies and proximity to distal anatomical landmarks typically challenge standard segmentation models. These results underscore the effectiveness of our architectural design in maintaining local precision while capturing the global context of the complete dental arch.

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical multimodal MoE for 3D medical vision-language; fits multimodal LLM and 3D pretrained modeling.
papers.title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
papers.tldr: MedHiVE uses hierarchical multimodal mixture-of-experts and contrastive learning to align anatomy-level and global information in 3D medical vision-language modeling.

papers.abstract: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.
bullets: Addresses poor coordination between object geometry and scene-level spatial organization in single-image 3D generation.
Predicts a color-coded voxel scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements.
Extracts each instance into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible scene anchor for refinement.
Reuses pretrained object-level generative priors while training scene components mainly for organization and anchor refinement.
Reports improved layout, geometry, visual quality, and generalization, with faster full-scene generation than SceneGen and SAM3D.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Generalization to diverse room scenes. The upper three rows compare reconstructions of a living room, a garage, and a classroom, with the input image followed by the results of DepR, PartCrafter, MIDI, SceneGen, SAM3D, and Bri3D. These examples cover different object categories, scales, and degrees of occlusion. The lower row shows a multi-room overview and reconstructions of its bathroom, bedroom, living room, and kitchen, each generated from a separate room-level input. Together, the examples illustrate object reconstruction across varied scene configurations and room types.

Figure 2 Overview of Bri3D. The Scene Scaffold Generator and Anchored Voxel Refiner replace the voxel-generation stage of a two-stage object generator, while its detail-synthesis stage remains frozen. SC-VAE denotes the StructureColor VAE, and snowflakes indicate frozen modules. The scaffold is generated in latent space and decoded at 1283; each object is refined to a 643 voxel support. The anchor initialization follows Eq. 5, including object-wise latent normalization.

Figure 3 Qualitative results on the 3D-FRONT [12] test set. Our method generates more plausible layouts and higher-fidelity geometry, consistent with the quantitative improvements. Red boxes indicate inferior baseline results.

Figure 5 Comparison of 3D scene layouts and failure cases. (a) Columns show the RGB input, ground-truth layout, and predictions from MIDI [18], SceneGen [28], SAM3D [3], and Bri3D. Red wireframe boxes mark the groundtruth object extents, making displacement, missing instances, and shape deviations visible. Bri3D better follows the reference arrangements in these examples. (b) Red rectangles highlight our failures: nearby objects may merge in the cluttered seating area (Case 1), and some instances may be omitted in the densely populated classroom (Case 2).

Figure 6 Color-coded scene scaffold vs. connected component analysis. From left to right: RGB input, instance label map, geometry-only CCA result, and the predicted color-coded voxel grid. In the upper example, CCA groups the refrigerator, microwave, and table into one connected region; in the lower example, it merges the touching bed components and teddy bear. The predicted instance colors provide additional separation cues at these contacts, allowing joint position–color clustering to recover distinct object anchors. Colors indicate instance identity rather than surface texture.

Figure 7 Preliminary attempt on structural elements. From left to right: RGB input, label map including structural regions, predicted color-coded voxel grid, and reconstructed scene mesh. The dining-area and bedroom examples include room surfaces together with foreground furniture, illustrating how structural labels can extend the scaffold beyond object instances. This extension depends on reliable labels for those regions and remains preliminary; floors, walls, and ceilings are excluded from the main Bri3D experiments and quantitative results.

Figure 8 Additional qualitative comparisons and robustness to imperfect segmentation. (a) Geometry and layout comparisons with MIDI and SAM3D on indoor and outdoor scenes; MIDI is shown with normal shading. Bri3D produces coherent layouts and faithful object geometry, while MIDI suffers from distorted shapes and implausible arrangements. (b) With an erroneous instance label map (Wrong Seg), Bri3D exhibits only local cracks, whereas SAM3D produces incorrect object partitions and collisions, including interpenetration between the teddy bear and the bed.

Figure 9 Robustness to instance segmentation granularity, label colors, and implausible partitions. From left to right: input image, input instance segmentation, predicted semantic voxel grid, and reconstructed textured meshes with bounding boxes. The first two rows show the same tabletop scene containing a bottle, a mug, a large box, a ball, and two small stacks of blocks. The segmentation changes only the grouping of these small stacks: each stack receives one label in the first row, while its individual blocks receive separate labels in the second row. The last two rows show deliberately implausible partitions of a chair, together with changes in instance label colors. papers.selection_reason: Single-image 3D scene generation with scene anchors; advances 3D generation.
papers.title: Bri3D: Bridging the Object-Scene Gap in Single-Image 3D Generation via Scene-Anchor
papers.tldr: Bri3D bridges scene layout and detailed object generation by using instance-aware voxel anchors to guide a frozen object generator in reconstructing coherent 3D scenes from a single image.

papers.abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection
bullets: Evaluates LBP, Gabor filters, wavelets, FFT, CNN features, and gray-level run-length features with several classifiers.
LBP combined with SVC and CNN showed high specificity and accuracy; statistical tests supported LBP’s relevance.
SHAP was used to identify the most influential features for classification.
On the reported small dataset, SVC reached 98.06% accuracy and CNN 97.8%; on a larger benchmark, CNN reached 98.9% and SVC 96.7%.
The study focuses on automated MRI diagnosis and evaluates performance across datasets, but the abstract does not detail clinical deployment or broader validation.

papers.tldr: A comparative MRI study finds that combining diverse image features with machine learning—especially LBP with SVC or CNN—supports accurate brain-tumor classification, with SHAP providing feature-importance explanations.

papers.abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MRI enables non-invasive assessment of left atrial (LA) scar, an imaging marker associated with atrial fibrillation ablation outcome. However, automatic scar segmentation is hindered by low contrast, the thin atrial wall, scarce labels, and extreme class imbalance. Conditional diffusion offers iterative mask generation, but its suitability for sparse 3D LA scar segmentation remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Conditional Mask Diffusion (CMDiff), which predicts clean masks using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet. We compared CMDiff with a deterministic baseline on identical cases in five-fold cross-validation of 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold. CMDiff achieved a scar DSC of 0.47 $\pm$ 0.08, HD95 of 12.89 $\pm$ 6.39 mm, and ASD of 1.91 $\pm$ 0.96 mm, compared with deterministic baseline values of 0.51 $\pm$ 0.08, 10.86 $\pm$ 5.39 mm, and 1.58 $\pm$ 1.03 mm, respectively. Under the same implementation, clean-mask prediction performed substantially better than the noise-prediction configuration evaluated in this study. Thus, CMDiff was technically feasible but did not improve segmentation performance: DSC was lower, and both HD95 and ASD were higher. Direct mask diffusion therefore provides an analytical alternative, but not a competitive performance advance for this task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jizhang02/CMDiff.
bullets: Addresses low contrast, thin atrial walls, scarce labels, and severe class imbalance in LGE MRI scar segmentation.
Uses a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet for iterative clean-mask generation.
Evaluated with five-fold cross-validation on 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects.
CMDiff achieved DSC 0.47 ± 0.08, HD95 12.89 ± 6.39 mm, and ASD 1.91 ± 0.96 mm, versus 0.51 ± 0.08, 10.86 ± 5.39 mm, and 1.58 ± 1.03 mm for the deterministic baseline.
Clean-mask prediction outperformed the evaluated noise-prediction configuration; source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.
bullets: Targets the gap between successful 2D vision foundation models and less effective 3D scene representation learning.
Replaces the hierarchical PTv3 backbone with a ViT-like Volume Transformer for 3D scenes.
Separates teacher and student roles for view matching, using clean teacher targets and stronger student perturbations.
Enforces masked-content prediction from visible geometry only and introduces view-consistent 2D-to-3D distillation.
Achieves substantial gains in dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, with strong out-of-domain transfer.

figures.caption: Figure 3: VINO Overview. Overlapping global and local views are sampled from a 3D scene. The EMA teacher encodes clean global views and softly assigns their tokens to learned prototypes, producing balanced targets. The prototypes are optimized independently by encouraging balanced and consistent assignments across global views. The student encodes strongly augmented local views and masked global views. Local-view embeddings, through a projection head, predict the targets of corresponding global-view tokens. Masked view embeddings provide context to a cross-attention-only predictor that predicts the targets at masked locations.

Figure 1: Self-supervised 3D Representations. We propose VINO, a framework for learning semantic representations of 3D scenes with no labels. Trained on 3D data only, VINO captures semantic similarity better than Sonata (Wu et al., 2025), as shown in PCA projections (top) and cosine-similarity maps (bottom). Sonata yields qualitatively similar representations across backbones, whereas VINO better distinguishes semantically different but geometrically similar regions, for example, chair and table legs, and captures semantic similarity across geometrically different instances, as illustrated by one plant strongly activating the other.

Figure 2: Comparison of Training Views. Sonata (Wu et al., 2025) geometrically corrupts all views and retains masked tokens in the student encoder. In contrast, VINO keeps the teacher’s global views clean, removes masked tokens from the student encoder, and applies geometric corruptions only to local views.

Figure 4: Representation Artifacts. We observe high-norm token artifacts in the representations (left). Register tokens largely eliminate these artifacts, but early in training, the learned representations still strongly reflect local voxel occupancy. Averaging voxel features within each patch removes this residual artifact (right).

Figure 5: Consistent 2D Targets. VFM (Oquab et al., 2024) features of the same 3D region vary across views. We learn prototypes in the frozen VFM feature space, optimized such that corresponding tokens across views produce matching soft assignments. These serve as our targets for 2D–3D distillation.

papers.title: VINO: Revisiting 3D Representation Learning with Volume Transformers
papers.tldr: VINO revisits self-supervised 3D representation learning with a Volume Transformer and redesigned learning objectives to produce stronger, transferable scene representations.

papers.abstract: Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian rendering combines compact textured surfaces with flexible 3D Gaussian primitives, offering an efficient alternative to purely Gaussian scene representations for structured environments. Existing scene-reconstruction hybrids commonly follow an additive formulation, where Gaussian residuals compensate for errors left by the mesh. However, not every Mesh-Gaussian conflict is caused by missing content: residual geometry errors, occlusion mismatch, texture-projection artifacts, and view-dependent appearance can make the same mesh content consistent in one view but inconsistent in another. We therefore formulate hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem and present Gaussolve, a subtract-and-refill framework that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content before residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. We introduce a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field, parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians, to learn where and from which viewing directions mesh content should be dissolved. A continuous transmittance fusion rule progressively exposes residual Gaussians behind the dissolved mesh, preserving their reconstruction gradients and avoiding hard visibility discontinuities. Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes demonstrate higher visual fidelity with fewer Gaussian primitives and faster rendering. Project page: https://ooosn.github.io/gaussians-can-subtract/
bullets: Frames hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem rather than purely additive mesh-error correction.
Uses a Neural Dissolve Field to predict which mesh regions should be dissolved and from which viewing directions.
Applies continuous transmittance fusion to reveal residual Gaussians smoothly while preserving reconstruction gradients.
Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes report higher visual fidelity, fewer Gaussian primitives, and faster rendering.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Gaussolve. The projection-textured mesh represents broad regular content, while the Neural Dissolve Field selectively suppresses mesh content that becomes inconsistent across views. Residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions, and all components are combined through continuous transmittance fusion.

Figure 1. Gaussians Can Subtract. Existing hybrids primarily compensate for mesh errors by adding Gaussian residuals. Gaussolve instead introduces a subtractive Neural Dissolve Field that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content and lets residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. This explicit subtract-and-refill decomposition improves visual quality while retaining a compact hybrid representation. Compared with existing methods, Gaussolve achieves a more favorable quality–compactness trade-off by allowing meshes and Gaussians to cooperate rather than compete.

Figure 5. Visualization of the subtract-and-refill mechanism. Compared with the projection-textured mesh and the Hard-Z hybrid baseline, Gaussolve selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content (Diss.) and lets residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions (Res.), producing cleaner boundaries and more accurate appearance. The red and blue boxes indicate the corresponding enlarged regions.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparisons on novel-view synthesis. Compared with 3DGS, PGSR, 3D-GES, and MeshSplatting, Gaussolve better preserves weakly textured surfaces. The red and blue boxes indicate the corresponding enlarged regions.

Figure 3. Hard-Z brittleness and gradient recovery. (a) Gaussians initially in front of the mesh frequently cross behind the Hard-Z visibility boundary during training. (b) For Gaussians whose reconstruction gradients are blocked by Hard-Z, Gaussolve recovers a substantial fraction of the ungated reference gradient. Curves and shading denote the four-scene mean and range.

papers.tldr: Gaussolve improves hybrid mesh–Gaussian rendering by selectively removing inconsistent mesh content so residual Gaussians can reconstruct it more accurately.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.
bullets: The dataset contains 12,068 objects and 311,886 Wikimedia Commons photos collected across people, years, environments, cameras, and physical instances.
It reconstructs camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks, while categorizing objects by whether they stay at one site, move between sites, or represent shared designs.
Recent feedforward models struggle most with objects that move or have multiple physical units.
Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting improves pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects and also improves performance on the NAVI benchmark.
Conventional benchmark performance remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Object-centric 3D reconstruction from found photos; fine-tunes foundation model.
papers.title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos

papers.abstract: Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, providing 3D masks as evidence. We curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic-spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.
authors: Yulu Xie, Zilong Li, Shen Xu, Yifan Bai, Liuhong Shi, Jiao Chen, Xianglei Kong, Wenchao Zhu, Na Shen, Xianghua Ye, Yang Yan, Jiaju Zheng, Yunsong Peng, Yanzhou Su, Chaohui Yu, Hao Luo, Fan Wang
bullets: Addresses the separation between textual CT interpretation and 3D anatomical segmentation.
Uses whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, trained with large-scale CT scans, instruction dialogues, and CT-mask pairs.
Evaluated across 346 tasks involving segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation.
Reported strong gains in multicentre validation, including 18.2-point improvement in lesion segmentation and 15.3-point improvement in report generation.
Shows bidirectional semantic–spatial synergy: language improves segmentation, while generated masks improve interpretation.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models enable dense monocular reconstruction without requiring camera calibration, but independently reconstructed submaps can accumulate scale drift, and even a valid revisit can yield an inconsistent cross-submap measurement. We extend VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with fixed-root scale anchoring and short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections. SALAD selects an image pair between the initial submap and each eligible new submap; joint VGGT inference then uses learned implicit semantic-geometric cues to supply a scale-only anchor while preserving the original overlap chain. For loop closure, neighboring image pairs support a consistency check and translation-scale alignment. Each accepted candidate contributes one robust Sim(3) factor between existing center-frame nodes, without an auxiliary loop submap. A 17-sequence comparison lowers mean Sim(3) ATE on nine TUM sequences from 0.1018 to 0.0451 m relative to the VGGT-SLAM 2.0 baseline. Anchoring improves all seven no-loop module ablations. On three Clio scenes, a fixed-loop comparison favors the direct connection pipeline over the tested auxiliary-submap pipeline. A separate candidate audit exposes additional rejections of visually overlapping pairs by the short-sequence check. These comparisons distinguish the gains from long-range scale anchoring and loop connection choices from the limitations of candidate verification.
authors: Ziyi Jin, Kangjin Yu, Beichen Wang, Can Jiang, Zhongpu Xia, Jie Xu
bullets: Addresses scale drift across independently reconstructed submaps and inconsistent measurements during revisits.
Uses fixed-root scale anchoring: selected cross-submap image pairs provide a scale-only constraint through joint VGGT inference while preserving overlap chains.
Uses neighboring image pairs to verify loop consistency and align translation scale, adding robust Sim(3) factors without an auxiliary loop submap.
On nine TUM sequences, mean Sim(3) ATE decreases from 0.1018 m to 0.0451 m versus VGGT-SLAM 2.0; anchoring helps all seven no-loop ablations.
Candidate verification can reject visually overlapping pairs, indicating a scope or limitation of the short-sequence consistency check.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Wenhao Dong, Jun Zhang, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed anchor representations and growing multi-view support sequences.
Routes spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers using coverage-cycled evidence routing.
Retains all decoder-facing anchor queries while reducing support-side fusion cost through pre-projection routing and joint context packing.
Achieves up to 26.12× faster cross-view fusion and 1.43× end-to-end acceleration without retraining.
Maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion on long input sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossPressor. We keep the original ZPressor [25] pipeline unchanged, including anchor selection, anchor–support grouping, the anchor-query pathway, and the downstream prediction modules. One representative anchor–support group is expanded to compare the fusion stage. The original dense fusion (top) uses all support features as K/V evidence for cross-attention, whereas CrossPressor (bottom) preserves the full anchor-query pathway and routes only the support-side features before K/V projection. For cluster stride sc, the sc × sc grid enumerates the s2c possible spatial sampling offsets. We index the offset assigned to support view v at fusion layer ℓ by pℓc,v = (rc(v) + κℓ) mod s2c , where rc(v) is the support-view rank and κ is the layer-wise increment. Moving across support views advances the sampling pattern by one offset, while moving across fusion layers advances it by κ, distributing the retained spatial evidence across both dimensions. The selected support features are gathered and packed into a compact sequence before the original K/V projection and cross-attention, producing the same updated-anchor interface for the unchanged downstream prediction pipeline.

Figure 1. Representation–fusion mismatch and CrossPressor. ZPressor [25] bounds the decoder-facing representation by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps. As more context views are assigned to these anchors, the dense support features used to construct each anchor continue to grow. CrossPressor keeps the anchor representation unchanged while routing a bounded support sequence across cameras and spatial locations, with spatial sampling offsets varied across fusion layers. Gray tokens denote dense support evidence, while green tokens indicate routed evidence from different support views.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CrossPressor, a training-free method for scalable cross-view fusion in 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing representation growth and fusion speed.
papers.title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: CrossPressor is a training-free fusion strategy that makes anchor-based feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting scalable for long multi-view sequences while preserving near-dense reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: We present the Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset, which adds dense semantic and instance-level labels to laser scans of the previously released Rohbau3D domain data from shell construction sites. The dataset comprises 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, each captured with a terrestrial laser scanner and stored in a scanner-centered local coordinate system. Unlike point clouds sampled from reconstructed meshes or synthetic building models, the data preserve the characteristic properties of real laser scanning, including non-uniform sampling, measurement artifacts, reflections, and fine geometric detail. Combined with manual labels, expert oversight during pointwise annotation, and full-scene review, this yields a high-quality benchmark for semantic scene understanding in complex built environments. The dataset includes 17 class labels of building components and one background class, along with instance annotations for object-level analysis. In addition to the 3D point clouds, the release also provides scripts for deriving geometrically aligned panoramic and cube-map representations of color, LiDAR reflection intensity, depth, surface normals, semantic labels, and instance labels from the 3D arrays. We describe the acquisition pipeline, annotation protocol, quality-control process, and panorama-generation procedure, and provide benchmark splits and baseline experiments for semantic segmentation. By combining precise terrestrial laser scans, dense annotations, and a wide variety of shell-construction scenes, Rohbau3D-Semantics bridges the gap among synthetic indoor datasets, mesh-derived benchmarks, and smaller construction-specific resources. The dataset is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics, and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment. Access and download the full dataset via https://github.com/RauchLukas/rohbau3d
bullets: Contains 504 point-cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, captured with terrestrial laser scanners.
Provides dense annotations for 17 building-component classes plus background, along with object instances.
Preserves real scanning characteristics such as non-uniform sampling, reflections, measurement artifacts, and fine detail.
Includes scripts for aligned panoramic and cube-map views of color, intensity, depth, normals, semantic labels, and instance labels.
Offers benchmark splits and semantic-segmentation baselines for construction-site and multimodal scene analysis.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D geometry generation requires maintaining global structural coherence alongside fine-grained surface details. While recent coarse-to-fine frameworks leverage Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to condition local queries, we reveal a critical training-inference resolution discrepancy: coordinate guidance and geometric supervision are aligned during training, whereas inference decodes high-resolution geometry from coarse spatial coordinates. This mismatch introduces a severe distribution shift that degrades fine details. To overcome this, we propose Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT), which anchors RoPE guidance at 512 resolution while supervising geometry at 1536, enabling robust detail extrapolation. Additionally, to eliminate high-resolution data bottlenecks, we present Dual3D-300K, a large-scale paired dataset comprising 300K watertight 3D point clouds explicitly aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RDT substantially improves sharp geometric regions, while Dual3D-300K offers a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.
authors: Jiale Zhang, Yang Liu, Chengyang Li, Jin Yuan, Qianxi Jia, Taicheng Huang
bullets: Identifies a training–inference resolution discrepancy that causes distribution shift and loss of fine surface details.
Uses Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT): RoPE guidance at 512 resolution with geometry supervision at 1536 resolution.
Introduces Dual3D-300K, a paired dataset of 300K watertight point clouds aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions.
Experiments show improved generation of sharp geometric regions and provide a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed RDT-3D framework. Training (Left): RDT-3D decouples spatial guidance from geometric supervision. Coarse point clouds (5123) provide spatial query locations injected into the DiT via ROPE, while fine point clouds (15363) are encoded into high-resolution GT shape latents for diffusion training. Inference (Right): Spatial queries sampled from a coarse mesh guide the trained DiT to generate fine shape latents, which are subsequently decoded into a high-fidelity 3D mesh via Marching Cubes.
Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Compared to existing approaches, our method captures significantly finer geometric details and produces sharper surface reconstructions.
Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison for ablation study. RDT recovers sharper edges and thinner structures.

papers.title: RDT-3D: Resolution-Decoupled Training for High-Fidelity 3D Geometry Generation
papers.tldr: RDT-3D addresses resolution mismatch in coarse-to-fine 3D generation by training coarse spatial guidance with high-resolution geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: While single-image 3D texture generation has advanced significantly, conditioning texture synthesis on multi-view reference images remains largely under-explored, despite its necessity for resolving surface ambiguity in unobserved regions. In this paper, we propose RouTex, a novel multi-reference 3D texture generation framework based on in-context Diffusion Transformers (DiT). Our key insight is that native 3D Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) inherently possesses spatial addressing capabilities. We introduce Positional Routing (PR) to reprogram 3D RoPE along spatial and semantic dimensions, establishing explicit reference-to-view correspondence without introducing additional parameters. To execute this routing efficiently, Dual-Granularity Attention (DGA) combines per-view local attention for fine texture fidelity with global joint attention over deduplicated references for cross-view consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RouTex achieves new state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.
authors: Chengyang Li, Yang Liu, Jiale Zhang, Qiang Rao, Wei Zhang, Taicheng Huang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in unseen surfaces that single-image texture generation cannot resolve.
Introduces Positional Routing to reprogram native 3D RoPE without adding parameters.
Uses Dual-Granularity Attention: local per-view attention for texture detail and global attention for cross-view consistency.
Experiments show state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.

papers.abstract: Super-resolution and quality enhancement of 1.5\,T brain MRI are normally validated with image-fidelity metrics, although their purpose is to improve downstream analysis. We study whether enhancement improves tissue segmentation, and for which segmenters. We propose an unpaired, physics-guided training pipeline for a lightweight ($\le$2.5\,M parameter) recurrent convolutional enhancer: a six-module stochastic 1.5\,T degradation operator, a residual adversarial network that adds scanner-specific texture without moving anatomy, and a cycle-consistent objective with an anti-identity penalty that rules out the copy solution. We then train U-Net, Swin-UNet and wavelet token-mixing segmenters \citep{jeevan2023wavemix} from scratch on either raw or enhanced 1.5\,T images of the same subjects, using identical labels and subject-level splits, for three enhancer variants and two datasets. On ABIDE (41 held-out subjects, FreeSurfer labels) enhancement significantly improves the wavelet segmenter (mean Dice $+0.014$, Wilcoxon $p=3.5\times10^{-5}$; CSF $+0.018$, grey matter $+0.013$), significantly degrades the U-Net ($-0.008$, $p=5.1\times10^{-4}$) and leaves Swin-UNet unchanged. On IXI, whose labels come from FSL-FAST, enhancement lowers Dice for all nine pairings, almost entirely through CSF; we trace this to spatially implausible CSF voxels in the labels that penalise smoother predictions. Enhancement of low-field MRI should therefore be validated per downstream model and against reliable labels.
bullets: The study evaluates enhancement by downstream segmentation rather than image-fidelity metrics alone.
It uses an unpaired, physics-guided pipeline with a lightweight recurrent convolutional enhancer, stochastic degradation, scanner-texture modeling, and cycle-consistent training.
On ABIDE, enhancement improved WaveMix segmentation, degraded U-Net, and did not change Swin-UNet performance.
On IXI, enhancement reduced Dice for all tested segmenter–enhancer pairings, mainly because of implausible CSF labels.
Results support validating MRI enhancement per downstream model and against reliable annotations.

papers.abstract: The release of SAM 3D Body is a recent development in human mesh recovery, demonstrating improved performance in producing clean, topologically coherent meshes from single images. By leveraging the Momentum Human Rig (MHR), it achieves robustness to occlusion and diverse poses. However, our evaluation reveals a specific and consistent limitation: the model struggles to reconstruct detailed anthropometric deviations, particularly in populations exhibiting distinctive morphological alterations such as geriatric muscle atrophy, scoliosis, or pregnancy, even when these features are prominent in the input image. In this paper, we investigate this phenomenon not as a failure of the model's capacity, but as a byproduct of the "perception-distortion trade-off". We posit that the architectural reliance on the low-dimensional parametric MHR representation, combined with semantic-invariant conditioning (DINOv3) and annotation-based alignment, creates a pervasive "regression to the mean" effect. We analyze these mechanisms to understand why individual biological details are smoothed out. Furthermore, we state our contributions by proposing specific, constructive pathways for future work, such as implicit-explicit hybrid representations and Medical-in-the-Loop alignment, to extend the baseline performance of SAM 3D Body into the high-precision medical domain.
authors: Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Ruting Cheng, James Hahn
bullets: Identifies consistent under-reconstruction of features such as geriatric muscle atrophy, scoliosis, and pregnancy-related morphology.
Attributes this to a perception–distortion trade-off and regression toward average body shapes.
Links the effect to the low-dimensional MHR representation, semantic-invariant DINOv3 conditioning, and annotation-based alignment.
Proposes implicit–explicit hybrid representations and Medical-in-the-Loop alignment as directions toward medical-grade fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates limitations of a 3D human mesh recovery foundation model and proposes pathways for improving anthropometric fidelity.
papers.title: Investigating Anthropometric Fidelity in SAM 3D Body
papers.tldr: SAM 3D Body produces coherent human meshes but tends to smooth distinctive anthropometric features, limiting high-precision medical reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.

papers.abstract: Dynamic driving scene reconstruction has made remarkable strides in recent years by leveraging generative priors, particularly in the quality of novel trajectory rendering. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between the generated data and real-world sensor observations, severely hindering further improvements in reconstruction fidelity. In this paper, we present ReconDreamer#, a self-evolving framework that synergizes reconstruction and generation for dynamic driving scenes, which substantially bridges the gap between synthesized novel trajectory data and recorded real-world observations. Within this self-evolving closed-loop framework, the generative and reconstruction models mutually reinforce each other through iterative refinement, ultimately yielding a significant enhancement in the 3D representation capability of the reconstruction model. Additionally, we introduce a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to further enhance the rendering quality of the reconstruction model. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks. Specifically on Waymo, at a 6-m lateral shift, ReconDreamer# improves NTA-IoU and NTL-IoU by 8.8% and 3.0%, respectively, and reduces FID by 15.1% relative to ReconDreamer++.
authors: Songling Liu, Guosheng Zhao, Xiaofeng Wang, Chaojun Ni, Guan Huang, Jiwen Lu, Xingang Wang, Zheng Zhu

papers.abstract: Large 3D repositories make it easy to collect assets, but difficult to determine whether they can be reused reliably across scene assembly, editing, rendering, game production, and training-data construction. An asset can look plausible in RGB while hiding disconnected geometry, problematic UV organization, or materials that fail to resolve correctly after import. We introduce Diagnostic Rendered Evidence (DRE): aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by pass-specific frozen ViT classifiers and combined through late fusion. On 1,234 human labeled TexVerse assets, nested grouped evaluation achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. On a separate, balanced 764 external reference test, DRE achieved 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy. Our method requires only an imported asset and renderer-derived evidence, without repository identity, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata at inference. Our results support cross-corpus portability and show that purpose built diagnostic views expose defects that just the beauty views can miss. Webpage: https://rbz-99.github.io/is-this-3d-asset-usable/
bullets: Addresses unreliable reuse of 3D assets whose geometry, UVs, or materials may fail despite plausible RGB renders.
Uses aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by frozen ViT classifiers and combined with late fusion.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

papers.abstract: Intracardiac flow is driven by complex, and time-varying cardiac motion and interaction with the heart valves, producing complex flow features that may provide valuable information for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. 4D Flow MRI enables non-invasive, time-resolved measurement of three-dimensional cardiovascular velocity fields. However, substantial noise and limited spatial and temporal resolution limit its ability to accurately resolve flow features. We propose 4D-MRAR (4D Magnetic Resonance Augmented Reconstruction), a deep learning (DL) method to super-resolve and denoise 4D Flow MRI data. Unlike prior DL methods that train and infer on static vascular regions, our method predicts intracardiac flow within hearts undergoing large deformation. Moreover, it uniquely allows for simultaneous super-resolution in 3D space and time. The method combines a residual convolutional neural network, a recurrent neural network, and an implicit neural field to predict high-resolution velocity and pressure fields while efficiently enforcing the governing equations of fluid flow during training. Trained on a synthetic dataset obtained from computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of left ventricle (LV) flow, our method generalizes to synthetic whole-heart 4D flow MRI data, and demonstrated promising performance on real 4D Flow MRI. The produced super-resolved flow fields exhibit significantly improved accuracy and greater consistency with the governing equations of blood flow compared with prior methods.
authors: Yusuf A. Ozturk, Jie Zheng, Fanwei Kong
bullets: Addresses noise and limited spatial-temporal resolution that obscure clinically relevant intracardiac flow features.

Trained on CFD-generated left-ventricle flow, it generalizes to synthetic whole-heart data and shows promising results on real 4D Flow MRI.
Produces more accurate, physically consistent flow fields than prior methods, though training relies on synthetic CFD data.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.
