papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.
authors: Fengzhi Guo, Nate Morrill, Shiqi Li, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified approach for 3D rigging and temporally stable 4D skeleton generation.
Generates an entire 4D sequence jointly in a single feedforward pass, while also supporting single-mesh 3D rigging.
Provides explicit control over skeleton count, uncertainty-based candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.
Uses a curriculum from large-scale 3D rigging data to mid-scale 4D mesh–skeleton data to reduce dependence on paired 4D training data.
Reports strong 3D rigging quality and high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FLOWRIG unifies rigging for both 3D and 4D meshes. Compared with prior methods such as Puppeteer (Song et al., 2025a) and UniRig (Zhang et al., 2025a), our model delivers accurate 3D rigging, preserves 4D temporal consistency, supports controllable bone count, achieves faster inference, and enables 4D skeleton prediction, including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.

Figure 2: FLOWRIG overview. We encode meshes into conditioning tokens, and initialize noisy skeleton slots, which are processed by a flow matching transformer to predict temporally aligned skeleton representations. The predicted features are decoded by the skeleton, graph, and uncertainty heads to recover 3D/4D rigging outputs, with uncertainty used for sample selection. n denotes the skeleton count, and ϕ denotes the unconditional token.

Figure 4: Static Reconstruction. Numbers from top to bottom are J2J, J2B, and B2B for each instance. Compared with baselines, our model preserves finer geometric details and achieves more accurate mesh alignment.

Figure 3: Data-efficient curriculum training. We first train on static 3D rigging, then adapt to 4D reconstruction, and finally enable prediction through masked conditioning. During the final stage, we use diverse masking patterns, including interpolation, forecasting, backcasting, and random masking, to expose the model to different temporal prediction settings. This schedule transfers large-scale 3D supervision to the data-scarce 4D setting.

Figure 5: Dynamic reconstruction and prediction. Blue indicates reconstruction with mesh guidance, while yellow indicates predictions without mesh guidance. In (b), from top to bottom, it shows interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting, respectively. Refer to the demo video for a clearer comparison.

Figure 6: Analysis of bone count control. Our model can freely control the number of bones to adjust skeletal detail, while existing baselines do not provide this level of controllable output granularity.

Table 1: Static skeleton reconstruction comparison. Our methods achieves strong reconstruction fidelity across diverse out-of-domain static datasets. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples and outperforms all baselines on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose. On ModelsResource, its zero-shot performance approaches that of RigAnything trained directly on the same dataset. See the "Baselines" paragraph for citations of these models.

Table 2: Dynamic quantitative comparisons on TexVerse dynamic dataset. N is time window length. PuppeteerD* means we finetuned Puppeteer-diverse model (Song et al., 2025a) on TexVerse training dataset. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples.
Table 3: Ablation studies on data sources. Metrics are evaluated on the TexVerse test set with T = 24.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified framework for 3D/4D skeleton generation using flow matching, bridging 3D vision, video generation, and robotic rigging/kinematics.
papers.title: FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for 3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching
papers.tldr: MoTWorld uses flow matching to generate controllable, temporally consistent skeletons for both static 3D and dynamic 4D meshes in one feedforward framework.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoLa3D, a simple and effective model for composable 3D scene decomposition that, given a single whole-scene latent from either a single image or an existing scene mesh as input, directly outputs a set of object meshes with consistent spatial layout that can be assembled back into a coherent scene. CoLa3D introduces a novel paradigm for 3D scene decomposition within a shared whole-scene latent, unlike alternatives that perform per-object generation in canonical spaces and then glue the objects back together with fragile pose and scale estimation. The network is a lightweight, flexible, and scalable query-based transformer that accepts various types of queries, including 2D masks, 3D points, and learnable queries, and learns to decompose the scene into objects in a compact latent space. On both synthetic and real-world datasets, CoLa3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on composable 3D scene decomposition, substantially improving global scene-level consistency and object-level quality while running 2 times faster and using less than 1% of SAM 3D's training data. Visible depth on par with MoGe2 further confirms that latent decomposition preserves accurate visible scene geometry while producing physically complete, decomposable object meshes.
bullets: Takes a single-image or existing-mesh whole-scene latent as input and outputs object meshes that reassemble into a coherent scene.
Uses a lightweight, scalable query-based transformer with 2D-mask, 3D-point, or learnable queries.
Performs decomposition directly in a shared latent space, preserving global layout and object-level quality.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real-world datasets, runs 2× faster, and uses less than 1% of SAM 3D’s training data.
Produces physically complete meshes with visible depth comparable to MoGe2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CoLa3D. Starting from an RGB image or a holistic scene mesh, CoLa3D first obtains a structured scene latent zs geo with TRELLIS.2 [76] and augments it with 3D semantic features zs sem from Utonia [87]. A lightweight decomposition transformer then uses mask, learnable, or point queries to decompose zs = zs geo + zs sem through L blocks of self-attention, cross-attention to frozen DINOv3 [52] features f img, and alternating Latent-to-Query/Query-to-Latent cross-attention. Finally, a multi-hot assignment extracts per-instance latents {zo k}, which are decoded in parallel by the shared decoder D into aligned object meshes and can be recomposed in the global 3D space.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on real-world scenes. CoLa3D produces coherent decompositions on Replica and ScanNet++ images, demonstrating robust generalization from synthetic training data.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons on synthetic data. Compared with baselines, CoLa3D produces spatially coherent object meshes with correct relative positions and scales.
Figure 5: Architecture details of the attention block used in the Query-Based 3D Latent Decomposition Transformer.
Figure 6: Decomposition from holistic scene meshes. CoLa3D produces coherent object-level meshes across generated and existing holistic scene meshes.
Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparisons on synthetic scenes. We show more results on the 3D-FRONT InstPIFU split and MetaScenes following the same layout as fig. 3.
Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparisons on real-world scenes. We show more zero-shot results on Replica and ScanNet++ following the same layout as fig. 4.
Table 5: Detailed per-dataset inference time. We report the average per-scene inference time in seconds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CoLa3D, a query-based transformer for decomposing 3D scenes into composable object meshes from single-image or mesh inputs, directly addressing 3D scene understanding and generation.
papers.title: CoLa3D: Composable Latent 3D Decomposition
papers.tldr: CoLa3D decomposes a whole-scene latent into spatially consistent, composable object meshes while avoiding separate canonical-space generation and fragile pose alignment.

papers.abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.
bullets: Addresses holes and unresolved geometry in image-based 3D reconstruction, which typically recovers only visible surfaces.
Combines partial-point conditioning with global scene tokens and local spatial evidence to preserve input geometry.
Uses metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation in fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency.
Outperforms strong baselines on Replica and SCRREAM, especially in sparse-view settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ANCHORCOMPLETE. From a partial, colored point cloud, Stage 1 generates a metric-scale octree coarse to fine, one window at a time, and Stage 2 generates shape latents on the finest level, which are decoded, merged and meshed once. Each window is conditioned on its parent occupancy and visible points through the local path (warm start) and on its points through anchor tokens read by cross-attention (global path).

Figure 4: Qualitative reconstruction results on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) and SCRREAM (Jung et al., 2024). Given the same DA3 point cloud as input, our method achieves better scene completion performance.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative results on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) at N=4. Top-down views of the meshes each method reconstructs from the same partial DA3 point cloud, with the ground truth in the last column.

Figure 10: Additional qualitative results on SCRREAM (Jung et al., 2024) at N=4. Top-down views of the meshes each method reconstructs from the same partial DA3 point cloud, with the ground truth in the last column.

Figure 7: Sparse-view conditional scene completion. The DA3 input (top) loses coverage as views are removed, while our completion (bottom) stays closed across the range. Bottom row: ANCHORCOMPLETE at level 0, N=4 to 14 views; Replica provides 10 input frames per scene, so N=12 and 14 add held-out frames of the same sequence.

Figure 5: Real-world scenes. Two real-world rooms from eight views, top-down with an inside view inset (same camera in every column); NKSR (Huang et al., 2023), SG-NN (Dai et al., 2020), Seen2Scene (Meng et al., 2026) and ANCHORCOMPLETE take the same input. The baselines leave surfaces holed where coverage thins, while ours closes them.

Figure 12: Failure cases under degraded imagery. Real captures with simulated low light (top) and motion blur/noise (bottom). The degraded inputs cause DA3 to miss large scene regions, and our model completes around these gaps rather than recovering them.

Figure 3: Coarse-to-fine levels. The same model stopped at levels 0, 1 and 2 on a room corner of a real-world scene, with the mean F-scores of Table 2(b) on the right. Only level 2 separates the ladder rungs and the legs of the chair.

Figure 8: Input robustness. F0.05 as the input is perturbed with Gaussian noise at a fixed 50k points (left) or thinned out (right), with no retraining, each on the DA3 cloud and on ground-truth points. The model is unaffected by noise up to the voxel scale and by sparsity down to a quarter of the points.
Figure 6: Sparse-view robustness on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) and SCRREAM (Jung et al., 2024) (mean across scenes).

Figure 11: Generation diversity. The input point cloud and five samples drawn from it with different seeds, rendered at level 0 with a model trained on InternScenes and SAGE. The observed structure is kept in every sample, and the samples differ only in the regions the input does not cover.

Table 1: Quantitative reconstruction evaluation on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) and SCRREAM (Jung et al., 2024) with Nviews = 4. The best result in each metric column is shown in bold, and the second best is underlined. ∗ denotes our scene finetune of TRELLIS, with its output aligned to the input cloud; the unstarred row is the released object-pretrained model. Runtime is per-scene reconstruction on an RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q.

Table 2: Ablation study. (a) Partial-point conditioning on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) (Nviews=4; the two ablated rows are trained on the TRELLIS backbone) and (b) the finest level of the coarse-tofine generation on held-out scenes; distances in metres.

Table 3: Generalization across input point-cloud sources on Replica (Straub et al., 2019). ANCHORCOMPLETE is evaluated without retraining on partial point clouds from multiple acquisition paradigms, using the default DA3 evaluation protocol (Table 1). Visual-SLAM and LiDAR use full trajectories/scans and therefore demonstrate source generality rather than budget-matched performance. † LiDAR uses conservative 5 cm range noise.

papers.selection_reason: Complete scene mesh reconstruction from partial point clouds built on TRELLIS.2, a generalist 3D foundation model.
papers.title: AnchorComplete: Recovering Complete Scene Meshes from Partial Point Clouds
papers.tldr: AnchorComplete reconstructs complete, globally consistent scene meshes from partial point clouds by anchoring generation to observed geometry and refining at metric scale.

papers.abstract: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how ``solved'' they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of refining or adding views in geometric foundation models that rely on one-shot or sequential-state prediction.
Uses an iteration-independent update operator that jointly updates previously solved and newly added views.
Trains the solver to preserve accurate reconstructions while correcting inaccurate intermediate states.
Caches solved-view representations as reusable geometric context for more compact and efficient iterations.
Demonstrates broad reconstruction capabilities without task-specific training or separate modules.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview. Left: A stationary transformer block repeatedly updates the multi-view state through frame-wise and global attention, initial-state injection, and state normalization. Right: The same operator continues refining the reconstruction across solver calls, allowing new views to be introduced at any stage and jointly updated with existing views. Camera poses, depth maps, and ray maps can be decoded from the current state after any solver call.

Figure 11. Streaming reconstruction. Qualitative comparison with window-based reconstruction [26], recurrent-state methods [21, 90], and geometric-context approaches [18] on long sequences, with camera trajectories colored by position error.

Figure 7. Mixed-progress solving. Left: pose accuracy when each view is initialized from a randomly sampled reconstruction stage. Right: rotation error as each view progresses through a pipelined reconstruction window, where views enter and leave after each solver call. Solv3R maintains accurate reconstruction across views with varying reconstruction stages, whereas DéjàView is sensitive to their computational progress.

Figure 12. Streaming accuracy vs. efficiency. Comparison of online reconstruction methods in terms of geometric-mean pose ATE and per-frame runtime; bubble size indicates peak GPU memory. For Solv3R, S/L denotes small/large memory configurations, and numbers indicate solver calls per frame (L8 is the default).
Figure 21. Offline reconstruction comparison. All methods see the same 100 images at once. VGGT, DA3-L, and VGGT-Ω misplace the second room, while Solv3R reconstructs both rooms in one piece.
Figure 22. Offline reconstruction comparison. All methods see the same 44 images at once. π3 and DA3-L misplace parts of the scene, while Solv3R keeps the walls and floor in place.
Figure 24. Streaming reconstruction comparison. The methods and settings are those of the streaming figure of the main paper. Camera trajectories are colored by position error.

Figure 23. Offline reconstruction comparison. All methods see the same 100 images at once, and the ceiling is removed for display. Insets show the predicted cameras in color and the reference cameras in gray, seen from above. Solv3R places the cameras closest to the reference, while VGGT and VGGT-Ω fold the room.

Figure 16. Memory on a long sequence. GPU memory over the 2000 frames of the long office sequence of TUM RGB-D, on a logarithmic axis. All methods are evaluated on a single H100 GPU. Crosses mark where a method runs out of the 80 GB of GPU memory (gray dotted line).

Figure 5. Stable and corrective solver dynamics. Left: pose accuracy and relative state update norm over solver calls. DéjàView is trained with up to 16 steps (shaded). Middle: camera rotation error and relative state update aligned to the solver call at which each window meets the stopping criterion of (5), showing median and interquartile range. Right: rotation error at call 16 after perturbations at call 8 using relative (rel.) or fixed-scale (fixed) Gaussian noise, or state resets (reset).

Figure 2. Comparison of geometric update mechanisms. Conventional GFMs [51, 88, 95] use successive layer-specific transformations, tying their intermediate representations to layer depth. Recurrent-memory models [21, 90] process incoming frames while updating a persistent scene memory across observations. Although DéjàView [12] shares transformer weights, its updates remain conditioned on the refinement step. Solv3R applies the same stationary update operator regardless of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated.

Figure 3. Continuing geometric solving with new observations. When new views are introduced, Solv3R continues solving from its existing state, jointly refining both previously reconstructed and newly added views. DéjàView struggles to maintain consistent reconstruction. Numbers indicate camera rotation errors in degrees.

Figure 9. Revisability and reuse. (a) Original-view rotation error when new views join at different refinement stages, compared with the no-join control; percentages indicate the fraction of improved windows. (b) Final pose accuracy versus total reconstruction time as the view set expands from 8 to 64. Solv3R improves existing estimates across different join times and achieves comparable accuracy to re-solving with less computation.

Figure 6. Warm-start convergence. Left: depth AbsRel along a KITTI [33] sequence, warm-starting each new frame from the previous solution with four solver calls. Right: percentage of new frames with rotation error below 2◦ versus solver calls in a 24-view window, comparing warm-starting with restarting from scratch. Solv3R remains stable under continued warm-starting and achieves accurate camera estimates with fewer calls, whereas DéjàView diverges.

Figure 20. One scene under the four arrival patterns. Shown as in Fig. 19. All four patterns end in nearly the same reconstruction, although the views arrive in different orders and receive different numbers of calls.

Figure 19. Reconstructions that grow as views arrive. Each row shows one scene at three stages of one arrival pattern. Offline solves all views jointly, incremental adds the capture in thirds, streaming adds video frames one at a time, and arbitrary order adds random groups of views. Views that join continue the running solve, and the views already in it keep their states. Above each panel are the number of views in the solve and the number K of solver calls run so far. Arrows give the views that joined, and orange marks their cameras.

Figure 10. Relocalization against a frozen map. Green dots are query estimates within 5 cm and 5◦ of the ground truth (gray rings), and red crosses are the others, linked to their ground truth. Above each panel are the cache size per map view and the fraction of queries within 5 cm and 5◦. With the smallest cache, Solv3R localizes as many queries as the most accurate baseline.

Figure 13. Stopping calls. Left: number of windows per stopping call, for the 144 of the 148 windows of the stability analysis that reach γ = 0.02, stacked by dataset. Right: rotation error of each window at its stopping call.

Figure 15. Initialization in streaming. ATE of on-arrival predictions with the L8 window for different numbers of calls per frame. Each new frame starts from its initial state z0 (cold start) or from z0 plus the solved offset of the previous frame (warm start).

Figure 17. Attention across solver calls. We show the three global-attention heads, out of 12, that best find ground-truth correspondences at call 16. These are the same heads in Solv3R (left) and DéjàView (right). Top: fraction of query patches whose strongest attention in an adjacent view falls within one patch of the ground-truth correspondence. Bottom: similarity to the call-16 attention map, measured as the share of the call-16 attention mass on the 64 most attended keys of each call and normalized to 1 at call 16. The shaded range is the 16-step schedule of DéjàView. Averaged over 82 windows of ETH3D and ScanNet++.
Figure 18. Failure case. In this window, views 5–8 share little content with views 1–4. Solv3R places them at a wrong position and orientation within 16 calls and keeps them there up to call 64.

Table 3. Streaming reconstruction benchmarks. Comparison with state-of-the-art streaming reconstruction methods across camera pose, video depth, and 3D reconstruction. We report per-frame runtime (ms) and peak GPU memory (GB), together with camera trajectory ATE (m), depth AbsRel and δ1.25, and reconstruction Chamfer distance (m) and normal consistency (NC).

Table 1. Standard (offline) multi-view reconstruction benchmarks. Quantitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods [12, 27, 42, 47, 51, 88, 89, 95] across five benchmark datasets [16, 40, 70, 71, 107]. We report camera pose AUC@3/@30 (↑), geometry relative L2 (↓), and inlier ratio (IR, ↑). TFLOPs are measured for 24 views. Solv3R (fixed) uses 16 solver calls, while Solv3R (adaptive) stops based on the relative state update criterion in Eq. (5) with γ = 0.02.

Table 4. Ablation study. All ablated variants are fine-tuned for 3k steps from the same pretrained initialization. The released DéjàView and the final Solv3R models are included as references. papers.abstract: Reconstructing detailed geometry and realistic appearance from a single RGB image is essential yet fundamentally challenging due to inherent ambiguities such as occlusion, lighting variations, and texture-geometry entanglement. While recent diffusion-based generative models have significantly improved novel view synthesis, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: lack of cross-view geometric consistency and insufficient cross-domain semantic alignment. To address these issues, we introduce UniCross3D, a unified cross-view and cross-domain diffusion framework designed explicitly for consistent and physically coherent 3D generation. UniCross3D features two novel contributions: (1) a cross-view latent regularization that enforces cross-view geometric consistency across synthesized viewpoints by penalizing latent variance, and (2) a cross-domain mutual information objective grounded in the physics of image formation, explicitly aligning synthesized color and normal maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniCross3D achieves significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly under challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.
bullets: Addresses ambiguities from occlusion, lighting, and texture–geometry entanglement in single-RGB-image 3D generation.
Uses cross-view latent regularization to reduce geometric inconsistencies across synthesized viewpoints.
Introduces a physics-grounded mutual information objective to align synthesized color and normal maps.
Experiments report better view consistency, semantic alignment, and reconstruction fidelity, especially for challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.

These issues become especially severe when generating views from novel, unseen viewpoints. papers.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: https://xiaokunsun.github.io/SeMo3D.github.io/.
bullets: Reframes all three tasks as synthesizing a selected region while retaining contextual content.
Uses region-selective denoising to train jointly on standard 3D assets without paired editing or completion data.
Introduces Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer supporting image, text, and point guidance.
Experiments across three benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across generation, editing, and completion, with controllability and consistency.
Supports natural-language-driven 3D creation for agents.

papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
bullets: Introduces drawing-to-render correspondence: deciding whether an orthographic drawing and shaded render depict the same part.
Builds BlueCAD-30K from 29,925 CAD models with aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings across six viewpoints, and surface metadata.
Frozen encoders achieve up to 65% Recall@1 with known viewpoints, falling to 43% when viewpoints are unknown.
Zero-shot vision-language models reach 0.52–0.67 verification accuracy and exhibit model-specific Yes/No biases.
LoRA fine-tuning slightly improves accuracy but does not solve viewpoint failures and intensifies bias.

papers.title: Blueprint2CAD: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Engineering Drawing-to-CAD Render Correspondence
papers.tldr: Blueprint2CAD introduces a benchmark showing that matching engineering drawings to CAD renders remains difficult, mainly because of viewpoint variation rather than encoder choice.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.
bullets: Motivation: Strong single-image benchmark performance does not guarantee coherent 3D structure over video or viewpoint changes.
Method: Evaluate predictions on real-world video sequences with moving cameras and use structure from motion to anchor affine-invariant depth to metric values.
Findings: The evaluation exposes challenges in achieving temporal consistency over long time periods.
Scope: It also reveals limitations in directly using structure from motion for metric grounding of monocular depth.
Contribution: A viewpoint-sequence benchmark methodology for assessing consistency and metric applicability of monocular depth models.

papers.abstract: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.
bullets: Motivated by the abundance of unlabeled 3D shapes and the cost of physics simulations, the work derives geometry-pretraining targets from the Euler-Lagrange equation for attached flow.
AREALS is a sign-free masked surface autoencoder using tokens that encode position, normal, and area, pretrained self-supervised on 61,822 raw meshes.
Sensors provide operating conditions, allowing one-pass completion of hidden fields without condition labels.
AREALS matches a scratch-trained model using half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++, and about one quarter on WindsorML.
With 20 sensors on DoubleDelta wings, it achieves 3.9× lower field error and 4.0× lower force error than GABI; pretraining also halves error beyond training angles.

figures.caption: Figure B.1. The Euler–Lagrange construction and its guarantees. Assuming only locality, the shift symmetry, rotations and Galilean boosts fixes the flow’s Lagrangian density as the pressure, with the gas’s equation of state the only free function; making its integral stationary gives the Euler–Lagrange equation, the law the flow obeys. Each guarantee on the right follows from this construction, and its last line says what AREALS builds in or learns from it.

Figure B.2. Near the wall the Euler–Lagrange equation needs only local geometry, the distance encodes it, and pretraining reads it (schematic; computed counterparts in Figure 2). (A) Bodies with the same wall around p, the wall point nearest x, have the same Euler–Lagrange equation at x, though not the same flow: in wall coordinates the Lagrangian density, the pressure times √ g, sees the shape only through the surface metric gS and the shape operator W at p. (B) The level sets and steepest lines of the distance are those coordinates; the value, Hessian and third derivative of ηS = 1 2 d2S give the wall, its normal lines and their spreading W (Lemma 1). (C) The pretrained decoder reads the distance and normal line at each query’s nearest wall point from nearby tokens; W is not supervised. Widths and the dashed radius in C are schematic; the 52% is measured on 16 DoubleDelta test wings (Section K).

papers.title: Large Geometry Models Are Priors For Fast Physics Pretraining
papers.tldr: Euler-Lagrange-informed geometry pretraining enables fast, sensor-conditioned prediction of physical fields from 3D shapes with substantially fewer simulations.

papers.abstract: Monocular semantic SLAM aims to reconstruct scene geometry and build semantic maps from RGB observations. Existing Gaussian-based methods often attach semantic labels or features to evolving Gaussian primitives, making semantic fusion difficult to maintain and increasing reconstruction overhead. Hybrid Gaussian--voxel representations provide more stable semantic support, but often rely on RGB-D input or known poses and do not revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates. We present UniGS-SLAM, an RGB-only framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics from Gaussian reconstruction while preserving bidirectional interaction. Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, while semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, enabling historical contributions to be revised as reconstruction evolves. The fused semantics further guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering, and geometric reconstruction performance among representative RGB-only methods, together with strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet. We also achieve a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/UniGS-SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses unstable semantic fusion and costly reconstruction in Gaussian-based monocular semantic SLAM.
Uses foundation priors to improve monocular depth and pose estimation while decoupling semantics from Gaussian reconstruction.
Stores semantics in a provenance-aware sparse voxel map, allowing historical evidence to be revised after geometry updates.
Uses fused semantics to guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement.
Reports leading performance among representative RGB-only methods on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360, with a 2.37× reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline.

papers.title: UniGS-SLAM: Monocular Gaussian SLAM with Enhanced Geometry and Open-Vocabulary Semantics
papers.tldr: UniGS-SLAM is an RGB-only monocular Gaussian SLAM system that jointly improves geometry, tracking, rendering, and open-vocabulary semantic mapping through bidirectional Gaussian–voxel interaction.

papers.abstract: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.
bullets: Replaces heuristic gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets with per-Gaussian loss-reduction decisions.
Uses efficient Taylor-based surrogates to estimate the objective change from primitive-level operations.
Extends second-order splitting to joint position-scale space for adaptive child locations and anisotropic extents.
Selects beneficial clones with principled opacity and applies selective soft decay to harmful primitives.
Improves rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets across standard 3DGS benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. (a) During training, we accumulate per-Gaussian surrogate statistics, including the joint splitting matrix and surrogate terms for cloning and opacity decay. At each densification interval, these surrogates determine whether each Gaussian is split, cloned, or assigned opacity decay. (b) For each Gaussian, we sequentially evaluate splitting, cloning, and opacity decay using accumulated loss-aware surrogate statistics. Joint splitting computes a loss-reducing direction in the joint position-scale space and initializes two children with corresponding position and log-scale perturbations. Cloning minimizes a local Taylor-based surrogate with respect to the duplicate opacity and appends a duplicate child when it is predicted to decrease the loss. Opacity decay similarly estimates a loss-reducing opacity decay strength and selectively decreases the opacity of Gaussians whose current contributions are predicted to be harmful.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on standard 3DGS benchmarks. Red boxes highlight zoom-in regions where our method better preserves fine details and object boundaries.

Figure 1: Intuition of our loss-aware adaptive density control (ADC). We visualize the effect of each density-control operation from the same intermediate state at the 3,000th training iteration. (a) Splitting: we compare the position-only split of [32] with our position-scale split, visualizing splitting Gaussians as ellipsoids. While the position-only split produces misplaced offspring around the thin bicycle handle, our position-scale split places offspring more appropriately and forms the handle structure more faithfully. (b) Cloning: we compare standard 3DGS and ours by individually cloning candidate Gaussians and measuring the resulting loss change; green/red indicate candidates whose duplication decreases/increases the loss. Our cloning selects mostly loss-reducing candidates and recovers missed structures, whereas heuristic cloning introduces loss-increasing candidates. (c) Opacity decay: we compare the opacity reset of standard 3DGS with our selective opacity decay. Opacity reset makes all Gaussian primitives nearly transparent, leading to unstable training. In contrast, our method weakens only Gaussians predicted to hinder optimization. (d) Component comparison: standard 3DGS relies on heuristics. SteepGS improves splitting with a position-only loss-aware rule but keeps cloning and opacity update heuristic. Our method applies loss-aware decisions to position-scale splitting, cloning, and opacity decay.

papers.selection_reason: Improves the adaptive density control mechanism in 3D Gaussian Splatting by using a loss-aware framework, directly contributing to the '3D Vision' subtopic of 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: Unified Loss-Aware Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: A unified loss-aware framework makes 3D Gaussian Splatting density control more targeted by predicting the local loss impact of splitting, cloning, and opacity decay.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.
bullets: Addresses feature collapse when jointly performing category discovery and test-time adaptation under domain shift.
Aggregates local 3D features using geometric density variations and enforces global class-wise prototype consistency for reliable pseudo-labels.
Models novel-category discovery as an optimal-transport assignment problem for globally consistent grouping.
Fuses semantic features from 2D vision foundation models with 3D features to create a more separable representation.
On three cross-domain benchmarks, achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 of 10 splits and improves mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

papers.abstract: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses weak grounded multi-step reasoning and text-centric inference in 3D large language models.
Interleaves task-relevant 3D scene evidence with textual chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses query-guided cross-attention to aggregate candidate objects while preserving ambiguity cues.
Introduces PointCoT, a 176.2K-instance 3D chain-of-thought instruction-tuning dataset covering captioning, QA, dialogue, and planning.
Experiments on six benchmarks report consistent improvements and state-of-the-art performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Construction of the 3D-text interleaved multi-modal CoT. Starting from a scene point cloud and a textual CoT, the framework first matches object-related mentions with candidate 3D objects, then performs query-based token fusion and ambiguity modeling to obtain evidence and ambiguity cues. These tokens are injected into the reasoning chain to form the final 3D-text interleaved multi-modal CoT.

papers.abstract: Advances in monocular depth estimation (MDE) now let an attacker generate depth from publicly available RGB images and submit forged RGB-D queries. Such attacks break a core assumption of RGB-D place authentication: that depth comes from a sensor. We study a presentation attack detection (PAD) classifier that uses geometric consistency between the enrollment and query views, as a software-layer defense. A three-stage evaluation shows how far this classifier detects software-injected depth, depending on how accurately the attacker knows the camera intrinsics. In the first stage, the attacker has only an estimate of the intrinsics, and the PAD classifier separates forgeries generated by all three MDE models with a validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997-0.999. In the second stage, the attacker obtains the exact intrinsics, and the original PAD classifier falls to near chance (AUC 0.54-0.61); a retrained PAD classifier, however, still has the registration residual between enrollment and query as a cue. In the third stage, an oracle evaluation, in which the evaluator fits warps using the ground-truth 3D geometry, shows that detection falls to near chance only in its strongest case, where every valid query keypoint is given its ground-truth 3D coordinate. Of the detection cues, the reprojection error captures the attacker's misestimate of the intrinsics, whereas the registration residual remains even when the attacker knows the exact intrinsics.
bullets: Generated depth from public RGB images violates the assumption that RGB-D authentication depth comes from a sensor.
With only estimated camera intrinsics, the classifier detects forgeries from all three evaluated MDE models with validation AUC of 0.997–0.999.
Knowing the exact intrinsics reduces the original detector to near-chance performance (AUC 0.54–0.61), while retraining preserves detection using registration residuals.
Reprojection error reflects intrinsic-parameter mismatch; registration residual remains informative even when intrinsics are known.
Under an oracle using ground-truth 3D geometry, detection becomes near chance only in the strongest attack case, where all valid query keypoints receive ground-truth 3D coordinates.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates attacks on depth estimation for place authentication, relevant to 3D geometry and security in embodied systems.
papers.title: Detecting Generated-Depth Injection Attacks on RGB-D Place Authentication
papers.tldr: Geometric-consistency PAD can detect generated-depth injection attacks, but its effectiveness depends strongly on the attacker’s knowledge of camera intrinsics and 3D geometry.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.
bullets: Targets CPU-based per-splat sorting, a major bottleneck in web and mobile viewers.
Groups splats into octree boxes of up to 128 and sorts only visible boxes; one dot product selects each box’s traversal direction.
Uses short order-aware fine-tuning while keeping 3DGS’s blending operator unchanged.
Across 13 standard scenes, loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average versus equally fine-tuned 3DGS and renders 4.5× faster in an OpenGL CPU-sorting viewer.
Also provides a 17-byte-per-splat format and a CUDA tile renderer using the same ordering scheme.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AbacusGS, an efficient rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that avoids per-splat sorting, improving the efficiency of 3D foundation models.
papers.title: AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
papers.tldr: AbacusGS accelerates Gaussian Splatting by storing approximate blending order in the scene, avoiding expensive per-splat depth sorting with only a small image-quality loss.

papers.abstract: Localized false-merge correction in connectomics requires converting an identified error into an executable native 3D partition. Still, neither intermediate correction predictions nor seeded graph solvers alone determine which native source-sink constraints should define that partition. We formulate this problem as a 3D-native partition-aware contact selection problem: selecting candidate contacts based on the complete partitions they induce. Our solution comprises two components: ContactCut (CC)-Auto, which uses learned single-contact selection, and ContactCut (CC)-Search, which enables bounded paired-contact search, generates compact alternatives, and applies learned panel ranking. On historical two-way false-merge corrections from MICrONS and FlyWire, CC-Auto improves failure-aware 3D partition (FA-3D Part.) mIoU by 5.9 and 3.4 points over the strongest graph-based controls and by 12.5 and 10.0 points over the best learned baselines. A MICrONS-trained ranker transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation. CC-Search expands oracle reachability and prioritizes near-oracle alternatives. The code is available at https://github.com/bentake/ContactCut.
bullets: Targets the gap between detecting a false merge and defining executable source–sink constraints for a native 3D partition.
CC-Auto learns to select individual contacts; CC-Search performs bounded paired-contact search and ranks compact alternatives.
On MICrONS and FlyWire corrections, CC-Auto improves FA-3D Part. mIoU over graph-based controls and learned baselines.
A ranker trained on MICrONS transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation.
CC-Search increases oracle reachability and prioritizes alternatives close to oracle solutions.

(b) Candidate contacts have centroids within 500 nm of the localized error cue x0 (red). Shown candidate centroids are green. The crossed marker denotes an excluded contact.

papers.abstract: Laser doppler vibrometer (LDV) scans can be used to detect defects and cracks in manufactured parts before they are deployed. This work presents a method for reconstructing the steady-state surface wavefield of a three-dimensional part by combining automated robotic manipulation with neural rendering. A six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) robotic manipulator (UFactory xArm6) with an embedded piezoelectric transducer presented an acoustically excited test article to a stationary LDV at a sequence of known orientations, yielding a set of complex-valued 2D scans with poses derived analytically from the arm kinematics rather than from image-based pose estimation. These scans were used to train a novel complex-nerfacto model, a modified Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) pipeline that replaces the standard three-channel RGB output head with a two-channel output. Complex-nerfacto represents the real and imaginary velocity components of a wavefield, preserving the complex measurement without quantization. Reconstructions of a welded aluminum cylinder and a welded T-bracket were evaluated against measured scans using Z-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). The complex-valued pipeline achieved a mean ZNCC of 0.60 at held-out viewing angles, compared with 0.28 for a baseline RGB nerfacto model trained on rendered images of the same data. The resulting surface wavefield reconstructions supported defect detection and characterization on complex components. We identify geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans as the remaining obstacle to practical deployment.
bullets: Automated 6-DOF manipulation presents parts at known poses to a stationary LDV, producing complex-valued scans.
A modified NeRF, complex-nerfacto, predicts real and imaginary wavefield velocity components without quantization.
Evaluated on a welded aluminum cylinder and welded T-bracket using Z-normalized cross-correlation.
The complex pipeline achieved mean ZNCC 0.60 versus 0.28 for the RGB nerfacto baseline at held-out viewing angles.
Practical deployment remains limited by geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans.

papers.abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
bullets: Addresses scarce, heterogeneous clinical data and the limitations of fixed, representation-based brain foundation models.
Pretrains a reusable, reconfigurable prior on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices.
Supports task-aligned synthesis for low-data prediction and post-training for image reconstruction.
Improved segmentation and classification across 48 downstream tasks and enabled high-fidelity enhancement across imaging conditions.
Multicenter stroke validation showed clinical applicability; radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy improved by 14% with AI assistance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of BrainGFM for Computational brain imaging. a. Heterogeneity in brain diseases, patient populations, clinical status, acquisition protocols, and clinical centers produces heterogeneous brain imaging distributions and limits the generalization of DL models. b. Our BrainGFM-1.3M comprises about 1.3 million axial slices spanning major MRI sequences and CT, providing a large-scale dataset for brain generative pretraining. c. Our BrainGFM learns a reusable brain-imaging prior from generative pretraining on our BrainGFM-1.3M dataset. d. Task-specific conditioning controls the pretrained generator where class labels are used for class-conditioned synthesis, segmentation masks for spatially conditioned synthesis, and source images for brain image reconstruction. These conditions are combined with task-specific adaptation as detailed in Fig. 6b,c. e. Evaluation spans 48 downstream tasks, comprising 20 segmentation, 8 classification, and 20 imageenhancement tasks. f. Clinical validation in a multicenter stroke cohort assesses BrainGFM for TOAST stroke subtyping, lesion segmentation, and MRI sequence transformation, as well as its clinical utility in reader studies and radiologist-AI collaboration.

Fig. 6 BrainGFM architecture, generative pretraining and downstream adaptation. a. BrainGFM pretraining consists of brain-domain adaptation of a multi-scale visual tokenizer and next-scale autoregressive generative pretraining. A shared encoder (E) and vector quantizer (Q) map brain images and segmentation masks into multi-scale discrete tokens using a shared visual codebook. The autoregressive Transformer learns the distribution of tokens through coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction under categorical modality and sequence conditions. The pretrained decoder (D) reconstructs brain images or segmentation masks from generated tokens. b. Task-aligned data synthesis adapts BrainGFM with limited supervision using LoRA. For classification, task-specific class conditioning enables the synthesis of class-labelled images for training ResNet50. For segmentation, BrainGFM generates task-specific masks and synthesizes corresponding images, producing image-mask pairs for training UNet. c. Task-adapted post-training adapts BrainGFM for image enhancement using paired source-target images. Source-image tokens condition autoregressive prediction of target-image tokens, while LoRA is optimized using token-level prediction and image-level reconstruction losses.

Fig. 7 Data flow and study design of BrainGFM. a. Eleven public brain-imaging resources comprising 64,754 3D volumes and 1,295,080 axial slices were collected and partitioned into pretraining and held-out subsets. The pretraining subset was used for two-stage generative pretraining, including visual tokenizer training and autoregressive modeling.Heldout samples from nine shared datasets, together with 15 additional public datasets, supported downstream evaluation across 48 tasks, including segmentation (20 tasks), classification (8 tasks), and image enhancement (20 tasks). Task-specific training data were constructed through labeled image–mask pair generation, class-conditioned image synthesis, and source– target image pairing. b. Six clinical stroke cohorts comprising 4,796 patients and 4,829 cases from two internal centers (JLH and NFH) and four external centers (NJH, WXPH, NJPH, and CZSPH) were collected. Task-eligible cases were selected according to task-specific imaging and annotation criteria for lesion segmentation, TOAST subtyping, and DWI-to-FLAIR transformation. Internal-center data were used for task-specific training, including low-data settings, while separate internal and external test sets were used for clinical validation.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Gaige Wang, Bowen Pan, Hao Ren, Jiangjing Lyu, Chengfei Lyu
bullets: Addresses poor orientation control and weak image-to-3D structural alignment in coarse 3D generation.
Uses a first-frame-anchored canonical space to align orientation with the input view while retaining object-centric normalization.
Combines a dual-tower DiT with auxiliary reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features.
Applies spatial-prior-guided attention using pixel-to-voxel correspondences.
Can replace existing coarse stages and consistently improves final 3D generation, with state-of-the-art performance reported.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Coarse3D. (A) First-frame Anchoring rotates the canonical geometry to zero the first view’s azimuth, turning orientation prediction into a well-defined, first-frameconditioned task. (B) Dual-tower DiT couples an Image-Tower, supervised by auxiliary tasks (Lrecon) to encode cross-view geometry, with a Geometry-Tower predicting the velocity field (Lgeo) via layer-wise cross-attention, trained end-to-end. (C) Spatial-prior-guided Attention regularizes cross-attention with a rasterized voxel-to-pixel prior (Lattn), strengthening 2D-3D correspondence.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison across three baselines (TRELLIS, TRELLIS2, and ReconViaGen). For each baseline, we show the original result (Baseline) and the result after replacing its first stage with our Coarse3D (+ Ours). Anchored by the first frame of the multi-view input (leftmost), our method yields (i) more controllable orientations, (ii) higher structural fidelity, and (iii) seamless plug-and-play integration without modifying subsequent stages.

Top: spatial prior Asp derived from geometric projection. Middle: base model attention Adense, which spreads diffusely across the object. papers.abstract: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.
authors: Armin Shafiee Sarvestani, Sheyang Tang, Jialu Xu, Zhou Wang
bullets: Addresses underconstrained HDR recovery and limited camera response function supervision from single-exposure LDR views.
Uses pseudo-HDR reconstructions as guidance while enforcing consistency with input LDR images through a closed reconstruction loop.
Learns a monotonic CRF prior to support plausible LDR re-exposure beyond the observed intensity range.
Factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and 3D gain field, reducing the impact of inconsistent pseudo-HDR targets and enabling HDR appearance editing.
Reports substantial superiority over baselines in extensive experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of PriorGS. Given single-exposure multi-view LDR captures of a scene, we reconstruct the 3D HDR scene as an LDR base extended by a 3D gain field. Input views supervise the LDR base, while pseudo-HDR targets generated by a 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction model impose LDR-to-HDR prior on HDR recovery. We then re-expose the HDR view by a priorconstrained learnable CRF to match the same input view, which closes the reconstruction loop.

Figure 1: Given the same single-exposure inputs, methods lacking learned LDR-to-HDR priors reconstruct the LDR novel view faithfully but fail at HDR radiance recovery. We leverage this prior to recover radiance much closer to the GT. HDR results are tone-mapped identically for visualization.

All curves are displayed using a logarithmic irradiance axis; the zero-irradiance samples are included during fitting but omitted from the visualization.

Increasing ρ for 3D HDR radiance scaling only shifts the histogram (equivalent to an exposure shift) and leaves the dynamic range (DR) unchanged. Our prior-constrained CRF maintains a plausible, monotonic response in this range, producing more faithful test-exposure renderings.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.
authors: Abdul Wasi, Akhil Gorugantu, Mahesh Bhosale, Anjan Dutta, Junsong Yuan, Sauradip Nag, David Doermann
bullets: Addresses limitations of whole-object rigging and 2D part-level handles in geometry-intensive image editing.
Uses CS-ARAP deformation with neighborhood covariance smoothing to reduce rotation discontinuities at part boundaries.
Introduces inversion-free selective texture transfer to move source appearance onto edited geometry through semantic matching.
Experiments report state-of-the-art geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the geometric editing pipeline. Stage 1 (Coarse 3D Editing): The input image is lifted to a 3D mesh and deformed using CS-ARAP with covariance smoothing and a bi-Laplacian solve (Lcoarse) to obtain a smooth mesh. Intermediate renderings and source views condition the diffusion model via IP-Adapter for identity preservation. Stage 2 (Global 3D Refinement): The Stage 1 Jacobian field is refined using Lrefine, combining handle constraints with SDS gradients from the diffusion model, producing a semantically plausible mesh for final rendering.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods. We compare RADI3N against other state-of-the-art methods across diverse object categories. Our method consistently produces geometrically faithful and photorealistic edits, while baselines exhibit artifacts, implausible geometry, or loss of scene context.
Figure 8. Extended qualitative comparisons across additional object categories. Each row shows the input, editing prompt, and outputs from all methods.
Figure 12. User Study: Comparing our method with FreeFine, GoodDrag, FlowDrag, Qwen-Image-Edit, ImageSculpting

papers.abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.
authors: Oliver Hahn, Rodrigo Marcuzzi, Sangeetha Grama Srinivasan, Alessandro Burzio, Sherwin Bahmani, Jiahui Huang, Stefan Roth, Shengyu Huang, Qunjie Zhou, Laura Leal-Taix\'e
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic generative 3D reconstruction and the semantic, instance-level understanding needed for robotics and physical AI.

Requires neither captured multi-view data, manual 3D annotations, nor per-scene optimization.
Supports novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, object grouping, and extension to structured dynamic scenes from monocular video.
Outperforms combined reconstruction and 3DGS-segmentation baselines on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks while preserving reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. Project Page: https://wzlwlm13.github.io/MLLM-GS
authors: Zhiliang Wu, Xinye Zheng, Kun Li, Fei Wang, Hao Guo, Yanyan Wei, Guanghui Yue, Beier Zhu, Wei Zhou, Xun Yang
bullets: Targets NVS under diverse extreme degradations without relying on degradation-specific models.

Optimizes 3DGS rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates to reduce computation, memory use, and optimization cost.
Experiments across multiple degraded scenes show effective degradation handling, high-quality synthesis, and substantially lower reconstruction time and memory consumption.
