papers.abstract: Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image requires realistic appearance, fidelity to the depicted object, and plausible physical behavior. Yet detailed geometry alone does not determine how an object should move or deform. We introduce PhysAg3D, which couples 3D generative models with agentic reasoning and tool use. A vision-language agent first infers semantic parts, candidate interactions, and physical priors from the image; a 3D generator then produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. A hierarchical interaction representation links these revisable priors to mechanisms and the generated surfaces they control, organizing interaction construction and refinement. Guided by this representation and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements guide targeted revisions within a fixed budget. The framework accommodates both rigid articulation and compliant deformation. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks demonstrate detailed, image-aligned assets with plausible interactions. Ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Project Page: supra-3d.github.io/PhysAg3D.
authors: Bi'an Du, Fanpeng Meng, Jiemin Fang, Chen Yang, Pufan Li, Daizong Liu, Qi Tian, Wei Hu
bullets: Targets single-image 3D asset generation with realistic appearance, visual fidelity, and physical interactivity.

Geometric and physical tools add rigid joints, deformable regions, and surface bindings while preserving useful generated geometry and materials.
Evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks show detailed assets with plausible interactions; ablations support bounded refinement and source-surface preservation.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.
authors: Mahmoud Elhadidy, Roshan M. D'Souza, Amirhossein Arzani
bullets: The study targets prediction of spatially resolved and spatially averaged time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) from sparse-view CT angiography.

Sampling and prediction were jointly optimized using Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K, and an agentic AI selector, alongside uniform and golden-angle baselines.
For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieved the lowest mean errors, with Agentic slightly better and notably stronger than fixed sampling under extreme sparsity.
Task-optimized projection masks focused on informative regions and differed fundamentally from masks optimized for image reconstruction.

papers.tldr: Agentic, task-aware projection selection can improve hemodynamic prediction from extremely sparse CTA acquisitions, even though its sampling patterns are poor for image reconstruction.

papers.abstract: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.
bullets: Addresses automatic extraction of reusable level chunks and higher-level graph structures from existing videogame levels.
Defines perceptual distance to measure relationships within level layouts.
Applies hierarchical clustering to segment levels into structural regions.
Compares the approach with prior StarCraft analysis and evaluates it on Super Metroid rooms.
Demonstrates proof-of-concept level generation using the resulting segments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The pipeline for computing the Perceptual Distance Segmentation shown on “Bubble Mountain” from Super Metroid. We begin by computing the probability of observing (angular area of) each visible surface (orange) from each point. The figure shows an example for a single point. Second, we use the Jensen-Shannon divergence of these probabilities to compute an approximate rate of change at each interior point (perceptual flux). We then find the minima of this field, and cluster the minima hierarchically based on the perceptual distance. Finally, the non-minima points are assigned to the cluster that they are closest to (in terms of perceptual distance).

Figure 11: A long hallway segmented with two different methods. In IJI, clusters below size 6 are also merged and the threshold value of 0.4 is chosen manually by the authors for best results. For PDS, the threshold value of 0.59 is the same as our other domains. papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at https://github.com/Jingong-Chen/GradSplat/.
authors: Jingong Chen, Linlian Jiang, Guangyuan Li, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Kwanghee Won
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap between feed-forward predictions and per-scene Gaussian optimization, mainly caused by Gaussian shape, scale, and rotation.
Uses log-anisotropy correction to adjust Gaussian axis ratios at constant volume.
Renders predicted Gaussians into input views and applies learned recurrent photometric-gradient updates, first to opacity and color, then to shape.
Requires no target view and preserves accuracy across 6–42 input views.
Reports best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods on complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, and strong zero-shot results on DL3DV and ScanNet++.

papers.abstract: Multi-source millimeter-wave (mmWave) observations offer an opportunity to learn human representations reusable across sensing tasks. However, sparse detections and multipath effects make these observations unstable, challenging existing point cloud pretraining methods. We propose PT$^3$, a prototype-guided self-supervised pretraining framework for mmWave human point clouds. PT$^3$ represents local states in spatial regions as sparse compositions of shared prototypes and learns their temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction. Observation consistency further stabilizes representations under radar perturbations. After pretraining on unlabeled sequences from multiple sources, the same frozen encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction on datasets not used for pretraining. Across these tasks, PT$^3$ outperforms the compared pretraining baselines and achieves competitive or superior performance to task-specific models.
authors: Ziyang Liu, Kieren Yu, Xiao Yang, Xin Yang, Kaishun Wu
bullets: Addresses sparse detections and multipath effects that destabilize mmWave point-cloud representations.
Represents local spatial states as sparse combinations of shared prototypes.
Learns temporal evolution through autoregressive prediction and improves stability with observation consistency.
A frozen pretrained encoder supports action classification, dense point generation, joint pose estimation, and future motion prediction across unseen datasets.
Outperforms compared pretraining baselines and is competitive with or better than task-specific models.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising alternative to per-scene optimization, enabling fast novel view synthesis by predicting Gaussian primitives directly from input images. However, it quickly faces a bottleneck of rendering efficiency while scaling from sparse to dense multi-view inputs, which offer more geometric constraints but produce a rapidly growing set of candidate Gaussians. Existing solutions cannot reliably distinguish redundant primitives, leading to many redundant primitives from repeatedly observed regions and increased rendering cost without much gain in visual quality. We propose BudSplat, a compact feed-forward 3DGS framework that learns to keep the most valuable Gaussians under a limited primitive count. BudSplat has two novel designs. The first is a detail-aware importance score that is extracted from multi-level visual tokens, providing an explicit cue for regions where pruning is likely to harm perceptual quality. The score can be injected into voxel fusion to preserve high-value local contributors during multi-view aggregation. The second is quality-aware Gaussian pruning that selects a compact set of primitives by jointly considering rendering contribution and detail importance. The quality-aware pruning enables local quota redistribution that helps avoid over-allocating primitives to large redundant regions. Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show that BudSplat achieves a favorable trade-off among rendering quality and efficiency.
authors: Muyu Xu, Fangneng Zhan, Yu Wei, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses the rapid growth of redundant Gaussian primitives as the number of input views increases.
Uses multi-level visual tokens to estimate detail-aware importance and preserve regions where pruning could hurt quality.
Introduces quality-aware pruning that jointly considers rendering contribution and visual detail.
Redistributes local primitive quotas to avoid wasting capacity on large, redundant regions.
Experiments on RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID show a favorable quality–efficiency trade-off.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudSplat. With dense geometry, confidence maps, and multi-layer tokens as predicted from multi-view RGB images by VGGT, the detail-aware decomposition first extracts residual token cues and predicts patch-level detail scores. The predicted scores are then propagated to the importance-preserving voxel fusion together with confidence and voxel support, retaining important local contributors during aggregation. Finally, the quality-aware pruning ranks the fused Gaussians by opacity, detail importance, and support-aware redundancy correction, followed by patch-level quota redistribution to select a compact set of retained Gaussian for rendering.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on challenging low-overlap target views. Red boxes highlight regions where baselines suffer from incomplete Gaussian coverage, blurred local structures, or uneven rendering quality. Our method allocates Gaussian budget more effectively, producing stable renderings and preserving perceptually important details with fewer Gaussians.

Figure 3: Target-view visualization of Gaussian density allocation and RGB rendering before and after pruning. Top row: projected Gaussian density before pruning, after pruning, removed density, and retention ratio. Bottom row: normal RGB rendering before pruning, after pruning, absolute difference, and reference image. The density diagnostic shows that pruning mainly removes redundant Gaussian support from low-frequency and highly overlapped regions, while preserving more support around high-frequency structures. The RGB difference map further shows that the remaining rendering changes are concentrated around edges, boundaries, and fine details rather than smooth regions.

papers.abstract: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
authors: Binjie Wang, Xinran Zhao, Shoubin Yu, Xiang Li, Silong Yong, Chenyang Yang, Tianyu Chen, Ruofei Du, He He, Chen Zhao, Tongshuang Wu

Evaluates 17 models using rendered outputs and human-reviewed checklists rather than code similarity alone.
Average success is 37%; even the strongest models solve fewer than 60% of structural and style edits.
As models improve, failures increasingly involve geometric foresight: executable code that produces the wrong shape.

Reviewer-model feedback describing render discrepancies helps more than additional reasoning effort or an agent harness, enabling a 27B model to exceed a 2.8T-parameter model’s single-shot performance.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT regress cameras and geometry in a single forward pass, but they report no uncertainty for the camera poses they predict: an incorrect relative pose looks no different from a correct one. We ask whether the frozen model nonetheless knows when its pose is wrong. On HardMatch, a benchmark of 1,000 deliberately difficult image pairs on which VGGT fails on 35% of pairs, a linear probe on VGGT's frozen features predicts pose failure on held-out categories with ROC-AUC 93.5%, compared with 79.7% for VGGT's own point-map confidence and 77.7% for a classifier trained on all of VGGT's outputs. The probe catches failures VGGT is confident about, lets a downstream system abstain on the pairs it distrusts, and transfers without retraining to rotation failures on PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500, beyond what co-visibility explains. This knowledge is absent from the per-image encoder: it is computed partway through the layers that fuse the two views, and the same holds for a second model, $π^3$. In essence, we find that VGGT knows more about its own failures than it reports.
bullets: VGGT fails on 35% of difficult HardMatch image pairs, but its frozen features reveal these failures.
A linear probe achieves 93.5% ROC-AUC, outperforming VGGT’s point-map confidence (79.7%) and a classifier using all outputs (77.7%).
The probe enables downstream systems to abstain on predictions likely to be incorrect.
Failure awareness transfers without retraining to rotation failures in PhotoTourism and ScanNet-1500.
This signal emerges during two-view feature fusion, not in the per-image encoder, and also appears in π³.

papers.abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. authors: Akshay Krishnan, Matias Turkulainen, Jamie Wynn, Zawar Qureshi, Mohamed Sayed, Guillermo Garcia-Hernando, Sara Vicente, James Hays, Michael Firman, Daniyar Turmukhambetov
bullets: Addresses unrealistic spatial layouts when generating views far outside the input viewpoints.
Uses cross-attention to combine posed street images with satellite-image conditioning while retaining pretrained diffusion priors.
Generates seamless novel views from only a handful of source views and no explicit 3D reconstruction.
Outperforms satellite-conditioned and street-view-conditioned baselines on outdoor datasets, particularly for targets with little source-view overlap.

papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) gives the electronic structure of materials, but its cost limits large-supercell calculations and materials screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonians bypass the self-consistent cycle but are usually system-specific; universal ones could cover new compositions and disordered solids. Such models must generalize across chemistry and keep downstream properties physical, while staying inexpensive for large cells. Here we introduce UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors rooted in density-functional tight-binding theory with deep learning. UniTB's network, which corrects a prior Hamiltonian, generalizes across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding. A projection bounds band shifts from the prior, suppressing spurious states and keeping downstream properties physical. We provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. The variant UniTB-Flash assembles its prior from two-center tables at $O(N)$ cost for $N$ atoms, against $O(N\log N)$ on a grid. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements. Without amorphous training data, both models agree with DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te. UniTB-Flash ranks candidates with no significant difference from UniTB, whose property values are more accurate; together they screen 16,195 crystals for five application domains of industrial relevance.
authors: Mingkang Liu, Zhanghao Zhouyin, Guanghui Wang, Daye Zheng, Lei Shen, Qiangqiang Gu
bullets: Addresses the high cost of DFT and the limited chemical scope of conventional machine-learned Hamiltonians.
Combines a density-functional tight-binding prior with a mixture-of-experts neural correction and charge equilibration.
Constrains band shifts to suppress spurious states and improve physicality of predicted properties.
Trained on 29,242 crystals, it achieves 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements.

UniTB-Flash enables linear-cost prior assembly and, with UniTB, screens 16,195 crystals across five industrial application domains; amorphous-material tests also agree with DFT without amorphous training data.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors with deep learning for materials science, fitting the 3D Foundation Models category.
papers.title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning
papers.tldr: UniTB uses physically structured, E(3)-equivariant machine learning to build fast, broadly transferable Hamiltonians for materials screening while preserving realistic downstream properties.

papers.abstract: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.
bullets: Addresses reduced MRI acquisition resolution, especially along the slice axis, without requiring a separate model for each geometry or scale.
Combines anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes, scale-conditioned frequency encoding, and exact measurement-consistency projection.
Uses one checkpoint per MRI contrast and supports arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic reconstruction resolutions.
Outperforms geometry-specific specialists at isotropic 2× and on perceptual metrics across geometries, though specialists achieve higher PSNR for anisotropic reconstruction.
Preserves downstream performance across segmentation, metastasis detection, and brain parcellation tasks, with reconstruction taking about 6 seconds per volume.

papers.abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) assisting human divers must continuously track not only the diver's 3D position but also their full-body orientation. However, vision-based perception is unreliable underwater, and forward-looking sonar -- despite being widely used -- discards the elevation information needed for orientation estimation, posing a fundamental limitation. Recently commercialized 3D sonar preserves elevation but produces sparse, noisy returns, and existing detectors are built for dense LiDAR data and for targets that remain upright and rotate only about the yaw axis (e.g., vehicles, pedestrians), making them unable to represent a freely pitching and rolling diver. To address this gap, we present two contributions. First, SonarVoxNet adapts a voxel-based encoder and an anchor-free center-based detection head to 3D sonar data, replacing the conventional yaw-only rotation representation with a continuous 6D rotation parameterization to predict full 9-DoF oriented bounding boxes -- to our knowledge, the first 3D sonar diver detector to do so. Second, Diver3D is the first public 3D sonar dataset with full 3D orientation labels for divers in diverse, non-upright poses, collected at a natural cave-diving site. Through controlled ablations over the backbone and detection head, we show that the dominant factor behind accurate 3D sonar-based diver detection is the transition from yaw-only rotation to full-SO(3) rotation. This transition substantially improves detection accuracy and reduces orientation error. These results demonstrate that full-body diver orientation is recoverable from 3D sonar alone, laying the groundwork for future work on diver pose estimation and diver-robot interaction.
bullets: Targets AUV diver tracking when vision is unreliable and conventional sonar lacks elevation.
Adapts voxel encoding with an anchor-free, center-based detection head for 3D sonar.
Uses continuous 6D rotations to predict full 9-DoF oriented bounding boxes, including pitch and roll.
Introduces Diver3D, a public cave-diving dataset with full 3D orientation labels.
Ablations show that replacing yaw-only rotation with full SO(3) rotation is the main driver of improved accuracy and lower orientation error.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
authors: Prakhar Kaushik, Soumava Paul, Alan Yuille
bullets: Addresses the memory and compute costs of radiance-field and splatting methods in resource-constrained settings.
Represents scenes and images with larger, locally planar hexagonal elements and first-order spatial color fields.
Across 34 scenes, improves PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB while using less training VRAM.
Delivers 2.31× faster FPS and up to 4.74 dB higher per-primitive quality than 2DGS in ablations.
Reduces reconstruction error by 28.9% on 15 DTU scans and achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods on 6 Tanks and Temples scenes.

papers.abstract: Existing evaluations of text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation largely emphasize semantic fidelity and physical validity at rest, leaving interaction-time physical reliability insufficiently assessed. To address this gap, we introduce ScIntBench, a unified benchmark centered on interaction readiness: it executes prescribed manipulation actions (e.g., pushing, opening, and surface probing) in physics simulation and measures task success, capability and progress, post-interaction integrity, and dynamic plausibility. Multi-view semantic and static physical evaluations complement these metrics and help explain interaction outcomes. We systematically evaluate 12 state-of-the-art scene generation systems across 10 room types. Our results reveal that strong semantic and static physical performance does not necessarily translate into interaction readiness: a system with near-perfect static plausibility completes only 11.54% of interactions, 7 of the 12 systems produce scenes that cannot support any interaction, and even the best system succeeds in only 36.92% of prescribed tasks. These findings highlight two fundamental challenges in generating interaction-ready scenes: providing the necessary physical interaction capabilities and ensuring reliable physical behavior under active manipulation.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.

Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.

papers.abstract: We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .
authors: Jaesung Lee, Hyeontaek Hwang, Gabriel Manalu, Daeyoung Kim
bullets: Targets referring expressions as both rendered 2D masks and explicit sets of 3D Gaussians.

It then performs QueryConditioned Cluster Scoring: the referring expression conditions the cluster tokens, and the MLP scorer ranks the candidates to select the Top-1 cluster as the explicit 3D target. Finally, Cluster-Level Mask Rendering assigns the selected cluster scores to Gaussians and renders a 2D mask supervised by the mask loss.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) remains unreliable under weak observations caused by long camera-to-person distances, occlusion, and motion blur. In challenging scenarios such as sports, these factors make the problem highly ambiguous, as different 3D poses may yield similar 2D projections. This ambiguity is especially severe for one-stage HMR, which recovers all meshes directly from the full image without person crops or external 2D cues. To handle this ambiguity, we present UT-HMR ( Uncertainty-guided Temporal HMR), to our knowledge the first one-stage HMR framework to capture correlated pose uncertainty across joints. Each person query predicts a Gaussian distribution over the full SMPL pose with a compact low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance, which is converted into joint-wise precision weights for heteroscedastic supervision while keeping inference deterministic. Temporal early fusion further injects neighboring-frame evidence before pose decoding, supplying the visual evidence needed to resolve the ambiguity that the uncertainty captures. With a lightweight ViT-B backbone, UT-HMR achieves state-of-the-art results on VIP-HockeyPose-v2 (ice hockey) and WorldPose (soccer), reducing MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, and PVE by up to 4.7%, 3.8%, and 5.6%, and remains competitive on 3DPW against methods with larger backbones and higher input resolutions.
authors: Zhibo Wang, Sirisha Rambhatla, Yuhao Chen, Maria Koshkina, David Clausi

The predicted covariance is supervised by the distribution loss and converted into joint-wise precision weights for the heteroscedastic joint loss.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.
authors: Gaurav Behera, Abhinav Raundhal, Archisha Panda, Saumya Balina, Gargi Shroff, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from faces, license plates, documents, and screens encoded in trained Gaussian splats.

Also introduces privacy-by-design training to prevent sensitive content from being embedded during optimization.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki, Boris Jutzi, Kwanghee Won, Kyle Gao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of geometry foundation models that assume pinhole cameras and lens-dependent image-position representations.

Evaluated across 13 central cameras and three datasets, Any3R is reported as the most consistently accurate method while predicting camera poses itself.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model robust to various camera types, advancing the capabilities of '3D Foundation Models' for heterogeneous data.
papers.title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
papers.tldr: Any3R enables feed-forward 3D reconstruction from images captured by arbitrary central camera types without lens-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

papers.abstract: Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.
bullets: Addresses a gap in isolated-asset and pose metrics: editable proxies must match the same object instance in its captured metric state.
Freezes the instance, cameras, scan-derived support, recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator while replacing only the object representation.
Defines the asset correspondence gap as lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry, without assuming the scan is complete ground truth.
Across two indoor RGB-D domains and two generation backends, generated assets lose 0.302–0.497 MaskIoU; disagreement involves both visible support and surface placement.
The evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover the mismatch, and generator preferences reverse across capture domains.

papers.abstract: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces (i) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and (ii) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer. Across 24 benchmarks, MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a scalable token interface that unifies medical image dimension, modality, and task usage.
bullets: Addresses fragmented tokenizers that are limited to specific image dimensions or modalities.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced rapidly with the development of foundation models that demonstrate strong zero-shot generalisation across diverse visual domains. However, the applicability of these models to visual perception for lower-limb prosthetics remains largely unexplored. Reliable depth perception is particularly important for prosthesis users, who often experience significant challenges when navigating stairs, uneven terrain, and other complex environments. To address this gap, we introduce the Lower-Limb Prosthesis (LP) dataset, a benchmark designed to evaluate depth perception from an emulated knee-level prosthetic viewpoint. Using this dataset, we evaluate four state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation foundation models. Our results provide the first systematic benchmark of monocular depth estimation performance from a prosthetic viewpoint, while highlighting both the challenges and the potential of deploying foundation models in prosthetic perception systems. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Ishivijay/lp_dataset.

papers.abstract: Recent multi-view Transformers (e.g., DUSt3R and VGGT) have advanced 3D reconstruction by scaling training data and model capacity from two views to many views and long sequences, subsuming the classical SfM/SLAM pipeline of feature extraction, matching, and pose estimation in a single feed-forward pass. Yet this subsumption hides the interfaces between pipeline stages---correspondences, geometry, and pose are entangled in a single forward pass, leaving supervised fine-tuning as the major path to improvement and offering no mechanism to correct predictions from geometric evidence at test time. We propose PosePlaner to close this gap by reviving the classical coupling between correspondences and pose via flow matching, treating pose refinement as a conditional generation problem that takes coarse geometric matches and initial pose as input condition and fuses the resulting pose hypotheses into a single refined estimate, providing a continuous, data-driven analog of RANSAC voting. Our method is trained efficiently on two-view data, yet serves as a periodic refiner for streaming n-view pose estimators with no retraining. Empirically, it corrects failures of feed-forward predictors, substantially improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces accumulated drift in long streaming sequences.
authors: Yihang Chen, Bin Tan, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu, Nan Xue
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of correspondences, geometry, and pose in modern multi-view Transformers.
Conditions pose refinement on coarse geometric matches and an initial pose, then fuses pose hypotheses into one estimate.
Provides a continuous, data-driven analogue of RANSAC voting.
Trained efficiently on two-view data and used as a periodic refiner for streaming multi-view pose estimators without retraining.
Corrects feed-forward failures, improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces drift in long sequences.

papers.abstract: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.
authors: Luke Hollis, Tianxing Fan, Heng Yang

papers.abstract: Significant advancements in 3D asset creation have enabled high-fidelity 3D generation from images. However, most existing representations remain inherently static, lacking the ability to model physically plausible behaviors under dynamic interactions. We present \textbf{PhysCreator}, a unified framework that directly generates simulation-ready 3D representations with spatially varying physical properties from images. Unlike prior approaches that treat physical attributes as simple post-hoc predictions or rely on expensive per-instance optimization, we reformulate physical property estimation within a unified 3D representation learning framework. We introduce a voxel-aligned latent space by lifting image observations into a spatially structured 3D representation, in which geometry, appearance, and physical properties are jointly modeled and inferred in a feed-forward manner. To enable scalable learning without densely annotated physical ground truth, we leverage vision-language distillation to transfer material-aware semantic priors from powerful vision-language models into spatially grounded voxel-level supervision. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior visual quality, physical plausibility, and generalization compared to prior approaches.
authors: Shiyan Zheng, Ming Li, Lei Han, Xiangyu Xu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static 3D representations that cannot model physically plausible behavior under interaction.
Uses a voxel-aligned latent space to jointly infer geometry, appearance, and physical properties.
Applies vision-language distillation to provide spatially grounded, material-aware supervision without dense physical annotations.
Experiments report improved visual quality, physical plausibility, and generalization over prior approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PhysCreator. Top: Given observations, our framework first constructs a voxel-aligned latent representation (the 3D latent). Built upon this shared representation, we decode simulation-ready 3D Gaussian primitives together with voxel-wise physical attributes, including Young’s modulus, density, Poisson’s ratio, and material category. Bottom: To provide scalable supervision, vision-language distillation generates part-level semantic and physical annotations, which are lifted into voxel-level labels for training the physical-material decoder. The predicted geometry and physical properties are then passed to an MPM simulator to evaluate and visualize dynamic behavior.

Figure 4 Effectiveness of spatially varying physical property modeling. Top: PhysCreator enables the flower to sway while keeping the pot stable, and allows the snow body to deform while preserving the hat; PhysGM produces implausible deformation due to uniform properties. 1D samples across time (space–time slices highlighted by dotted lines) are included to better visualize the temporal dynamics. Bottom: PhysCreator localizes motion to the flower while keeping the pot and chair stable, whereas PhysGM causes all components to move together. The blue dashed axes highlight this unintended coupled motion.

Figure 1 We present PhysCreator, a physics-aware 3D generative model that produces simulation-ready 3D Gaussians with spatially-varying, semantically-consistent physical properties directly from images. Our method enables the joint prediction of geometry and physically meaningful attributes, such as material type, stiffness, and density, with strong generalization across diverse objects. The generated 3D Gaussians can be seamlessly integrated into simulations, yielding realistic and dynamic physical behaviors.

Figure 3 Qualitative comparison of simulated dynamics under gravity. PhysCreator produces stable and physically consistent motion with realistic contact and deformation. papers.abstract: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving both global spatial consistency and fine geometric details in single-shot fringe projection profilometry.
Uses a Swin-based U-shaped encoder–decoder with visual state space modeling at an intermediate resolution.
Introduces an axial and dilated vision state space block with local, dilated, and axial convolutions plus four-directional selective scanning.
On a public FPP dataset, outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet across MAE, RMSE, absolute relative error, and SSIM.
Achieves 0.548 mm RMSE and 0.9985 SSIM from a single deformed fringe image; evaluation is limited to the reported public dataset and metrics.

papers.abstract: Language-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced language-driven 3D scene understanding by incorporating semantic and relational cues into reconstructed scenes. However, relation-aware grounding depends not only on representing such information, but also on whether the underlying scene-side evidence is reliable and sufficient. Multi-view semantic aggregation can incorporate weak observations, while object relations can remain under-observed along the available camera trajectory, leading to ambiguous evidence for target disambiguation. We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines semantic and relational evidence for 3D visual grounding. RelateGS suppresses unreliable observations during semantic feature uplifting and consolidates multi-view object observations into a persistent 3D graph. The graph further identifies under-observed object relations and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames to complement their evidence. Experiments on Sr3D+ and Nr3D demonstrate competitive 3D grounding performance, improving the previous best by 7.9 and 1.7 percentage points at Acc@0.25, respectively.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous target disambiguation caused by weak semantic observations and incomplete relational evidence.
Suppresses unreliable multi-view observations during semantic feature uplifting.
Builds a persistent 3D object-relation graph from multi-view observations.
Uses the graph to identify missing relations and re-query informative existing frames.
Improves prior best Acc@0.25 by 7.9 points on Sr3D+ and 1.7 points on Nr3D.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RelateGS. Given a reconstructed 3D Gaussian scene and posed RGB-D observations, RelateGS selectively refines the scene-side evidence used for relation-aware grounding. At the Gaussian level, weak multi-view observations are filtered during semantic uplifting. At the object level, multi-view observations are consolidated into a persistent graph, whose current state identifies under-observed object pairs and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of relation-aware 3D visual grounding on ScanNet. The ground-truth column shows the target object in green and distractor objects in red. For each method, green denotes the ground-truth target, yellow indicates a correctly grounded prediction, and red indicates an incorrect prediction. Compared with language-embedded Gaussian representations and RelateGS without relational re-querying (w/o RQ), the full RelateGS more reliably resolves targets from relational expressions by complementing underobserved relational evidence.

Figure 1. Motivation of RelateGS. Existing methods can suffer from (A) unreliable semantic evidence due to weak multiview observations and (B) insufficient relational evidence due to limited viewpoint coverage. RelateGS addresses these issues by (A) filtering weak observations during semantic feature uplifting and (B) complementing under-observed relations through graphguided re-querying of informative existing views.

papers.abstract: Medical image segmentation remains fragmented along two axes: segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality. Existing methods are typically developed separately for semantic, in-context, and interactive segmentation, and are further specialized to either native 2D images or 3D volumetric data. In clinical practice, however, segmentation workflows take many forms: a case may be initialized by semantic prediction, reference-guided segmentation, or user interaction. Regardless of how it begins, fine-grained refinement is naturally performed on 2D views; for volumetric scans, such 2D edits must propagate coherently to the rest of the volume. We present UniPro, a unified model that bridges segmentation paradigms and data dimensionality, using propagation to extend 2D segmentation to 3D volumes. Our key insight is that volumetric propagation and in-context segmentation share the same reference-conditioned prediction mechanism, differing only in whether the reference image-mask pairs come from other cases or from previously segmented neighboring slices. Building on this view, UniPro supports semantic, in-context, interactive, and propagation-based segmentation within a single slice-based framework, using class priors, reference exemplars, user clicks, and neighboring-slice predictions as mode-specific conditioning inputs. To improve propagation reliability, UniPro further incorporates bidirectional and 3D supervision to regularize slice-wise propagation beyond per-slice losses. Extensive experiments across diverse modalities and anatomies show that UniPro achieves strong performance across all segmentation settings, enabling annotation-efficient 3D segmentation from sparse 2D initialization and reducing slice-by-slice correction effort.
bullets: Addresses fragmented segmentation methods across paradigms and 2D/3D data.
Uses a shared slice-based framework conditioned on class priors, reference examples, user clicks, or neighboring-slice predictions.
Treats volumetric propagation as reference-conditioned prediction, analogous to in-context segmentation.
Adds bidirectional propagation and 3D supervision to improve consistency beyond independent slice losses.
Experiments across modalities and anatomies show strong performance and enable sparse-initialization 3D annotation with fewer slice corrections.

figures.caption: Figure 2: UniPro overview. (a) A unified slice-based segmentation pipeline for semantic, in-context, interactive, and propagation-based segmentation. UniPro uses a shared image encoder and decoder, with different settings instantiated through mode-specific conditioning inputs. Conditioning signals are converted into dense 2-D fusion features and sparse 1-D queries, which are jointly fed to the MoE Transformer decoder. Notably, propagation is formulated as in-context segmentation over neighboring slices, enabling coherent volumetric segmentation. (b) Two-stage training strategy. Stage 1 jointly pretrains semantic, in-context, and interactive segmentation with the shared backbone. Stage 2 further adapts the model to propagation with bidirectional and 3D consistency supervision.

Figure 1: Comparison of medical image segmentation paradigms. Existing task-specific, universal, and propagation-based models cover only part of the design space, with limitations in segmentation modes, data dimensionality, or propagation capability. UniPro unifies multi-mode segmentation, native 2D and 3D data, and volumetric propagation in a single slice-based framework.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on pancreas segmentation under the single-click propagation setting. Each row shows a different method propagating from a single positive click (⋆) on the seed slice (z = 34) to representative slices at z = 22, 28, 43, 48, with the resulting 3D reconstruction shown in the rightmost column. UniPro produces masks that closely follow the ground-truth pancreas boundary across the entire volume, while baselines exhibit boundary leakage (PAM, iSegFormer), partial coverage (nnInteractive, MedSAM2), or large over-segmentation toward neighboring organs (SAM2). Per-volume 3D Dice is reported next to each method name.
Figure 3: Ablation analysis of UniPro’s 3D propagation behavior.

Figure 6: Selected success and failure cases on LiTS, KiTS, and BraTS. Each row shows the seed slice (red border), four additional slices ordered by absolute distance from the seed, and 3D ground-truth and predicted surfaces. Green contours and orange overlays denote ground truth and predictions; 3D surfaces use the same colors. z is the slice index and ∆ the absolute index distance in the preprocessed volume.
Table 1: Propagation-based segmentation (3D Dice, %, ↑). All methods are initialized from a single positive click on one seed slice and propagated to the remaining slices.

Table 2: Semantic and in-context segmentation across internal and external datasets (Dice, %, ↑). All in-context models use one-shot inference; propagation is applied only to 3D volumes. nnU-Net (3D) is reported as a fully supervised upper bound. Best results in each block are in bold.
Table 3: Ablation studies on Stage-2 propagation training.

Table 7: Statistical analysis of propagation performance. (a) UniPro’s mean Dice (%), SD, and 95% CI. (b) Paired comparisons with MedSAM2, where ∆ denotes the Dice difference in percentage points. Bold p-values indicate significance at the unadjusted p < 0.05 level.

Table 5: Comparison between standard full-volume Dice (%) and target-containing-slice Dice. Results are averaged over organs within each dataset when applicable. ∆ denotes target-containing-slice Dice minus full-volume Dice, reported in percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Unified 2D/3D medical segmentation via propagation; relevant to generalist 3D perception models.
papers.title: UniPro: Unified Multi-Mode Medical Image Segmentation from 2D Images to 3D Volumes via Propagation
papers.tldr: UniPro unifies semantic, in-context, interactive, and 3D medical image segmentation by propagating conditioned 2D predictions across volumetric slices.

papers.abstract: Developing multiple instance learning pipelines for the classification of whole-slide images involves many interdependent design decisions and expertise in both pathology and machine learning. We present AutoMIL, an open-source framework that applies principles from the field of automated machine learning to tackle this task by automating integral pipeline steps, such as preprocessing, training and evaluation. In a benchmark evaluation with default settings, AutoMIL reached ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam and 0.93-0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset, comparable to specialised pipelines in related work. Ensembling mainly improved performance on imbalanced data, showing that an automated pipeline must adapt to dataset characteristics. AutoMIL thus provides an accessible baseline for whole-slide image classification without manual pipeline configuration.
authors: Jonas Waibel, Frank Kramer, Dominik M\"uller
bullets: Addresses the expertise and configuration burden of designing whole-slide image classification pipelines.
Automates preprocessing, training, and evaluation using automated machine learning principles.
Achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.94 on UBC-OCEAN, 0.99 on PCam, and 0.93–0.96 on a TCGA-NSCLC subset.
Ensembling primarily benefits imbalanced datasets, highlighting the need to adapt automation to dataset characteristics.
Provides an open-source baseline without manual pipeline configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Applies automated machine learning to whole-slide image classification, fitting the 3D Vision category (specifically 3D Foundation Models).
papers.title: AutoMIL: Automated Multiple Instance Learning for Whole-Slide Image Classification
papers.tldr: AutoMIL automates key multiple instance learning pipeline decisions for whole-slide image classification, providing an accessible baseline with competitive benchmark performance.

papers.abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.
authors: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
bullets: Pattern-matching 3D MLLMs struggle to distinguish geometrically similar objects, with accuracy dropping sharply on highly ambiguous samples.
The method reverses the usual information flow: geometry → function → identity, using part-level segmentation and functional chain-of-thought supervision.
PFIR trains on 507K functional QA pairs with a progressive curriculum and combines functional reasoning with descriptive grounding through dual-objective GRPO.
Under Objaverse→ModelNet40 and XYZRGB→XYZ-only zero-shot evaluation, accuracy improves from 60.5% to 66.7%.
Improvements are concentrated 2.6× more on geometrically ambiguous samples, supporting part-level functional reasoning for recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Part-level functional reasoning in 3D MLLMs to improve generalizable 3D recognition; relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
papers.tldr: PFIR improves generalizable 3D object recognition by inferring function from parts before identifying the object, especially in geometrically ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D scene construction is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Recent methods such as SAM-3Dfy enable end-to-end reconstruction of 3D assets and their scene layouts, but still struggle with fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality. Meanwhile, specialized 3D object generators provide detailed object geometry, while 3D foundation models offer strong and generalizable spatial understanding. We propose Easy-3Dfy, a compositional workflow that decouples object generation from scene layout estimation, allowing specialized models to fully exploit their respective strengths. An RPF-based aligner then bridges these capabilities by establishing geometric correspondence between object-local meshes and partial scene pointmaps, recovering object layout for scene composition. Without requiring complete scene-level supervision, the proposed workflow consistently outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200. Our results demonstrate that explicit geometric composition can effectively combine high-quality object generation with strong spatial understanding, while enabling the workflow to benefit independently from advances in both 3D object generation and foundation models.
authors: Ziang Zhang, Wenyou Yi, Zehan Wang, Jiachen Xu, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Targets limitations in fine-grained scene geometry and asset quality in existing end-to-end methods such as SAM-3Dfy.
Uses specialized 3D object generators for object geometry and 3D foundation models for spatial understanding.
An RPF-based aligner matches object-local meshes with partial scene pointmaps to recover object layouts.
Requires no complete scene-level supervision and outperforms SAM-3Dfy across multiple geometric metrics on Scene-Maker and 3D-FUTURE200.
Its modular design can independently benefit from advances in object generation and foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Single-image 3D scene construction via geometric composition, linking 3D object generation with spatial understanding from foundation models.
papers.title: Easy-3Dfy: Object-Level Geometric Composition for Single-Image 3D Scene Construction
papers.tldr: Easy-3Dfy improves single-image 3D scene reconstruction by separately generating detailed objects and estimating their spatial layout, then aligning them geometrically for composition.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language world model with geometric/spatial reasoning and counterfactual simulation directly fits world models, spatial intelligence, and 3D reasoning.
papers.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
papers.tldr: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively combines visual, linguistic, geometric, and simulated reasoning for flexible physical-world inference.

papers.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.
authors: Chao-Yeh Chen, Tiffany Chen, Lin Duan, Tianyi Hu, Yu-Hsiang Huang, Umar Iqbal, Jiefeng Li, Edy Lim, Yanchen Liu, Yihan Pang, Hang Qiu, Jun Saito, Shao Su, Qingsi Wang, Xiufeng Xie
bullets: Addresses accurate 3D hand reconstruction from challenging egocentric video.
Trains on a 14-million-image corpus combining synthetic, in-the-wild, and multi-camera motion-capture data.
Uses SOMA-Hand with a transformer encoder, camera cues, and an auxiliary 2D branch for geometric and image consistency.
Performs strongly on zero-shot HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O evaluations, with approximately 9.69 ms inference latency.
Model and source code are released under the OpenMDW license with free commercial use.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model trained on egocentric video. This falls under 3D Vision and involves learning from human videos, which is relevant to embodied AI and 3D perception.
papers.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoHand reconstructs 3D hands from monocular egocentric video using diverse training data and camera-aware transformer modeling, achieving strong zero-shot generalization and fast inference.

papers.abstract: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.
authors: Marek Wodzinski, Kamil Kwarciak, Daria Hemmerling, Mateusz Daniol
bullets: Evaluated three pretrained models on 239 cranial defects, including carved synthetic defects and real post-craniectomy cases.
None outperformed simply using the patient’s remaining bone on 210 carved defects; only one improved beyond chance on 29 real cases.
